questions: How do the neighborhoods our agency serves reflect the policies Rothstein describes, and what local records could document that?
Where do our current siting, zoning, or voucher practices reinforce patterns created by past de jure segregation?
If segregation was state action, what duty does that create for a public agency today, and how would we act on it?

title: When Affirmative Action Was White: An Untold History of Racial Inequality in Twentieth-Century America
editionNote: First published 2005 · W. W. Norton · 238 pages
overview: When Affirmative Action Was White is a work of political history by Ira Katznelson, a professor of political science and history at Columbia University. Katznelson examines the major social programs of the New Deal and the postwar era, including Social Security, labor law, and the GI Bill. He argues that they were designed and run in ways that gave their benefits overwhelmingly to white Americans, while excluding or shortchanging Black Americans. He calls this pattern a form of affirmative action for whites. He argues that it should change how we frame the debate over affirmative action for Black Americans.
summary: Katznelson opens by recasting a familiar question. Public debate about affirmative action usually begins in the 1960s and asks whether race-conscious remedies are fair. He proposes instead to begin in the 1930s and ask who received the huge public investments that built the American middle class. His answer is that those investments were not race-neutral. In part, they created the racial gaps in wealth and opportunity of the late twentieth century.

The central mechanism was the political power of the Southern Democratic bloc in Congress. The New Deal depended on Southern votes, and Southern lawmakers demanded that federal programs leave the region's racial order alone. The result was a set of compromises that Katznelson documents in detail. Social Security and the Fair Labor Standards Act at first excluded farm and domestic workers. Those were the jobs that most Black Southerners held. Unemployment insurance followed the same pattern. Where programs did not exclude people by job category, they were handed to local officials. That let Southern officials hand out relief, farm payments, and public works jobs in a discriminatory way.

A chapter on labor shows how the Wagner Act, which protected the right to organize, let unions exclude Black workers. It also shows how the Taft-Hartley Act's later limits were shaped by Southern fears that organizing would cross racial lines. Katznelson argues that the resulting pattern of union membership gave white workers decades of wage gains and benefits that Black workers were denied.

The book's most detailed case is the GI Bill of 1944. Katznelson describes it as the largest targeted, fully national program of support in American history. Its education, training, housing, and business-loan benefits were formally open to all veterans. In practice, though, local veterans' offices, banks, and colleges ran the program. Black veterans in the South and elsewhere were routinely steered into vocational programs, denied mortgages, and turned away from segregated universities. Katznelson presents evidence that the gap in benefits received was large. The bill therefore widened racial inequality rather than narrowing it, even as it lifted millions of white families into homeownership and college.

Katznelson then turns to the 1960s. He reads Lyndon Johnson's 1965 Howard University speech as a clear statement of why affirmative action was needed. Johnson argued that a person held back for years cannot fairly be placed at a starting line and told to compete. Katznelson examines how affirmative action grew through executive orders and court decisions. He argues that its defenders lost the argument by framing it as diversity rather than as a remedy for specific, documented harm.

In the final chapter he proposes a standard. Affirmative action should be justified as corrective and tied to the specific injuries that federal policy caused. It should be designed to be temporary and aimed at those injuries. He argues that this approach holds up better in court and persuades the public better than arguments based on diversity. It also returns the debate to the question of what the country owes for its own policy choices.
mainPoints: Southern lawmakers shaped the New Deal and postwar programs that built the white middle class so that they would preserve racial hierarchy.
Social Security, labor standards, and unemployment insurance at first excluded farm and domestic workers, who were disproportionately Black.
Local control of federal programs allowed benefits to be handed out in discriminatory ways.
Labor law let unions exclude Black workers, steering wage gains to white workers.
The GI Bill, though formally race-neutral, gave far more to white veterans because of local control.
These programs added up to large-scale affirmative action for whites and helped create the racial wealth gap.
Johnson's Howard University speech framed affirmative action as a remedy for past harm rather than as diversity.
Later defenses of affirmative action lost ground by dropping the remedial argument.
Katznelson proposes affirmative action justified as corrective, tied to specific documented injuries, and designed to end once they are addressed.
The history of who received public investment should be part of any debate about fairness today.
relevance: This is a foundational text for anyone who must explain to staff or the public why group-based disparities exist and why race-conscious or targeted remedies are proposed. It is especially useful for benefits, workforce, and veterans' services agencies whose predecessors ran the programs described. Policy staff can treat one of its arguments as a design warning: programs that are neutral on paper but leave room for local discretion produce unequal outcomes. Trainers should note that the book is a historical argument, not a program manual. Historians widely accept its evidence. The debate is over its policy conclusion. Katznelson's remedial framework for affirmative action fits uneasily with the diversity rationale many institutions used. It also fits uneasily with later court decisions that restricted race-conscious programs.
questions: Which of our current programs rely on local or caseworker discretion in ways that could repeat the patterns Katznelson describes?
How does framing equity work as a remedy for documented harm, rather than as diversity, change how we would explain it to the public?
What records would show whether past benefits programs in our jurisdiction were handed out unequally, and what could we do with that knowledge?

title: The Color of Money: Black Banks and the Racial Wealth Gap
editionNote: First published 2017 · The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press · 371 pages
overview: The Color of Money is a history of Black banking in the United States by Mehrsa Baradaran, a law professor who specializes in banking law and financial inclusion. Baradaran traces Black-owned banks from the Reconstruction era to the present. She uses their story to explain why the racial wealth gap has barely moved since emancipation. Her central claim is that banks working inside a segregated economy could not create wealth for their communities. She also argues that the repeated political call for Black self-help through banking has stood in for the structural remedies that would have worked.
summary: Baradaran starts from a stark figure. At emancipation, Black Americans held a tiny fraction of the nation's wealth, and more than a century and a half later the share remains small. She asks why decades of effort to build Black financial institutions have not changed this. To answer, she examines how banks actually create wealth. Banks take deposits and lend them out, and wealth grows when loans pay for assets that rise in value. Now picture a community where incomes are low, segregation holds down property values, and borrowers are shut out of the wider credit market. A bank there has nowhere profitable to lend. It either takes on risky loans or parks its deposits in safer white-owned institutions. Either way, it drains capital out of the community it was meant to serve.

The early chapters cover Reconstruction and the Freedman's Savings Bank. This federally chartered bank collected the deposits of formerly enslaved people and then failed in 1874 after its white trustees mismanaged it. Baradaran treats this as a first lesson: Black savers bore the losses of an institution they did not control. She then follows the rise of Black banks during Jim Crow, often tied to fraternal societies, churches, and insurance companies. She describes figures such as Maggie Lena Walker in Richmond. These banks served a community shut out of white institutions. But they worked with small amounts of capital in neighborhoods whose property could not rise in value.

A central theme is the political uses of Black capitalism. Baradaran shows how, at moment after moment, leaders across the political spectrum promoted Black banking and business as the answer to racial inequality. Booker T. Washington urged economic self-reliance over political rights. After the civil rights movement, Richard Nixon embraced "Black capitalism" as a way to answer demands for economic justice without redistributing resources or desegregating credit markets. Later administrations kept funding minority-bank programs and community development financial institutions. Baradaran argues that these efforts were small. They were often offered in place of policies such as fair lending enforcement or housing integration. And they put the burden of closing the wealth gap on the very community that had been made poor.

She gives close attention to the ways of exclusion that made the trap impossible to escape. These include redlining and FHA policy, discriminatory lending, and the exclusion of Black families from postwar mortgage subsidies. They also include the later targeting of Black neighborhoods by predatory and subprime lenders. In each era, she notes, Black banks were expected to make up for structural exclusion with far fewer resources than white banks had.

The final chapters bring the story to the 2008 financial crisis. The crisis destroyed a disproportionate share of Black wealth and wiped out several Black banks. The chapters then turn to current proposals. Baradaran argues that relying on community self-help and financial literacy gets the problem wrong. Policy created the wealth gap, through enslavement, exclusion from land and credit, and discriminatory subsidy. Only policy at a similar scale can close it. She points toward reparations, including a program aimed at formerly redlined neighborhoods, as the kind of action that matches the size of the harm.
mainPoints: The Black share of national wealth has barely changed since emancipation, despite generations of effort to build Black financial institutions.
Banks create wealth by lending for assets that rise in value; in a segregated economy there is little such lending to do.
The structure of the economy forced Black banks to hold deposits in or send capital to white institutions, draining their communities.
The failure of the Freedman's Savings Bank set a pattern in which Black savers absorbed losses from institutions they did not control.
Political leaders from Washington to Nixon promoted Black capitalism as a substitute for structural change.
Minority-bank programs and similar efforts were too small to offset the exclusion they were meant to counter.
Redlining, FHA policy, and predatory lending again and again undercut Black efforts to build assets.
The 2008 crisis destroyed a disproportionate share of Black wealth and Black banks.
Framings based on financial literacy and self-help put responsibility on the harmed community rather than on the policies that harmed it.
Closing the gap requires public action on the scale of the policies that created it.
relevance: This book is valuable for practitioners in economic development, benefits, housing, and financial-empowerment programs. It challenges a common belief that financial education and support for minority-owned institutions are enough as equity strategies. It helps explain the racial wealth gap to staff and stakeholders. It also gives historical grounding for asset-building and fair-lending work. Policy staff should take seriously its warning that symbolic programs can replace substantive ones. The book is a legal and historical argument rather than a program guide. Its policy conclusions, including support for reparations, are debated, and some economists stress income and employment factors more than Baradaran does. Practitioners should present its claims as one well-documented interpretation.
questions: Which of our economic-empowerment or financial-literacy programs assume that changing individual behavior can close a gap created by policy?
How do we judge whether support for minority-owned institutions is building community wealth rather than symbolic inclusion?
What would an asset-building effort on a scale that matches the harm look like in our jurisdiction?

title: Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents
overview: Caste is a work of narrative nonfiction by Isabel Wilkerson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and author of The Warmth of Other Suns. Wilkerson argues that the United States is best understood not only through the lens of race but also through the older and broader idea of caste, which is a fixed, inherited ranking of human groups that assigns worth and position at birth. She compares the American system with the caste system of India and the racial hierarchy of Nazi Germany, and from that comparison she contends that race in America serves as the visible marker of a deeper caste structure, one that has outlasted slavery and legal segregation.
summary: Wilkerson opens with a distinction. Race, she argues, is the skin; caste is the bones. Race is a fairly recent invention tied to the transatlantic slave trade, but it was put to work as the signal of a caste hierarchy whose purpose is to fix who belongs on top and who on the bottom. Caste is not about individual feelings or hatred; it is a structure of power that people can keep in place without holding any conscious prejudice at all. She uses the image of an old house inherited from earlier owners: the people living there now did not build the flaws in the foundation, but they are responsible for what they do about them.

The first part of the book sets up the comparison among three systems. India's caste system, with its thousands of jatis and its long-excluded Dalits, provides the oldest and most developed model. Nazi Germany's racial laws, she shows, were drafted by officials who studied American Jim Crow statutes and laws against interracial marriage, and in some cases they found the American laws too harsh to copy. The third is the American system, built on enslavement and extended through segregation, lynching, and ongoing patterns of exclusion. Wilkerson does not claim that the three are identical, but she argues that they share a common architecture.

The book's central section describes that architecture as the eight pillars of caste. The first is a belief in divine will or natural law to justify the hierarchy, and the second is heritability, so that position passes down by birth. Others are control of marriage and mating to keep bloodlines separate, and ideas of purity and pollution that police contact. There is also a ranking of jobs that confines the lowest caste to the most degrading labor. The remaining pillars are dehumanization and stigma; terror as enforcement and cruelty as a means of control; and claims of inborn superiority and inferiority. For each pillar she pairs historical cases from the three systems. Here she draws on records of lynching, the testimony of Dalit scholars, and Nazi documents.

The book's later sections show how caste works in everyday life. Wilkerson recounts her own experiences as a Black journalist being disbelieved, ignored, or treated as out of place. She adds the stories of others: a Black Little League player barred from a city pool in 1951, Satchel Paige's career confined by segregation, and Martin Luther King Jr. being told in India that he was recognized as a fellow untouchable. She describes the health costs of living in a lower caste, drawing on research on stress and life expectancy. She also describes the psychological toll on members of the dominant caste who must constantly defend their position. She discusses the role of the middle castes, including immigrants who learn where they are expected to stand. And she discusses the anxiety of dominant-caste members who see demographic change as loss.

Wilkerson closes with the chance of change. She notes that Germany confronted its past through memorials, education, and law in ways the United States has not. She argues that individual goodwill alone cannot dismantle caste, though individuals can refuse to enforce it. She describes the idea of "radical empathy," the effort to understand another person's experience from within rather than from above. The book ends with a plea for a world in which worth is not assigned at birth.
mainPoints: Race in America is the visible marker of a deeper caste structure, an inherited ranking that assigns worth at birth.
Caste is a structure of power, not a matter of individual prejudice, and people without conscious bias can keep it in place.
The American, Indian, and Nazi German systems differ in detail but share a common architecture.
Nazi officials studied American race laws when drafting their own.
Eight pillars hold up caste: divine justification, heritability, control of marriage, purity rules, a ranking of jobs, dehumanization, terror, and claims of inborn superiority.
Caste is enforced in everyday interactions, not only through law, and it shows up as disbelief, exclusion, and surveillance.
Living in a lower caste carries measurable health and mental costs.
Middle groups, including immigrants, are pressured to place themselves within the hierarchy.
Demographic change stirs anxiety in the dominant caste, and that anxiety shapes politics today.
Germany's reckoning with its past offers a model of memorials, education, and law that the United States has not matched.
relevance: Caste is widely used as a reading-group and training text. Its narrative style makes structural inequality concrete for general audiences, and because it separates structure from personal prejudice, it can also lower defensiveness in discussions. Practitioners can use the eight pillars as a lens for examining institutional practices such as job segregation, enforcement patterns, and whose accounts are believed. The book is debated. Some scholars argue that the caste framework plays down the specific economic history of American racism. Others say the comparison with India is imprecise and that the focus on hierarchy leaves class and policy remedies thin. Trainers should present it as a frame rather than a complete analysis and pair it with texts focused on policy.
questions: Where in our organization does worth or credibility seem to be assigned by group position rather than by individual contribution?
Which of the eight pillars are visible in the practices of the systems we work within, such as hiring, enforcement, or service eligibility?
Drawing on Wilkerson's comparison with Germany, what would a public reckoning with our jurisdiction's history look like?

review.authorDecisionReason: Publisher credits Isabel Wilkerson. Additional catalogue contributors do not replace the principal author credit.

editorialCheck.finding: Publisher credits Isabel Wilkerson. Additional catalogue contributors do not replace the principal author credit.

title: The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness
editionNote: First published 2010 · The New Press · 290 pages (available to borrow)
overview: The New Jim Crow is a legal and social argument by Michelle Alexander. She is a civil rights lawyer and former director of the ACLU of Northern California's Racial Justice Project who later became a law professor. Alexander contends that the American system of mass incarceration, driven by the War on Drugs, works as a racial caste system. In its effects, she says, it is comparable to Jim Crow segregation. Her core claim is that the system labels large numbers of Black men as criminals. That label then makes legal the same kinds of discrimination that civil rights law was supposed to have abolished, in employment, housing, voting, and public benefits.
summary: Alexander opens by describing how she came to her thesis. While working on racial profiling cases, she saw a flyer claiming that the drug war was a new form of Jim Crow, and at first she dismissed it as overstated. Over time, she decided the comparison was closer to the truth than the mainstream civil rights view. That view treated mass incarceration as simply one of many disparities. The book is her attempt to make the case.

The first chapter traces the history of racial control in the United States as a series of systems. Slavery was followed, after a brief Reconstruction, by Jim Crow, a system of legal segregation and stripping of voting rights. When the civil rights movement took Jim Crow apart, Alexander argues, a new system arose within a generation. It was built on the language of law and order and crime rather than race. She describes how the "Southern strategy" used appeals about crime and welfare to attract white voters upset by civil rights gains. The War on Drugs, declared in 1982 before crack cocaine became a public issue, provided the vehicle.

Alexander then describes how the system works. Police have broad discretion to stop and search. Supreme Court decisions have made it nearly impossible to challenge stops on racial grounds without proof of explicit intent. Federal grants and asset forfeiture laws gave police departments money-based reasons to pursue drug arrests. Prosecutors hold enormous power over charges. Mandatory minimum sentences, including the hundred-to-one disparity between crack and powder cocaine, push defendants to plead guilty. Drug use rates are roughly similar across racial groups, she notes, but enforcement focused on Black neighborhoods produced a prison population that was heavily Black and brown.

A central chapter concerns what happens after release. A felony conviction brings lawful exclusion from jobs through background checks, from public housing and food assistance, from jury service, and, in many states, from voting. Alexander argues that these consequences recreate a status of second-class citizenship through the criminal label. That status was once imposed through race directly. Because the system is officially colorblind, she argues, it is harder to challenge than Jim Crow was, and its targets are blamed for their own condition.

Alexander also asks why the civil rights establishment was slow to confront mass incarceration. She points to the stigma of criminality and to a preference for affirmative action and respectable plaintiffs, and she also points to the way a small Black professional class could rise even as the caste system hardened. She argues that colorblindness as an ideal has served to hide racial hierarchy rather than fix it. Movements focused narrowly on individual rights, she says, have struggled to address harm built into the system.

The final chapter calls for a social movement rather than piecemeal reform. Alexander argues that ending the drug war, reforming sentencing, and removing collateral consequences are needed, yet they are not enough unless the public consensus that treats Black men as criminals changes. She warns that without such a shift, a new system of control will replace the current one. Later editions of the book include a preface reflecting on the reform movement that followed its publication.
mainPoints: Mass incarceration works as a system of racial control that followed slavery and Jim Crow.
The War on Drugs was launched as a political strategy and grew through federal incentives to police.
Court decisions have given police and prosecutors wide discretion while making claims of racial bias almost impossible to prove.
Drug use is similar across racial groups, but enforcement focused on Black communities.
Mandatory minimums and plea bargaining pressure defendants into convictions whether or not they are guilty.
A felony record legally permits exclusion from jobs, housing, benefits, juries, and voting.
Those exclusions recreate second-class citizenship through a criminal label rather than an openly racial one.
Colorblind ideology makes the system harder to see and challenge than Jim Crow was.
Civil rights organizations were slow to make incarceration a priority because of stigma and strategic choices.
Lasting change requires a movement that shifts public consensus, not only legal or sentencing reform.
relevance: This is a central text for human-services and public-sector practitioners. The collateral consequences Alexander describes are carried out by public agencies: background checks in hiring, eligibility rules for housing and benefits, and licensing limits. HR staff can use it to review fair-chance hiring practices. Program and policy staff can look at where exclusions based on criminal records appear in their own rules. The book shaped a decade of reform and is widely assigned. It is also contested. Critics such as legal scholar James Forman Jr. argue that it plays down violent-crime convictions as a driver of prison growth and overstates the drug war, and they also say it gives too little attention to support within Black communities for tougher policing. Others note that some statistics have since shifted. Practitioners should present it alongside current local data.
questions: Where do exclusions based on criminal records appear in our hiring, eligibility, or licensing rules, and which does the law require and which come from habit?
How does the ideal of colorblind administration in our agency help or hinder our ability to see outcomes patterned by race?
Which critiques of Alexander's argument matter in our local context, and how do they change which reforms we would put first?

title: Disability Visibility: First-Person Stories from the Twenty-First Century
overview: Disability Visibility is an anthology of first-person essays, interviews, testimony, and manifestos by disabled writers, edited by the activist Alice Wong. Wong was a disabled Asian American organizer who founded the Disability Visibility Project in 2014. She put the collection together for the thirtieth anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. Wong died in November 2025. The book's core claim is that disabled people are experts on their own lives. Their stories, told in their own voices, are richer, angrier, funnier, and more political than the stereotypes that usually stand in for them.
summary: Wong opens with a short introduction explaining where the book came from. The Disability Visibility Project began as an oral history partnership with StoryCorps. It grew into an online community, a podcast, and a platform for disabled writers. Wong notes that roughly one in five people in the United States has a disability, yet disabled people remain nearly invisible in media and publishing. She is clear that the collection is not meant to be representative or complete. It is a sampler, weighted toward writers who are also people of color, queer, trans, or marginalized in other ways. It also leans into the range of disability itself: physical, sensory, intellectual, psychiatric, chronic, visible and invisible.

The book gathers roughly three dozen pieces, grouped into four parts: Being, Becoming, Doing, and Connecting. The first part centers on identity and lived experience. The best-known entry here is Harriet McBryde Johnson's "Unspeakable Conversations." It is a reprint of her account of debating the philosopher Peter Singer about whether lives like hers are worth living. Other pieces in this section describe growing up with a disability in a family or community that had no language for it. They also describe the work of coming to claim disability as an identity rather than a flaw. The section also includes an account by a Deaf man who was denied interpreters and basic communication during years in prison.

The second part, Becoming, follows writers through change: diagnosis, loss of function, and the reshaping of ambition. It includes testimony to Congress by a man who survived a large public institution and now speaks up for community living. Other contributors write about chronic illness, mental illness, and the way medical systems can erase the person in front of them.

Doing, the third part, is about work and activism. Ellen Samuels's widely cited essay on "crip time" describes how disability bends a person's relationship to clocks, deadlines, and the expected pace of a life. A blind astronomer, Wanda Díaz-Merced, explains how she turned telescope data into sound so she could keep doing science. The section also describes the daily labor of organizing. That labor includes fighting for accessible transit, for communication access, and for a seat at the table.

The final part, Connecting, turns to community, love, and interdependence. Contributors write about friendships among disabled people, about finding one another online, and about building forms of care that do not depend on institutions. Some pieces on disability justice connect to the performance collective Sins Invalid and its co-founder Patty Berne. These pieces link disability to race, class, and queer politics. Stacey Milbern, a disability justice organizer, writes about disabled ancestors and the idea of a lineage of disabled people across time. Several writers insist that interdependence, rather than independence, is the honest description of every human life. Disabled people, they say, simply make it visible.

Several themes repeat across the collection. One is the rejection of pity and inspiration, since contributors do not want to be seen as brave for existing. Another is the gap between legal rights on paper and access in practice, three decades after the ADA. A third is intersectionality, meaning the way different parts of identity overlap. Many authors cannot separate their disability from their race, gender, immigration status, or poverty. They argue that a disability movement that ignores those connections will fail.

A young adult adaptation of the anthology followed, and the Open Library record combines information from both editions. The adult edition is the one most often used in reading groups and training settings.
mainPoints: Disabled people are the authorities on disabled lives; first-person accounts correct the distorted picture painted by media, medicine, and charity.
Disability is hugely varied, and no single story, including any one in this book, speaks for the whole community.
Many contributors live with disability together with racism, poverty, homophobia, or transphobia, and these cannot be examined separately.
"Crip time" names the way disability changes a person's relationship to pace, deadlines, and the expected timeline of a life.
Institutions, prisons, and medical settings routinely strip disabled people of communication, autonomy, and dignity, as testimony in the book shows.
Independence is a myth for everyone; interdependence and mutual care are the realistic basis for community.
Legal protections such as the ADA matter, but they have not produced equal access in daily life.
Disability justice, as distinct from disability rights, centers the leadership of disabled people of color and of queer and trans disabled people.
Pity and "inspiration" are forms of distance that turn disabled people into objects for nondisabled people to look at.
Disabled people have a history and a lineage, and connecting to it is a source of strength.
relevance: For HR, training, and program staff, this collection is a practical way to put disabled voices at the center of a learning session instead of relying on compliance checklists. Individual essays are short enough to assign for a lunch-and-learn or a staff book group. The testimony on institutions and prisons is directly relevant to human services agencies. Practitioners should expect strong language and sharp critiques of professionals, including social workers and clinicians. They should treat that as data rather than something to soften. One caveat: the book is an anthology with no single argument. Facilitators need to choose pieces with care rather than assign the whole thing and hope a theme emerges.
questions: Which story in the collection most challenged an assumption you held about disability, and what was the assumption?
Several contributors describe professionals, including caseworkers and clinicians, as obstacles. What in your own agency's practices could produce that experience?
How does the idea of interdependence change how you think about "independence" as a program goal?

title: Year of the Tiger: An Activist's Life
overview: Year of the Tiger is the memoir of Alice Wong, the disabled Asian American activist best known for founding the Disability Visibility Project and editing the anthology of the same name. It is not a conventional life story but a scrapbook. It mixes original essays, pieces published earlier, conversations with other activists, photographs, graphics, and commissioned art. Wong's central claim is that a disabled life is not a story of overcoming but a story of building. She builds community and culture, and she holds on to the stubborn pleasures of being alive on her own terms.
summary: Wong was born in 1974, the Year of the Tiger in the Chinese zodiac, to parents who had moved from Hong Kong to Indianapolis. She had spinal muscular atrophy, a progressive condition of the nerves and muscles. She used a wheelchair from childhood and a ventilator as an adult. The early sections describe growing up as a disabled Chinese American kid in the Midwest. She writes about family meals, church, school, and being the only person like herself in most rooms. Wong writes with affection about her parents and sisters. She is also frank about the isolation of a childhood spent dealing with stairs, stares, and well-meaning people who did not expect much of her.

The book is organized by theme rather than by date. Wong moves through her education, including her move to the San Francisco Bay Area for graduate study in medical sociology, and she also covers her years working as a researcher at the University of California, San Francisco. She explains how she drifted from academic research toward activism and storytelling. She was frustrated that disabled people were studied far more often than they were heard. In 2014 she launched the Disability Visibility Project as an oral history effort tied to the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. It grew into a media platform, a podcast, and a network of disabled writers and organizers.

Several chapters deal with Wong's time in public life. She served on the National Council on Disability under President Obama. In 2015 she attended a White House reception for the ADA anniversary by telepresence robot. She tells this story with humor and with a sharp eye for what it says about access. She describes co-founding #CripTheVote, an online campaign to make disability a visible issue in electoral politics, and she also reflects on what it means to do activism from bed, through a screen, with limited energy. Her tools are words, relationships, and a wide-ranging curiosity about disability culture.

Food is a thread that runs through the book. Wong writes about her love of eating, Chinese cooking, and the social life built around meals. Later chapters describe how her disability progressed and changed her relationship to eating. She treats that loss with honesty rather than sentiment. Pop culture gets similar attention. This is a deliberate choice that insists disabled lives include small joys and not only struggle.

The pandemic fills a large part of the later sections. Wong describes the fear of being judged expendable and the early triage policies that ranked disabled lives lower, and she also describes her fury as public health messages treated the deaths of "people with underlying conditions" as acceptable. She records how disabled communities responded with mutual aid, information sharing, and demands for vaccine access. Interviews and conversations with other disabled activists, writers, and artists appear throughout. In this way, the book also works as a portrait of a generation of the movement.

Wong frames herself as a "disabled oracle." She can see where society is going because disabled people live in the future that everyone else is heading toward: aging, chronic illness, and dependence on technology and on one another. She resists being read as inspirational; instead, she asks readers to think about what they owe each other. The book closes with an imagined conversation among Wong's younger, present, and older selves, reflecting on her survival. Wong died in 2025. For readers coming to the memoir now, that gives its reflections on lineage and mortality added weight.
mainPoints: A disabled life does not need to be told as triumph over adversity; Wong presents hers as a life of building community and culture.
Identity is layered: disability, being Chinese American, gender, and class all shape Wong's experience at once.
Disabled people have long been research subjects; Wong's move from academia to storytelling was a move toward being heard rather than studied.
Activism can happen from bed, online, and through media; organizing does not require a body that can march.
Technology, from ventilators to telepresence robots to social media, is part of disabled life and part of access, not a substitute for it.
Public policy, including electoral politics and emergency planning, routinely ignores disabled people unless they force the issue.
The pandemic showed how quickly institutions were willing to write off disabled lives, and how disabled communities organized in response.
Joy, food, humor, and fandom belong in disability stories as much as pain and barriers do.
Disabled people see the future first: over time, aging and illness make everyone's life more like theirs.
Lineage and ancestors matter; remembering who came before keeps the movement going.
relevance: This memoir is useful for staff who need a concrete, personal picture of what access and exclusion look like day to day. It is told by someone who worked both inside government advisory bodies and outside them. Its scrapbook format makes it easy to excerpt. A single chapter on the pandemic, on telepresence, or on growing up can anchor a training session. Program designers and emergency planners will find the pandemic chapters especially pointed on triage, communication, and who gets consulted. One caveat: the nonlinear structure frustrates some readers who want a straightforward story. Wong's tone is also deliberately blunt about professionals and institutions, and some audiences may need to be prepared for that.
questions: Wong calls herself a "disabled oracle." What does your agency's current planning look like if you assume most clients and staff will be disabled at some point?
How did Wong's pandemic experience differ from the official public health story your organization told at the time?
What role did humor, food, and pop culture play in the book, and why might Wong have insisted on including them?

title: Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist
overview: Being Heumann is the memoir of Judith Heumann, one of the central figures of the American disability rights movement, written with Kristen Joiner. Heumann got polio as a toddler in 1949, and she spent her life fighting for access, first for herself and then for everyone, from a Brooklyn school basement to federal office in Washington. The book's core claim is simple and insistent. Disabled people are not sick, broken, or in need of charity; they are a minority denied civil rights, and those rights are won by organizing.
summary: Heumann begins in Brooklyn, where she grew up in a Jewish family whose parents had fled Germany. Polio paralyzed her at eighteen months, and she used a wheelchair from early childhood. When her mother tried to enroll her in the neighborhood public school, the principal turned her away as a "fire hazard." She received only a few hours of home teaching a week until her mother forced the system to place her in a special class, held in a school basement and kept apart from nondisabled children. Heumann uses these early chapters to show how ordinary and bureaucratic exclusion was, and how it was justified by concern for her safety. She also describes summers at Camp Jened, a camp for disabled teenagers in the Catskills, where she first knew a community in which disability was normal, and there many future activists met.

The next section covers her college years at Long Island University and the fight that made her a public figure. After finishing her teaching degree, she passed the written and oral exams, but the New York City Board of Education denied her a license on medical grounds. Officials reasoned that a teacher in a wheelchair could not get students out in an emergency. Heumann sued in 1970, the case drew press attention, and the city settled and issued her license. She became the first wheelchair user to teach in New York City public schools. After the publicity, she co-founded Disabled In Action, an organization built on direct protest rather than providing services, and she led demonstrations, including a traffic blockade in Manhattan after President Nixon vetoed the Rehabilitation Act.

The heart of the book is the 1977 occupation of the federal building in San Francisco. Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 barred any recipient of federal funds from discriminating against disabled people, but for four years no administration had issued the regulations needed to enforce it. By then Heumann was deputy director of the Center for Independent Living in Berkeley, and she helped organize a nationwide sit-in at regional offices of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. The San Francisco occupation lasted more than three weeks, the longest sit-in of a federal building in American history. Heumann describes the practical details. After the phones were cut, Deaf participants relayed messages in sign language through windows. The Black Panther Party delivered hot meals, and attendants and nurses kept people alive. A delegation flew to Washington to confront Secretary Joseph Califano, and he signed the regulations. Heumann treats the sit-in as proof of what made the win possible: solidarity across disabilities and alliances with other movements.

Later chapters follow Heumann into roles inside institutions. She co-founded the World Institute on Disability and served under President Clinton as Assistant Secretary in the Department of Education. She also worked at the World Bank, and she became the State Department's first Special Advisor for International Disability Rights under President Obama. She reflects on the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 as the product of the organizing described earlier, and on how far practice still lags behind law. Throughout, she is frank about anger and about the toll of always being the one who has to ask. She is also frank about the difference between being included on paper and being wanted in a room.

The memoir also deals with private life: friendship, marriage, the search for accessible housing, and the near-constant work of arranging personal assistance. Heumann refuses to present these as individual problems, since each one, she says, is a design choice that society made. The "unrepentant" in the title is a stance. She apologizes for nothing, and she asks readers to stop expecting disabled people to be grateful for partial access.
The book came out the same year as the documentary Crip Camp, in which Heumann is a central figure, and the two are often paired. Heumann died in 2023.
mainPoints: Keeping disabled children out of school was routine and framed as safety; Heumann's childhood shows how ordinary discrimination looked before civil rights law.
Spaces where disability is the norm, such as Camp Jened, build confidence, community, and future leaders.
Heumann's 1970 lawsuit won her the teaching license that the New York City school system had denied her on medical grounds.
Direct action, not polite requests, moved policy; Disabled In Action was built on protest.
Section 504 sat unenforced for four years until the 1977 sit-ins forced the government to issue regulations.
The San Francisco occupation succeeded through cooperation across disabilities and support from allies such as the Black Panther Party.
The ADA grew out of decades of organizing; it was not granted from above.
Law changes faster than attitudes; Heumann spent her later career inside government pushing agencies to follow rules already on the books.
Personal assistance, housing, and transportation are civil rights issues, not private misfortunes.
Disabled people owe no gratitude for access; "unrepentant" is a political position.
relevance: This memoir is a strong introduction to the history behind Section 504 and the ADA for staff who know the laws only as compliance rules. It is especially useful for public-sector readers because Heumann tells both sides. She was the activist outside the building and, later, the official inside it, trying to make agencies act. Training designers can pair chapters with the film Crip Camp. Direct service staff will recognize the pattern of exclusion in the name of safety that she describes, and they can use it to examine their own policies. The book is admired across the field. Its main limit is that it is one person's view, centered on physical disability and on the movement's best-known leaders.
questions: The principal who barred Heumann from school cited fire safety. What safety rules in your organization might work as exclusion?
The 504 sit-in depended on allies from other movements. Who are the natural allies for disability access work in your agency, and are those relationships in place?
Heumann worked both as a protester and as a federal official. What did each role allow her to do that the other did not?

review.authorDecisionReason: Catalogue repeats Judith Heumann with and without middle initial; both supplied authors present.

title: Care Work: Dreaming Disability Justice
editionNote: First published 2018 · Arsenal Pulp Press · 263 pages
overview: Care Work is an essay collection by Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha, a queer, disabled, nonbinary femme writer and performance artist of Sri Lankan and Irish-Roma descent. The author draws on years of organizing with the collective Sins Invalid and in sick and disabled queer communities of color. The book is both a record and a manifesto. Its core claim is that when disabled people organize care among themselves, it is not a burden or a charity but a form of politics and a way of making the future.
summary: Piepzna-Samarasinha opens by explaining disability justice. Disabled people of color and queer and trans disabled activists developed this framework from 2005 onward, among them Patty Berne, Mia Mingus, Stacey Milbern, Leroy Moore, and Eli Clare. Disability justice differs from the earlier disability rights movement in two ways. It centers people who are disabled and also Black, brown, Indigenous, poor, queer, or trans. And it treats ableism, or prejudice against disabled people, as bound up with racism, capitalism, and colonialism. The author is clear that she is one voice in a larger movement and that the book is a set of "dreams" and working notes rather than a finished theory.

The early essays describe what the author calls sick and disabled queer communities and the practice of building spaces by and for them. She recounts organizing performances, gatherings, and tours where access was planned from the start rather than added at the end. She is honest about how often this failed, how exhausting it was, and how it was done with almost no money. A central idea here is collective access, which holds that access is a shared duty of everyone in a space, worked out together, rather than a service that an organization provides to the few people who ask.

The opening essay takes up care webs, the author's term for informal networks in which disabled people care for one another outside of state systems, paid attendants, or family. She draws on examples from her own life and from collectives organized around individual disabled people. She looks at what works: clear asks, rotating duties, and attention to the fact that caregivers are often disabled too, and she also looks at what fails. Burnout, unspoken resentment, and the way care webs can copy the hierarchies of the systems they replace are all risks. The book does not romanticize mutual aid; it treats it as skilled labor that needs structure.

The collection's most personal essays address emotional labor and suicide. One long piece argues that femmes, especially femmes of color, carry an unrecognized load of emotional care in movements, and it proposes thinking about that labor as an economy that could be made fair. Another set of essays deals with suicide in queer and trans communities. The author writes from her own experience of suicidal feelings and of losing friends. She rejects both the medical script of hospitalization and the activist script that treats despair as a failure of politics; instead, she describes staying alive as a shared, ongoing practice.

Later chapters turn toward art and the body. Piepzna-Samarasinha writes about what it means to tour as a disabled queer performer of color, facing inaccessible venues, exhausting travel, and audiences that want inspiration. Elsewhere she develops the idea of "crip emotional intelligence," which names the skills disabled people build in reading situations, pacing themselves, and surviving institutions. She argues these are expertise rather than deficits. A conversation with Stacey Milbern adds a historical dimension as they discuss crip lineages, disabled ancestors, and the fear of being forgotten.

The book also imagines the future. In one essay, the author lays out "wild" disability justice dreams. She pictures a world in which disabled people lead the response to climate change, where care is plentiful and chosen, and where no one has to prove they deserve help. She treats the apocalypse not as a metaphor but as the condition disabled people already live in. She argues that the survival skills built in disabled communities are what everyone else will need.
mainPoints: Disability justice is a framework developed by disabled people of color and queer and trans disabled activists; it treats ableism as linked to racism, capitalism, and colonialism.
Disability rights won legal protections, but a rights framework alone leaves out people whose disabilities overlap with other forms of marginalization.
Collective access makes everyone in a space responsible for access, replacing the model of accommodations that individuals must request.
Care webs are informal networks of mutual care among disabled people; they require structure, honesty, and attention to caregiver burnout.
Emotional labor in movements falls heavily on femmes and women of color and is rarely counted.
Suicide in queer, trans, and disabled communities needs responses rooted in community, beyond hospitalization and crisis lines.
Crip emotional intelligence names the survival skills disabled people build and reframes them as expertise.
Disabled artists face concrete barriers in venues, travel, and audience expectations that limit whose work gets seen.
Disabled ancestors and lineages are a source of knowledge that institutions tend to erase.
Disabled people already live in the "apocalypse" and have skills the rest of society will need in climate and health crises.
relevance: Care Work is most useful for practitioners who want to understand why many disabled advocates are skeptical of approaches based on accommodations and demand something broader, especially disabled people of color. Program designers can borrow the collective access framework for events and meetings, and the care web essays offer a frank look at what peer support models require. Readers in human services should note that the author openly criticizes social work, psychiatry, and nonprofit structures. Her language and politics are openly anti-capitalist and abolitionist, and the book is best used with that context named. It is widely assigned and respected in disability studies, though some readers find its essays uneven in form.
questions: How would a meeting or event planned on the principle of collective access differ from one planned under your current accommodation process?
Where in your organization is emotional labor done but not counted, and who does it?
The author argues that disabled people are already experts in surviving crisis. How could that expertise shape your emergency and continuity planning?

title: The Future Is Disabled: Prophecies, Love Notes and Mourning Songs
editionNote: First published 2022 · Arsenal Pulp Press · 333 pages
overview: The Future Is Disabled is the pandemic-era follow-up to Care Work, written by the disability justice writer and organizer Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha during two years of isolation. The book mixes essays, letters to disabled queer and trans readers of color, eulogies for friends, and practical notes on surviving. Its core claim is in the title. A future shaped by climate crisis, pandemics, and authoritarian politics will be a disabled future, and the knowledge that disabled communities already hold is what will get everyone through it.
summary: The author begins by observing that COVID-19 was, among other things, a mass disabling event. Millions of people developed chronic illness. Millions more lived for the first time under conditions disabled people already knew: confinement at home, reliance on delivery and remote work, and uncertainty about medical care; they also learned that institutions might decide their lives were expendable. Piepzna-Samarasinha argues that the nondisabled world briefly caught up to disabled reality and then tried to forget it. The book is a refusal to forget.

Much of the book documents what disabled communities did during the Trump years and the pandemic. The author describes mutual aid networks that delivered groceries and medicine and shared masks and air filters during wildfire season. These networks also organized online when gathering in person was impossible. She draws on the example of Stacey Park Milbern, a friend and organizer who died in 2020. She offers these stories as evidence that disabled people were not passive victims of the crisis. They were among its most capable responders, often while getting the least support.

A key idea is crip interdependence, carried forward from the author's earlier work. Care Work described care webs among disabled people. This book considers what it means to care across a whole community when nearly everyone is sick, grieving, or exhausted. Piepzna-Samarasinha writes about how disabled mutual aid differs from mutual aid organized by nondisabled people, and she also writes about the disabled friends who taught her how to live with illness. And she addresses the limits of mutual aid. It can be exhausting, it can fall apart, and it cannot replace the public infrastructure that governments refuse to build.

Parts of the book are openly mournful. The author writes honor songs for disabled people who died during these years, many of them queer and trans people of color. She treats grief as political. Disabled deaths, she argues, routinely go uncounted, and a movement that does not mourn its dead cannot sustain itself. The book also takes up the ongoing erasure of long COVID. It names the ableism of a "return to normal" that treated continued precautions as hysteria.

Other essays address disabled joy and art as ways of surviving. The author writes about disabled performers, writers, and online communities that kept making work through the crisis, and she also writes about the pleasure of disabled friendship. She includes "recipes for survival," some of them literal recipes, along with practical pieces such as a sample access rider. Writing on disabled families and kin networks widens the book's scope.

The book also offers the prophecies promised in the subtitle. Piepzna-Samarasinha sketches futures in which disabled knowledge and care help everyone survive climate change, fascism, and pandemics, and she also imagines darker futures. She insists that disabled communities will survive them too, because surviving is what they have always done. The book speaks first to disabled queer and trans readers of color. It is also written for anyone who cares about disability justice, the care crisis, and surviving the apocalypse.
mainPoints: COVID-19 was a mass disabling event that made disabled living conditions universal for a time; most institutions then worked to forget this.
Disabled communities met the pandemic and climate disasters with mutual aid networks that often moved faster than official systems.
Crip interdependence means caring for one another when everyone is tired and sick, not only when a few people need help.
Disabled mutual aid works differently from mutual aid organized by nondisabled people, and newer efforts can learn from it.
Mutual aid has limits; it cannot stand in for public infrastructure, and it can collapse under its own weight.
Disabled deaths go uncounted and unmourned; grieving them is a political act.
Long COVID is a disability, and the push to "return to normal" was itself a form of ableism.
Disabled art, humor, and friendship are survival practices, not luxuries.
Disability justice offers a way to survive fascism, climate change, and pandemics.
The future is disabled; planning for it means centering disabled knowledge now.
relevance: Public-sector and human services readers will find this book a direct challenge to how their agencies handled the pandemic and how they plan for the next crisis. It touches, if indirectly, on emergency management, public health communication, and workforce policy on remote work and sick leave. The mutual aid chapters are useful for anyone designing peer support or community resilience programs. Its discussion of long COVID bears on HR accommodation practice. There are caveats. The book is written for an insider audience and is openly abolitionist and anti-capitalist. Some readers find the form loose and the grief heavy. It works best after Care Work and with facilitators who can hold its tone.
questions: What did disabled staff or clients in your organization learn during the pandemic that your official after-action reviews did not capture?
The author describes mutual aid as both essential and not enough. Where does your agency rely on informal care that it should be funding?
How does your organization now treat long COVID and other newly acquired chronic conditions, and does that match the book's account?

title: Skin, Tooth, and Bone: The Basis of Movement Is Our People, a Disability Justice Primer
overview: Skin, Tooth, and Bone is a short primer on disability justice by Sins Invalid. Sins Invalid is a performance project founded in the San Francisco Bay Area by Patty Berne and Leroy Moore. It centers disabled artists of color and queer and gender-nonconforming disabled artists. The primer first circulated in 2016 and was revised in a second edition in 2019. It is the closest thing the disability justice movement has to a founding text. Its core claim is that disability cannot be addressed apart from race, class, gender, and sexuality. A movement, it argues, must be led by those who live where these identities meet.
summary: The primer begins by explaining why disability justice was needed. The disability rights movement of the 1970s through the 1990s won major legal victories, including Section 504 and the Americans with Disabilities Act. But its leaders and framing were largely white, and it relied on a single-issue approach based on rights. Disabled people of color, queer and trans disabled people, and disabled immigrants found that laws written for a generic disabled citizen did not reach their lives. Beginning around 2005, a group of activists began to put a different framework into words. They included Patty Berne, Mia Mingus, Stacey Milbern, Leroy Moore, Eli Clare, and Sebastian Margaret. Sins Invalid became one of the framework's main vehicles.

The heart of the primer is the ten principles of disability justice. Intersectionality holds that each person carries several identities and that systems of oppression work together. Leadership of those most impacted means that the people who face the most layered marginalization should direct the work. Anti-capitalist politics rejects the idea that a person's worth depends on how much they produce. Cross-movement solidarity links disability work to racial, economic, queer, and environmental justice. Recognizing wholeness treats every person as complete, not as a problem to be fixed. Sustainability insists that organizing must be paced so that disabled people can stay in it. Cross-disability solidarity values people across physical, sensory, intellectual, and psychiatric disabilities, including those usually left out. Interdependence replaces the myth of independence with mutual reliance. Collective access makes access a shared, creative responsibility. Collective liberation states that no one is free until everyone is.

The primer then places ableism in historical context. It describes how ideas of the normal, productive body were tied to colonialism, slavery, eugenics, and industrial capitalism. It also shows how disabled people of color faced institutionalization, sterilization, and police violence in ways that a purely legal analysis misses. Here the primer explains Sins Invalid's own origin as an arts project. Putting disabled bodies of color on stage as beautiful and sexual is itself a political act. It pushes back against a culture that treats them as objects of pity or disgust.

Practical sections follow. There is guidance on access for events and organizations. It covers planning for wheelchair access, interpreters, scent-free spaces, and rest areas. It also covers the needs of people with chemical sensitivities and psychiatric disabilities. The primer presents these as starting points, not a checklist. It argues that access should be budgeted and designed from the beginning. It also suggests how nondisabled organizers and organizations can show up as allies without taking over. And it includes a glossary of terms used in the movement.

The second edition adds material reflecting a decade of practice. It includes new writing on Audism and Deafhood by D/deaf contributors and a call to action from survivors of environmental injury. It also adds disability justice timelines, a glossary, and a resource list. The authors caution that disability justice is not a brand or a set of words to add to a mission statement. Organizations that adopt the language without changing power relations are missing the point. The primer closes with the phrase in its subtitle. The basis of movement is people, their bodies and relationships, not policy alone.
mainPoints: Disabled people of color and queer and trans disabled people developed disability justice when they found that the rights movement did not reach their lives.
The framework rests on ten principles, including intersectionality, leadership of those most impacted, anti-capitalism, and collective liberation.
Ableism is tied in history to colonialism, slavery, eugenics, and the demand for productive bodies.
Cross-disability solidarity means including people with psychiatric, intellectual, and chemical sensitivities, who are often left out even within disability organizing.
Sustainability requires pacing work so disabled people can stay in it rather than burning out.
Interdependence, not independence, describes how people actually live.
Collective access makes access everyone's responsibility and a creative practice, not a service for a few.
Access should be planned and funded from the start, not added when someone asks.
Art and performance by disabled people of color are political acts against a culture that makes them invisible or pitiable.
Adopting the language of disability justice without shifting leadership and resources misuses the framework.
relevance: The ten principles are now widely cited in nonprofit, foundation, and public-sector equity work, and this primer is the source document. HR and training staff can use it to understand what advocates mean when they say "disability justice" rather than "disability inclusion." Program designers can use its access guidance for events and meetings. Practitioners should take seriously the warning about borrowing language without changing power. The authors are explicit that the framework is anti-capitalist and rooted in movements, which may sit uneasily with institutional settings. Some critics in the disability rights tradition argue that the framework undervalues legal strategy. The primer's authors would reply that law was never enough.
questions: Which of the ten principles is hardest for your organization to practice, and why?
The primer warns against adopting disability justice language without changing who leads. What would leadership of those most impacted look like in your program?
How does your current access planning compare with the primer's guidance on events, and where is access treated as an afterthought?

title: Demystifying Disability: What to Know, What to Say, and How to Be an Ally
editionNote: First published 2021 · Ten Speed Press · 176 pages
overview: Demystifying Disability is a short, plain-language guide to disability for nondisabled readers. Its author, Emily Ladau, is a wheelchair user, writer, and longtime disability rights advocate. Ladau wrote it as the book she wished she could hand to people who want to do the right thing but are afraid of saying the wrong thing. Its core claim has three parts. Disability is an ordinary part of human diversity, ableism is learned, and allyship is a set of practices anyone can pick up by listening to disabled people.
summary: Ladau opens with her own story. She was born with Larsen syndrome, a genetic condition that affects joints and bones. Her mother has the same condition, and Ladau was raised to see disability as a normal part of life. She describes the mix of curiosity, pity, and awkwardness she meets daily. She sets a friendly, direct tone: she is not going to shame readers for not knowing, but she expects them to learn. She also explains her own position as a white, physically disabled woman, and she notes where other disabled people's experiences differ from hers.

The first two chapters ask what disability is. Ladau walks through the main ways disability has been defined. The medical model treats disability as a defect in the person, something to be cured or managed. Disabled activists developed the social model, which places disability in the barriers society builds: stairs, inaccessible communication, and discriminatory attitudes. Ladau favors the social model. But she grants that impairment and pain are real and that some disabled people want medical treatment. She stresses that disability includes physical, sensory, intellectual, developmental, psychiatric, and chronic health conditions. Many disabilities are invisible.

These chapters also take up language and intersectionality. Ladau explains the difference between person-first language ("person with a disability") and identity-first language ("disabled person"). She notes that preferences vary among individuals and communities, and she advises asking. She lists terms to avoid, including euphemisms such as "differently abled" and "special needs," and she explains why. She then argues that disability must be understood together with race, gender, sexuality, and class.

The book gives a compact history of disability in the United States, which Ladau labels incomplete on purpose. It covers institutionalization, eugenics and forced sterilization, and the "ugly laws" that barred visibly disabled people from public spaces. It also covers the independent living movement, the Section 504 sit-in of 1977, and the passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990. The aim is to show that disabled people have a civil rights history. Today's access requirements were won through protest.

One chapter deals with ableism and accessibility. Ladau defines ableism as discrimination and prejudice based on disability. She shows how it ranges from obvious exclusion to small assumptions. She describes accessibility broadly, from physical access to digital access such as image descriptions and captions. She offers practical guidance for workplaces, events, and online spaces, and she stresses that access benefits everyone.

A chapter on etiquette answers the questions readers are most afraid to ask. Should you offer help? Ask first. How do you talk to a Deaf person using an interpreter? Address the person. Should you touch a wheelchair? No. The chapter also covers how to respond to children's questions. The chapter on media examines "inspiration porn," the practice of using disabled people as feel-good content for nondisabled audiences. It also reviews other stereotypes, such as stories driven by pity and portrayals of mental illness. Ladau asks readers to notice who tells disability stories and whether disabled people are present.

The conclusion is about allyship. Ladau frames it as ongoing action rather than an identity. It means listening, amplifying disabled voices, and pushing for access when disabled people are not in the room. It also means accepting correction and not expecting praise. She closes with a reminder that most people will experience disability in their lifetime. That makes the work a matter of self-interest as well as justice.
mainPoints: Disability is a normal part of human diversity, and about one billion people worldwide have one.
The medical model places disability in the body; the social model places it in barriers. Ladau favors the social model while taking impairment seriously.
Language preferences differ; ask individuals, avoid euphemisms, and accept that both person-first and identity-first usage are valid.
Disability intersects with race, gender, class, and sexuality; experiences of ableism are not all the same.
Disabled people have a civil rights history, including institutionalization, eugenics, the 504 sit-in, and the ADA.
Ableism ranges from exclusion to everyday assumptions about what disabled people can do or want.
Accessibility applies to physical and digital spaces and should be built in rather than requested.
Basic etiquette: ask before helping, speak directly to the person, and do not touch mobility equipment.
"Inspiration porn" and media stereotypes shape how nondisabled people see disability and should be questioned.
Allyship is action, not a label; it includes listening, advocating, and accepting correction.
relevance: This is the most accessible introductory text in the disability section. It is well suited for new-employee orientation, training for staff who work with the public, and managers who need a foundation before policy discussions. Its guidance on language, etiquette, and digital accessibility carries straight into style guides and communication standards. Trainers should pair it with first-person accounts from disabled people of color, since Ladau herself notes the limits of her point of view. The book is widely recommended and seldom debated. Its limit is depth. It is an introduction by design and does not engage in detail with disability justice critiques of allyship frameworks.
questions: Which common phrases or practices in your workplace does Ladau identify as ableist, and how would you change them?
How does the social model of disability change the way you would describe a client's or employee's barriers in a case note or a report?
Ladau says allyship is action, not identity. What is one access improvement you could push for without being asked?

title: A Disability History of the United States
overview: A Disability History of the United States is a survey of American history from before European contact to the present. The historian Kim E. Nielsen wrote it as part of Beacon's ReVisioning American History series. Nielsen's core claim is that disability is not a side topic but a central organizing idea in American life. Ideas about who counts as able have shaped citizenship, labor, immigration, slavery, and gender. And disabled people have been actors in that history, not only its objects.
summary: Nielsen begins with Indigenous North America before 1492. Drawing on the limited sources available, she argues that many Indigenous communities understood difference in terms of relationships and contribution rather than a fixed category of disability. A person who could not walk or see might still have a defined role. What mattered was whether one was part of the web of shared obligation. This opening sets up the book's method. Disability is defined differently in different times and places, and tracing those definitions reveals how a society organizes itself.

The colonial chapters show English settlers bringing a different framework. Colonial law and poor relief sorted people by their ability to work and support themselves. Towns "warned out" those likely to become dependent. Terms such as "idiot," "lunatic," and "distracted" entered legal records. Families and communities, rather than institutions, provided most care. Nielsen also examines how disability was used to justify slavery. Enslaved Africans were described as naturally deficient, and physicians invented diagnoses that explained resistance and escape as illness. At the same time, the violence of slavery caused disability on a massive scale.

The nineteenth century brought institutions. Nielsen traces the rise of asylums and of schools for deaf and blind students. Later came custodial institutions for people labeled feeble-minded. She shows both the reform goals behind them and the way they became tools of control and segregation. The chapter on the late 1800s links nativism, or hostility to immigrants, to oralism. The movement to suppress sign language in deaf education drew on the same fears about foreignness and national unity that fueled limits on immigration. Immigration law itself, from the 1882 act onward, excluded people judged likely to become a public charge. Officials applied this standard by inspecting bodies and minds at ports of entry.

Nielsen gives close attention to eugenics. State laws allowed the sterilization of people labeled feeble-minded or unfit, and the Supreme Court upheld the practice in Buck v. Bell in 1927. The "ugly laws" of several cities barred people with visible disabilities from appearing in public. Industrialization injured large numbers of workers and raised questions about compensation and responsibility. Wars, meanwhile, produced disabled veterans whose claims on the state were stronger than those of other disabled people. Nielsen notes early organizing, including the League of the Physically Handicapped. During the 1930s, it protested job discrimination in federal relief programs.

The final chapters follow the twentieth-century movement. Nielsen presents a civil rights history with its own leaders and strategies. It runs through rehabilitation programs after the world wars, the polio epidemics, deinstitutionalization, and parent advocacy for children with intellectual disabilities. It continues with the independent living movement in Berkeley, the 1977 Section 504 sit-ins, the Deaf President Now protest at Gallaudet in 1988, and the passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990. Nielsen closes by noting how much is still contested. Disabled people still face high poverty rates and continued institutionalization. There is also a tension between a rights framework and the economic realities disabled people face.

Throughout, Nielsen uses disability as a lens of analysis in the way historians use race and gender. She shows that arguments against women's suffrage, against Black citizenship, and against immigrants all relied on claims of bodily or mental deficiency. The book is short and written for general readers and undergraduates. It is now the standard starting point for the field.
mainPoints: Disability is a central category of American history, used to define who could be a citizen, a worker, a voter, and an immigrant.
Many Indigenous societies understood difference through relationship and contribution rather than a fixed disability category.
Colonial law sorted people by their ability to work; care was local and family-based, and the "unproductive" faced exclusion.
Slavery both relied on claims that Africans were deficient and caused disability through violence.
Nineteenth-century institutions began as reforms and became tools of segregation and control.
Limits on immigration and the suppression of sign language drew on the same nativist fears.
Eugenics, upheld by the Supreme Court in 1927, led to forced sterilization and shaped law for decades.
Disabled veterans and injured workers won state support that other disabled people did not, revealing a ranking of who was seen as deserving.
Disabled people organized throughout American history, from Depression-era protests to the ADA.
Arguments against the rights of women, Black Americans, and immigrants routinely invoked disability, linking ableism to other systems of exclusion.
relevance: This book gives practitioners the historical background that most disability training skips. Policy staff will find the sections on public charge rules, institutionalization, and sterilization directly relevant to current debates in immigration, benefits, and guardianship. Trainers can use the book to show that disability exclusion was built into law on purpose and was changed by organizing. Its intersectional argument is that disability was used to deny rights to many groups. That argument helps connect disability work to other equity efforts. The book is widely respected. Its main limit is brevity, so it surveys each period rather than examining any one in depth.
questions: Nielsen shows that "ability to labor" defined who deserved support in colonial America. Where does that standard survive in current benefit and service rules?
How were claims of deficiency used against women, Black Americans, and immigrants, and what does that suggest about linking disability work with other equity efforts?
Which institutions or policies described in the book have direct descendants in your agency's work today?

title: No Pity: People with Disabilities Forging a New Civil Rights Movement
overview: No Pity is a journalist's account of the American disability rights movement by Joseph P. Shapiro, then a reporter for U.S. News & World Report and later with NPR. It came out three years after the Americans with Disabilities Act. It was the first widely read book to present disabled Americans as a political minority rather than as patients or charity cases.
