Prizant argues that trust and control come before building skills. Where do your intake or support processes give the person real choice, and where do they not?
How would you evaluate a vendor, therapy, or training program using Prizant's test of understanding versus control?

title: Neurodiversity at Work: Drive Innovation, Performance and Productivity with a Neurodiverse Workforce
overview: Theo Smith is a recruitment and talent professional and podcaster who is himself neurodivergent. Amanda Kirby is a physician, professor, and founder of Do-IT Solutions, a company that builds neurodiversity screening and support tools. Their book is a practical guide for employers who want to hire, support, and keep neurodivergent people. This includes people with ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia, dyscalculia, and Tourette syndrome. Its core claim is that organizations lose talent and performance when they design work for a narrow idea of a typical brain. Modest, steady changes to hiring and management fix much of this.
summary: The authors begin with definitions. "Neurodiversity" describes the natural variation in how human brains work. "Neurodivergent" describes a person whose way of thinking differs from the majority. The authors stress that these conditions overlap heavily and that many adults are undiagnosed. Every person's profile is a mix of strengths and challenges that shift with context. They also set out the business case. Large shares of working-age people are neurodivergent, and unemployment among autistic adults in particular is very high. Organizations that recruit only in their own image lose people with unusual abilities in pattern recognition, creativity, persistence, and problem-solving.

A second strand introduces the models that shape how people think about disability and difference. The authors contrast the medical model, which places the problem in the individual, with the social model, which places it in environments and attitudes. They favor a biopsychosocial view. This view recognizes real individual differences while holding organizations responsible for removing barriers. The framing matters for the rest of the book because it shifts attention from diagnosis to design. An employer does not need to know a person's label to make work more accessible.

The heart of the book walks through the employee life cycle. On attracting and recruiting staff, the authors look at how job ads, application portals, psychometric tests, and interviews screen out neurodivergent candidates. These tools reward social polish and fast verbal recall instead of the skills the job needs. The authors recommend plain-language ads that list only essential requirements. They suggest sharing interview questions in advance, offering work samples and trials, and training interviewers not to read eye contact or fidgeting as lack of interest. They also discuss specialist hiring programs run by large companies. They note what these programs achieve, but warn that separate pipelines can become a substitute for fixing mainstream processes.

On onboarding and daily management, the book covers reasonable adjustments. In the UK these are a legal duty, and in the US they match reasonable accommodation. The authors describe common adjustments: written follow-up to spoken instructions, noise-reducing headphones, flexible hours, assistive software, clear task priorities, and quiet spaces. They argue that most of these cost little and help many people beyond those with a diagnosis. They pay special attention to line managers, whom they see as the point where policy succeeds or fails. They offer guidance on talking about needs without requiring disclosure.

Later chapters address career growth, performance management, and wellbeing. The authors note that neurodivergent employees are often promoted less, disciplined more, and more likely to leave. They trace these patterns to appraisal systems that reward conformity. They cover intersectionality, including how gender, race, and class affect who gets diagnosed and who is believed. They also discuss remote and hybrid work, drawing on the pandemic period. They see it as both an opportunity and a new source of barriers.

The book closes with guidance on building a neurodiversity strategy. Steps include winning leadership sponsorship, setting up employee resource groups, gathering data responsibly, training managers, and measuring outcomes. Throughout, the authors include first-person accounts from neurodivergent workers and case examples from organizations that have changed their practices. The tone is practical rather than inspirational. The authors are honest that awareness campaigns without process change achieve little.
mainPoints: Neurodiversity is normal human variation. A large share of any workforce is neurodivergent, whether or not people are diagnosed or disclose.
Conditions such as ADHD, autism, dyslexia, and dyspraxia overlap, and each person's profile is a unique mix of strengths and challenges.
A biopsychosocial model keeps attention on removing barriers in the organization rather than on fixing or labeling individuals.
Standard recruitment, especially unstructured interviews and timed psychometric tests, screens out capable candidates for reasons unrelated to job performance.
Sharing questions in advance, using work samples, and training interviewers improve hiring for everyone, not only neurodivergent applicants.
Most reasonable adjustments are inexpensive and help the wider team. The obstacle is usually process and attitude, not cost.
Line managers decide whether neurodivergent staff thrive. They need training and simple tools for conversations about needs.
Performance and promotion systems that reward conformity drive neurodivergent employees to leave.
Specialist hiring programs can help, but they should not replace making mainstream processes accessible.
A neurodiversity strategy needs executive sponsorship, employee voice, data, and measurement, not just awareness events.
relevance: This is one of the more directly usable books on the list for HR and workforce development staff. Its chapters follow the employee life cycle. That makes it a handy tool for reviewing job postings, interview protocols, onboarding checklists, accommodation procedures, and appraisal forms. Public-sector employers will need to translate the UK legal framing to the ADA and state law, but the practices carry over cleanly. Some cautions apply. The book leans on the business case for inclusion, which some advocates see as making inclusion conditional. Also, its co-author runs a company that sells screening tools, and readers should keep that in mind when weighing those recommendations.
questions: Review one of your organization's current job postings. Which requirements are essential, and which are habits that screen out neurodivergent candidates?
What would it take for your managers to offer adjustments without requiring a diagnosis or formal disclosure?
Where in your performance management process are people rewarded for conformity rather than results, and who loses out because of that?

title: Sitting Pretty: The View from My Ordinary Resilient Disabled Body
overview: Rebekah Taussig is a writer and former high school teacher from Kansas City. She has been paralyzed since early childhood, after cancer treatment. She holds a PhD in creative nonfiction and disability studies and built an audience through the Instagram account @sitting_pretty. This memoir in essays describes life in a wheelchair in a world built for walking bodies. It argues that disability is an ordinary part of human life, one that our culture insists on treating as tragedy, inspiration, or spectacle.
summary: Taussig opens by describing the stories about disability she grew up with. In films, books, and church, disabled people were saintly, pitiable, or villainous, and they existed to teach a lesson to nondisabled characters. Growing up as the only visibly disabled person in most rooms, she had no model for an ordinary disabled life. She absorbed the message that her body was a problem to be managed or overcome. The book sets out to tell a different kind of story. In it, disability is complicated and sometimes painful, but it is also simply part of who she is.

Several essays look at the gap between good intentions and real help. Taussig writes about strangers who grab her chair to push it without asking, who insist on carrying her bags, or who interrupt her to pray that she will walk. She explores kindness that serves the giver, where the nondisabled person's need to feel helpful overrides what the disabled person has said she wants. She contrasts this with access, which is built into environments ahead of time and does not depend on anyone's charity.

Another thread concerns dependence and independence. Taussig describes the exhausting work of planning every trip around whether there will be a ramp, an accessible bathroom, or a parking space. She shows how ableism shows up not as hostility but as absence: the step at the door, the narrow aisle, the event held upstairs. She questions the value placed on doing everything alone. Everyone depends on others, she argues, and disabled people simply make that dependence visible. She draws on the social model of disability, which places the problem in environments and attitudes rather than bodies. At the same time, she is honest that pain and fatigue are also real.

The book is frank about intimacy, romance, and the body. Taussig writes about dating, about her first marriage and its ending, and about the assumption that disabled women are not sexual beings. She also writes about her work as a teacher and how her students resisted her lessons on disability.

Throughout, Taussig turns to media and representation. She analyzes "inspiration porn," a term she borrows from the late Australian activist Stella Young. It describes using disabled people as motivational props for nondisabled audiences. She shows how these images shape everyday encounters and how they shape disabled people's view of themselves. She also considers what better representation would look like: stories in which disabled characters have inner lives, bad days, ambitions, and humor.

The book ends with reflections on disability as a shared human condition. Taussig notes that most people will experience disability at some point, through aging, illness, or injury. A society that designs for disabled bodies, she argues, designs for everyone's future. She does not offer a program so much as an invitation to see differently. She asks readers to notice the steps and the stares, to ask before helping, and to treat disabled people as the authorities on their own lives.
mainPoints: Dominant stories cast disabled people as tragic, inspiring, or monstrous. These stories leave no room for ordinary disabled lives.
Ableism most often shows up as absence and oversight, such as the missing ramp, rather than as open hostility.
Help that is not asked for, and does not respect the person's answer, serves the helper more than the disabled person.
Access designed into environments in advance is different from charity, which depends on individual goodwill.
Everyone depends on others. Disability makes interdependence visible rather than creating it.
The social model of disability is useful, but bodily pain and fatigue are real and deserve honest acknowledgment.
Disabled people are routinely assumed to be nonsexual, and that assumption shapes daily interactions.
"Inspiration porn" uses disabled people as props for nondisabled audiences and harms how disabled people see themselves.
Good representation gives disabled characters inner lives, humor, and ambition rather than using them as lessons for others.
Most people will experience disability over a lifetime, so accessible design is an investment in everyone's future.
relevance: Practitioners in human services meet disabled clients and colleagues every day. This book is a readable corrective to the service mindset in which help is given rather than asked about. It is useful in staff training on disability etiquette and in discussions of facility and event accessibility. It also helps in communications work, where its analysis of inspirational framing can guide how agencies tell client stories. Because it is a memoir, it speaks from one woman's experience as a white, educated wheelchair user. Readers should pair it with accounts from disabled people of color and people with intellectual or psychiatric disabilities. Its arguments are widely shared in disability studies and are not seriously contested in the field.
questions: Taussig describes help that serves the helper. Where in your program's culture does staff kindness override client choice, and how would you know?
Think about your last public event or client meeting. What would a wheelchair user have needed to plan in advance to attend, and who was responsible for that?
How does your organization tell stories about the people it serves, and would those stories pass Taussig's test for representation?

title: The Pretty One: On Life, Pop Culture, Disability, and Other Reasons to Fall in Love with Me
overview: Keah Brown is a journalist and essayist from western New York who was born with cerebral palsy. In 2017 she started the hashtag #DisabledAndCute, which spread widely and brought her national attention. This essay collection describes what it means to be a young Black disabled woman in a country whose media and institutions treat whiteness and able bodies as the norm. Its core claim is that self-love for disabled people is both hard-won and political, and that the stories a culture tells shape whether that self-love is possible.
summary: Brown begins with the origin of the title. She has an identical twin sister who does not have cerebral palsy, and people in their lives called her sister "the pretty one." The book traces how that label, and the comparisons it implied, shaped her sense of her own body for years. She describes a long period of self-hatred, including depression and thoughts of suicide, and she is clear that the hatred came from outside before it came from inside. The culture around her, from classmates to movies, told her that a body like hers was something to hide or overcome.

The essays then move through different parts of her life. She writes about school and the particular loneliness of being both the only Black student and the only disabled one in many rooms. She writes about her family, her mother's care, and the tensions and loyalty between the twins. She writes about her physical reality in specific terms: the uneven gait, the hand that does not fully open, the surgeries, the fatigue. She also notes the way doctors and strangers talk about her body as though she is not there. She resists the urge to make these experiences uplifting, and she insists on the ordinary pleasures of her life alongside its difficulty.

Pop culture is the book's second major subject. Brown is a devoted fan of television, music, and film, and several essays analyze how disability appears on screen. She lists the familiar patterns: disabled characters played by nondisabled actors, disability used as a plot device to be cured or killed off, and the near total absence of disabled Black women. She explains why representation matters to her: not as an abstract principle but as a practical question of whether a disabled kid can imagine a future. She also writes warmly about the shows and musicians that gave her joy. She argues that the right to be a fan, and to care about frivolous things, is part of being seen as a full person.

A central essay tells the story of #DisabledAndCute. Brown posted photos of herself with the hashtag on a day when she felt good about how she looked, and thousands of disabled people around the world responded with their own. She describes the elation and the backlash, including criticism from within the disability community that "cute" was too narrow a standard. She reflects on the limits of social media activism. Still, she defends the campaign's core point: disabled people are allowed to find themselves attractive, and saying so in public challenges a culture that makes them invisible.

Later essays take up romance and desire. Brown writes about the frustrations of dating when potential partners cannot see past the disability, and about whether she wants children. She also writes about her career as a writer, about being asked to write only about disability, and about the economics of freelance journalism for a person with medical needs. An essay on physical accessibility describes the everyday indignities of inaccessible venues. It shows how being carried up stairs strips away a person's adulthood.

The book closes on the self-love its subtitle promises, but Brown presents it as a practice rather than an achievement. She describes choosing, on hard days, to speak kindly to herself, and she frames this choice as a form of resistance in a culture that profits from disabled people's shame. Throughout, the tone is conversational and funny, and the book speaks as much to disabled readers looking for company as to nondisabled readers looking for understanding.
mainPoints: Self-hatred among disabled people is learned from a culture that treats disabled bodies as lesser. It is not an inevitable response to impairment.
Being Black and disabled creates experiences that neither racial justice nor disability advocacy, taken alone, fully addresses.
Comparisons to nondisabled siblings and peers begin early and shape identity for years.
Media portrayals of disability are scarce, usually inaccurate, and almost never include disabled Black women.
Representation matters because it shapes whether disabled young people can imagine their own futures.
The right to enjoy pop culture and ordinary pleasures is part of being recognized as a full person.
#DisabledAndCute showed both the reach of social media activism and its limits, including debates within the disability community.
Disabled adults are routinely treated as nonsexual and left out of conversations about romance and parenting.
Inaccessible spaces impose indignities that undermine adulthood and independence.
Self-love is a daily practice and a political act, not a one-time arrival.
relevance: This book is short, candid, and easy to read, which makes it a good entry point for staff who have not read disability memoir before. For practitioners, its value lies in its intersectional lens. It shows how race and disability combine in ways that programs focused on one issue miss. That insight bears directly on outreach, case management, and workforce inclusion efforts. Communications teams can use its analysis of representation when choosing images and stories. Readers should note that the book is a personal account rather than a policy argument. Some disability advocates also questioned whether the campaign at its center reinforced standards based on appearance, and Brown takes up that critique herself.
questions: Brown describes being the only Black person and the only disabled person in most rooms. How does your organization account for people who are marginalized in more than one way?
What images of disabled people appear in your agency's materials, and who chose them?
Brown argues that self-love for disabled people is political. What does that claim suggest about how services should talk about client strengths and goals?

title: Accessibility for Everyone
editionNote: First published 2017 · A Book Apart · 166 pages
overview: Laura Kalbag is a British designer and co-founder of the Small Technology Foundation, which advocates for ethical technology that respects privacy. This short book is part of the A Book Apart series for web professionals. It introduces digital accessibility to designers, content creators, and product teams who do not see themselves as specialists. Its core claim is that accessibility is not a technical add-on done at the end of a project. It is a mindset to apply from the first sketch, and doing so improves products for every user.
summary: Kalbag begins by reframing what accessibility means. She does not treat it as a narrow compliance rule for people who use screen readers. Instead, she presents it as the practice of making products usable by people across the full range of abilities and circumstances. She describes disability through the social model, in which design choices, not bodies, create barriers. She widens the frame to include temporary and situational impairments: a broken arm, a noisy train, bright sunlight on a screen, a slow connection. Designing for the edges, she argues, produces products that work better in the middle.

The second chapter surveys the ways people experience disability online. Kalbag walks through visual, hearing, motor, cognitive, and speech-related impairments and explains what each means for using a website or app. She introduces assistive technologies such as screen readers, screen magnifiers, switch devices, voice control, and captioning. She stresses that users combine these tools in their own ways. She also discusses the risks of designing for a stereotype, such as assuming that all blind users are the same. She recommends involving disabled people in research and testing.

The book then turns to planning. Kalbag argues that accessibility decisions belong in project scoping and content strategy, when teams decide what the product will do and say. She covers writing accessible content: plain language, clear headings, meaningful link text, descriptive alternative text for images, and transcripts and captions for audio and video. She treats content as a design material, not filler to add later. She notes that clear writing helps readers with cognitive disabilities, readers whose first language is different, and readers in a hurry.

Later chapters cover visual design and interaction. Kalbag explains color contrast, the dangers of showing information through color alone, typography and line length, and why keyboard users need visible focus states. She discusses layout, including why content order and visual order should match. She also addresses motion and animation, which can cause problems for people with vestibular disorders. She then covers structure and semantics. This means using proper HTML elements so assistive technology can read a page, labeling forms, and making custom components work with a keyboard. She introduces ARIA, the set of attributes that adds to HTML for complex interfaces, and she warns against overusing it.

A chapter on testing and evaluation describes how to check work. Kalbag covers software checking tools and their limits. She also covers manual checks, such as moving through a page with only a keyboard, trying a screen reader, and zooming in. Above all, she stresses the value of testing with disabled users, which nothing else can replace. She refers to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) as the standard most laws and policies point to. She explains its principles of perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust content, without turning the book into a checklist.

The book also addresses the organizational side. Kalbag discusses how to make the case for accessibility to colleagues and clients, including legal risk, audience reach, and quality. But she cautions that the strongest argument is simply that excluding people is wrong. She describes building accessibility into process and culture so that it does not depend on a single champion. The title sums up the argument. Accessibility is for everyone because everyone benefits, and because everyone on a team shares responsibility for it.
mainPoints: Accessibility is a design mindset applied from the start of a project, not a technical fix added before launch.
The social model places barriers in design choices, and removing them is the designer's job.
Impairments can be permanent, temporary, or situational, so accessible design helps far more people than a narrow count of disabled users suggests.
People with disabilities use many assistive technologies in their own combinations. Designing for a stereotype fails real users.
Content is a design material. Plain language, clear structure, alt text, and captions are core accessibility work.
Visual design choices such as contrast, color use, typography, focus states, and motion directly affect who can use a product.
Correct HTML semantics do most of the work for assistive technology. ARIA adds to them but should not replace them.
Software testing tools catch only some problems. Keyboard and screen reader checks and testing with disabled users are essential.
WCAG provides a shared standard, but meeting it is a floor rather than a goal.
Accessibility succeeds when it is built into process and culture rather than depending on one advocate.
relevance: Public agencies and nonprofits must make digital services accessible under the ADA, Section 508, and state law. This book is a fast, nontechnical orientation for the communications, program, and procurement staff who shape websites, forms, PDFs, and social media. It is useful for setting expectations with vendors and for building accessibility checks into content workflows. The book is introductory and dates from 2017, so technical details on tools and ARIA have moved on. Readers responsible for compliance should consult current WCAG versions. Its arguments are mainstream in the field and are not contested.
questions: Which of your agency's public-facing digital services were designed with accessibility in mind from the start, and which had it added at the end?
Kalbag treats content as a design material. Who in your organization writes for the public, and have they been trained in plain language and alt text?
How does your procurement process confirm that a vendor's product is accessible, beyond asking for a compliance statement?

title: A Web for Everyone: Designing Accessible User Experiences
overview: Sarah Horton is a user experience and accessibility consultant with a long career in higher education technology. Whitney Quesenbery is a user researcher and usability expert who has advised government on civic design, including ballot and election accessibility. Their book brings accessibility into the mainstream of user experience (UX) practice. Its core claim is that accessible design and good design are the same thing. Teams that ground their work in the real needs of diverse people, they argue, will build products that work for everyone.
summary: The authors open by describing the state of the web for people with disabilities. Much content is unusable because it was designed with a single imagined user in mind. They argue that accessibility has been treated as a compliance task owned by developers, separate from design. This split produces products that technically pass tests but remain frustrating to use. Their alternative is to make accessibility a UX concern from the start. It should draw on the same research and empathy that drive good design for anyone.

A key tool in the book is a set of personas. These are imagined profiles, based on research, of people with a range of disabilities and circumstances. The personas include people who are blind, have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have motor impairments, have cognitive or learning disabilities, or have age-related changes. They also include people whose challenges come from limited technology or literacy. Each persona has goals, habits, preferred tools, and frustrations. The authors use them throughout the book to show how a design decision plays out for different users. They encourage readers to adopt and adapt them for their own projects.

The book follows a set of design principles the authors propose, each rooted in both WCAG and broader UX practice. The principles cover people-first design, clear purpose, solid structure, easy interaction, helpful wayfinding, clean presentation, plain language, accessible media, and universal usability. Each chapter takes up one principle, explains why it matters, connects it to the personas, and gives practical guidance. For example, the chapter on structure explains how headings, landmarks, and semantic markup make a page easy to navigate for screen reader users. The same features help sighted users scan. The chapter on interaction addresses keyboard use, focus management, and forms. The chapter on wayfinding covers navigation, page titles, and links that make sense out of context.

Several chapters address content rather than code. The authors treat plain language as an accessibility requirement. They explain how clear writing helps people with cognitive disabilities, people reading in a second language, and people under stress. They discuss accessible media, including captions, transcripts, audio description, and the design of players. They also address visual presentation, with guidance on contrast, text sizing, and layouts that reflow.

The book connects design principles to process. The authors describe how to build accessibility into each phase of a project, from research and requirements through design, development, and testing. They urge teams to include people with disabilities in user research and usability testing, and they explain how to do this in practice. They cover the roles of software checkers, expert review, and testing with assistive technology. They stress that these methods add to one another rather than replace one another.

The closing chapters take up the organizational side. The authors discuss how accessibility fits with laws and standards, including Section 508 and WCAG. They show how to use those standards as a framework rather than a finish line. They describe the roles of different team members, from executives and product managers to designers, writers, and developers. Shared responsibility, they argue, is the only approach that lasts. They end with a vision of universal usability. In it, designing for the full range of human diversity becomes the normal practice of the field rather than a specialty.
mainPoints: Accessible design and good user experience are not separate goals. The practices that serve disabled users improve products for everyone.
Treating accessibility as a developer compliance task produces products that pass tests but fail people.
Personas with disabilities, based on research, help teams keep real users in view during design decisions.
A small set of principles, including clear purpose, solid structure, easy interaction, and plain language, covers most of what accessibility requires.
Structure and semantics give assistive technology what it needs and also help sighted users scan and navigate.
Keyboard use and clear focus are basic to interaction design, not advanced features.
Plain language, captions, transcripts, and audio description are design requirements, not afterthoughts.
Accessibility belongs in every phase of a project, and people with disabilities should take part in research and testing.
Software checkers, expert review, and assistive technology testing each catch different problems.
Standards such as WCAG and Section 508 provide a framework. Meeting them is a floor, and shared team responsibility is what keeps results going.
relevance: This book is especially useful for public-sector teams. One author has worked extensively on civic design and government services, and the persona approach suits agencies that must serve the whole public. Program managers, web content owners, and procurement staff can use the principles as a plain-English checklist for reviewing websites, online applications, and digital forms. The personas can anchor staff training. The book predates the current WCAG version and the 2024 federal rule on state and local government web accessibility, so legal details should be checked against current sources. Its approach is standard in the UX field and widely endorsed.
questions: Pick one online form or service your agency offers. Walk through it as each of the book's personas would. Where does it fail?
The authors argue that accessibility fails when only developers own it. Who owns it in your organization, and who should?
Does your user research or community feedback include people with disabilities? If not, what would it take to include them?

title: Inclusive Design for a Digital World: Designing with Accessibility in Mind
overview: Regine Gilbert is a user experience designer and educator who teaches at New York University and has consulted widely on accessibility. Her book is a practical introduction for designers, developers, and product managers who want to build accessible digital products but do not know where to begin. Its core claim is that inclusive design depends on mindset and process as much as technique. Teams that start with the full range of human ability and situation will build better products, at lower cost, than teams that fix things after the fact.
summary: Gilbert opens by placing accessibility within the larger idea of inclusive design. She separates the terms. Accessibility refers to whether people with disabilities can use a product. Universal design means designing one solution for the widest possible range of people. Inclusive design is a method that draws on human diversity to guide choices. She traces the history of disability rights and accessibility law, including the ADA and Section 508 in the United States and the development of WCAG. This history shows readers why the obligations exist and how they came about.

A chapter on understanding users describes the range of disabilities and the assistive technologies people use. Gilbert covers visual, hearing, motor, cognitive, and neurological conditions. She extends the frame to aging, temporary injury, and situational limits. She introduces the "curb cut effect": features built for disabled people, like sidewalk ramps, end up helping many others. She uses it to argue that accessibility is an investment in the whole user base. She stresses that nothing replaces talking with disabled users, and she gives practical advice on recruiting them for research.

The core of the book walks through the design process. Gilbert covers research and discovery, including how to write inclusive personas. She explains how to run interviews and usability sessions with participants who use assistive technology. She then addresses information architecture and content, arguing that clear structure and plain language are the foundation of accessible products. Chapters on visual design cover color and contrast, typography, iconography, motion, and layout, with concrete checks a designer can apply. Chapters on interaction cover keyboard navigation, focus order, forms and error messages, and custom components. They explain how screen readers and switch devices interpret each of these.

Gilbert gives extended attention to mobile and emerging technologies. She discusses touch targets, gestures that have no keyboard equivalent, screen orientation, and the accessibility features built into iOS and Android. She also considers voice interfaces, virtual and augmented reality, and wearables. She notes where these raise new accessibility questions that standards have not yet caught up with. This material gives the book a broader reach than guides that focus only on websites.

A practical chapter on testing explains the tools available. These include browser extensions and software checkers, color contrast analyzers, screen readers such as VoiceOver, NVDA, and JAWS, and manual testing steps. Gilbert explains what each one catches and misses. She recommends a layered approach that ends with testing by disabled users. She includes guidance on writing accessibility notes for developers so that the design's intent is not lost in handoff. She also discusses accessibility documents such as conformance reports.

The book also takes up the organizational work of building an accessibility practice: training, governance, assigning roles, and making the case to leadership. Gilbert argues that accessibility champions burn out when they work alone, and she urges spreading responsibility across teams. Throughout, she includes interviews with practitioners and short case examples. She writes in a friendly voice meant to make the subject less daunting for newcomers, not to serve as a complete technical reference.
mainPoints: Accessibility, universal design, and inclusive design are related but distinct. Inclusive design is a method that uses human diversity to improve decisions.
Legal duties such as the ADA, Section 508, and WCAG grew out of disability rights activism. Knowing that history helps teams see them as more than box-checking.
The "curb cut effect" shows that features built for disabled users help many others.
Direct research with disabled users cannot be replaced, and recruiting them is a practical problem that can be solved.
Structure and plain language are the foundation of accessible content. Visual polish cannot make up for confusing organization.
Visual design choices about color, type, motion, and layout have specific accessibility effects that can be checked.
Keyboard use, focus order, and clear error handling are core requirements for interaction design.
Mobile, voice, and immersive technologies raise accessibility questions that standards are still catching up with.
Software checkers, manual checks, and user testing catch different problems and should be layered.
An accessibility practice lasts only when responsibility is shared and backed by governance and training.
relevance: Many agencies and nonprofits build or buy apps, portals, kiosks, and mobile services. For them, this book is a useful bridge between legal duties and the practical choices of design teams. Its coverage of mobile and emerging technology makes it relevant to organizations updating client-facing services. Its chapter on handoff and annotation helps nontechnical program staff explain requirements to vendors. The book is introductory, and some tool references have aged. Readers responsible for compliance should check current WCAG criteria and federal rules. Its approach reflects mainstream practice and is not contested.
questions: Gilbert separates accessibility from inclusive design. Does your organization aim only to meet standards, or does it use human diversity to guide design decisions?
What assistive technologies do the people you serve actually use, and has anyone tested your mobile or web services with them?
Who on your staff is the accessibility champion, and what would happen to your practice if that person left?

title: Universal Design for Learning: Theory and Practice
authors: Anne Meyer, David H. Rose, and David Gordon
overview: Anne Meyer and David Rose co-founded CAST, the nonprofit research organization that developed Universal Design for Learning (UDL). David Gordon is a CAST editor and publisher. This book is the authoritative statement of the UDL framework from the people who created it. Its core claim is that learner variability is the norm, not the exception. Curricula designed for an imagined average student create barriers. Those barriers could be removed by building flexibility into goals, materials, methods, and assessments from the start.
summary: The authors begin with the roots of UDL in the universal design movement in architecture. There, features such as ramps and automatic doors were built in for disabled users and turned out to help everyone. CAST applied this idea to education in the 1980s and 1990s while developing technology for students with disabilities. The researchers came to believe that the disability was not in the student but in a rigid curriculum. Printed textbooks, lectures, and timed written tests all assumed one way of learning. The book presents UDL as a response to the "myth of the average learner," the idea that there is a typical student for whom teaching can be designed.

A central chapter lays out the framework's basis in learning science. The authors describe three broad networks in the brain that are involved in learning. Affective networks govern why we learn, including engagement and motivation. Recognition networks govern what we learn, including perception and understanding. Strategic networks govern how we learn, including planning, action, and expression. The authors stress that these networks vary from person to person. They also vary within one person depending on context. That is why no single method works for all.

From these networks the authors draw the three UDL principles: provide multiple means of engagement, multiple means of representation, and multiple means of action and expression. Each principle is spelled out through guidelines and checkpoints that make up the UDL Guidelines, a reference tool that CAST maintains and updates. Under engagement, for example, the guidelines address sparking interest, sustaining effort, and self-regulation. Under representation, they address perception, language and symbols, and comprehension. Under action and expression, they address physical action, expression and communication, and executive functions. The book explains each in plain language with examples.

The authors then turn to curriculum design. They name four parts of a curriculum: goals, methods, materials, and assessments. They show how each can be designed with flexibility built in. A key move is to separate the goal of a lesson from the means of reaching it. Say the goal is to understand a historical event. Then requiring students to read a particular text is a means, not the goal, and options such as audio, video, or discussion should be available. The authors stress that UDL means planning for variability in advance, rather than accommodating individuals after the fact.

A chapter on expert learners describes the framework's aim. The authors want students to become purposeful and motivated, resourceful and knowledgeable, and strategic and goal-directed. The point of flexibility is not to lower expectations. It is to remove obstacles so that all students can work toward rigorous goals and build the ability to direct their own learning.

The later chapters address putting UDL into practice in classrooms, schools, and whole systems. They cover professional development, leadership, policy, and the role of technology. The authors grant that technology makes many UDL practices easier, but they insist the framework does not depend on it. They also discuss UDL's growing place in federal policy, where the Higher Education Opportunity Act of 2008 recognized it. The original edition was published as a multimedia online book, itself designed to show UDL principles at work.
mainPoints: Learner variability is universal and predictable. The "average learner" is a statistical fiction that harms instructional design.
Barriers to learning usually lie in rigid curricula rather than in students.
Three brain networks, affective, recognition, and strategic, match the why, what, and how of learning. They vary across people and contexts.
UDL's three principles are multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression.
The UDL Guidelines turn the principles into specific checkpoints that designers can apply.
Goals should be stated separately from the means of reaching them so that multiple paths stay open.
UDL plans for variability in design rather than responding to individuals after the fact. This sets it apart from individual accommodation.
Flexibility is meant to keep rigor, not lower it. The aim is expert learners who can direct their own learning.
Technology helps but is not required. UDL is a way of thinking about design.
UDL has been recognized in US federal education policy and applies beyond K-12 to higher education and training.
relevance: Trainers, program designers, and anyone who runs workshops, orientations, or client education can apply UDL directly. They can state goals separately from methods, offer content in more than one format, and let participants choose how to show what they know. They can also build in ways to sustain engagement. HR and learning teams will find it a useful framework for making required training accessible without separate tracks. Practitioners should know that UDL is widely adopted, but researchers note that the evidence on its effect on outcomes is still developing. Some critics argue the framework is so broad that it is hard to evaluate. CAST has also updated the Guidelines since this edition, so readers should consult the current version.
questions: Take a training or workshop your organization delivers. What is its actual goal, and which of its requirements are means that could be made flexible?
Where does your organization rely on individual accommodation to fix problems that could be designed out in advance?
How would you know whether a UDL-based redesign improved outcomes for participants, rather than simply feeling more inclusive?

title: Reach Everyone, Teach Everyone: Universal Design for Learning in Higher Education
authors: Thomas J. Tobin and Kirsten T. Behling
editionNote: First published 2018 · West Virginia University Press · 312 pages
overview: Thomas Tobin is a faculty developer and distance-education specialist. Kirsten Behling directs student accessibility services at a university. Both have long experience with disability services and online learning. Their book adapts Universal Design for Learning (UDL) for colleges and universities, where it has caught on far more slowly than in K-12 schools. Its core claim is that UDL will spread in higher education only when it is framed as a way to reach every learner, not as a disability accommodation. That includes the growing number of students who study on mobile devices in the gaps of busy lives.
summary: The authors open by explaining why UDL has stalled on campuses. Faculty hear "universal design" and assume it is about students with disabilities, a small group served by a separate office. They see it as extra work with no reward, and they worry it means lowering standards. Disability services staff, meanwhile, are stretched thin handling accommodation requests one at a time. Tobin and Behling argue that this framing is the problem. As long as UDL is sold as a disability initiative, it will stay a niche concern.

Their alternative is the "plus-one" approach. It does not ask instructors to redesign everything. Instead, it asks them to find the one place in a course where students most often get stuck or ask questions. Then they add one more way to engage with it: a short video alongside a reading, a choice of essay or recorded presentation, an outline alongside a lecture. This step-by-step method makes it easier to start and lets faculty see results quickly. The authors argue that small changes add up over time to a fully flexible course.

A second reframing concerns who the students are. The authors point to a shift in who attends college: adult learners, parents, workers, commuters, and first-generation students. Many of them reach course materials on phones during commutes, breaks, and late nights. The authors argue that these learners face the same kinds of barriers that students with disabilities face, such as content that requires sitting at a desk with full attention. Designing for mobile, time-pressed access solves both problems at once. They introduce the idea of designing for "access-to-time," so that learners can make progress in whatever slices of time they have.

The book then reviews the UDL framework itself, drawing on CAST's three principles: multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. The authors translate the principles into the language of higher education. They give examples across disciplines, from lab sciences to writing courses. They take on the standards objection directly. UDL, they argue, changes how students show their learning, not the learning outcomes themselves. The exercise often leads to clearer outcome statements.

Several chapters speak to different campus audiences. A chapter for faculty gives step-by-step guidance on applying plus-one thinking to syllabi, assignments, assessments, and feedback. A chapter for instructional designers and faculty developers covers how to build UDL into course design services and training. A chapter for disability services staff describes how to move from reacting to accommodation requests toward consulting with faculty ahead of time. Over time, this reduces individual requests. A chapter for administrators addresses policy, incentives, and the data leaders need to support adoption, including retention and completion figures.

The authors also take up legal and accessibility compliance. They explain how UDL relates to the ADA and Section 504 and to lawsuits about the accessibility of online course content. They argue that UDL does not replace accommodation, since some students will always need individual adjustments. But it reduces demand and improves the experience for everyone. The book closes with a chapter on building a movement across a campus. This includes finding early adopters, documenting results, and keeping change going through leadership turnover. Case studies and practical templates run throughout.
mainPoints: UDL has stalled in higher education mostly because it is framed as a disability initiative rather than a way to improve teaching.
The "plus-one" approach asks instructors to add one alternative where students most often struggle, rather than redesign everything at once.
Today's college students are often adults, workers, and parents who learn on mobile devices in small slices of time. Designing for them also serves disabled students.
Designing for access to time, as well as access to content, is central to reaching mobile learners.
UDL changes how students show their learning, not what they must learn, so it does not lower standards.
Faculty, instructional designers, disability services staff, and administrators each have distinct roles and need guidance suited to them.
Disability services can shift from reacting to requests toward consulting on course design, which reduces the number of requests over time.
UDL reduces but does not end the need for individual accommodation.
Administrators should link UDL to retention, completion, and legal risk to justify investment.
Lasting adoption requires early adopters, documented results, and leadership support that survives turnover.
relevance: Although written for campuses, this book carries over easily to workforce training, continuing education, and any organization that teaches busy adults. Its plus-one method is a realistic starting point for trainers who cannot overhaul their programs. Its reframing of accessibility as a mainstream quality concern is useful when making the case to leadership. HR and learning teams can borrow its guidance on moving from case-by-case accommodation toward planning ahead in design. Readers should note that the book's stress on the business and retention case is a strategic choice that some disability advocates question. Evidence on UDL outcomes in higher education also remains limited.
questions: Where in your organization's training do participants most often get stuck or ask questions? What one alternative could you add there?
The authors argue that designing for busy mobile learners also serves disabled learners. Does that framing help or hinder your accessibility goals, and why?
How much of your accommodation workload could shrink if programs were designed differently in the first place?

title: Academic Ableism: Disability and Higher Education
editionNote: First published 2017 · University of Michigan Press · 254 pages
overview: Jay Dolmage is a professor of English at the University of Waterloo and a leading scholar in disability studies and rhetoric. This book is a critical history and analysis of how colleges and universities have been built, both physically and culturally, around keeping disabled people out. Its core claim is that ableism is not an unfortunate side effect of higher education but one of its organizing principles. Reforms such as accommodation offices and universal design are valuable. But they have often been absorbed in ways that leave the deeper structure untouched.
summary: Dolmage begins with the image of the "steep steps" that lead up to the main building on many old campuses. These steps, he argues, are both real barriers and a symbol of what the university has stood for. It is a raised-up place that only certain bodies and minds were meant to reach. He traces the history of American and Canadian higher education alongside the history of eugenics. Many of the same institutions that claimed to advance knowledge also produced the science used to classify, sterilize, and exclude disabled people, immigrants, and racial minorities. In his account, the university did not merely tolerate eugenics. It was one of its main engines, and that legacy lives on in how the institution defines merit and intelligence.

The book then examines the metaphors through which higher education has taken in disability. Dolmage names the "retrofit" as the main way institutions respond. Examples include a ramp bolted to the side of a building, a separate entrance, or an accommodation letter processed after a student has already fallen behind. Retrofits are presented as solutions. But they keep disability at the margins and mark disabled people as exceptions. They also force disabled people to ask again and again for what others receive by default. He is especially critical of how accommodation systems put the burden of proof on students. Students must get documentation, disclose, and negotiate with each instructor.

A third metaphor is universal design. Dolmage credits the universal design movement and Universal Design for Learning with pointing toward a better approach, in which flexibility is built in from the start. But he warns against treating universal design as a checklist or a finished product. When it is reduced to a set of techniques, he argues, it can become another retrofit. The same happens when it is marketed as helping everyone while quietly moving disabled people away from the center. He proposes seeing universal design as an ongoing process of negotiation. That process keeps disabled people's perspectives central and never claims to be complete.

The middle chapters look at specific sites of academic ableism. Dolmage analyzes campus architecture, admissions and standardized testing, and the rhetoric of rigor and excellence. He also looks at how institutions handle mental health and disclosure, and at the position of disabled faculty, who are rarely counted and often invisible. He discusses the language of "accommodation" and "special needs" and how it frames disabled students as costly exceptions. He also addresses the cultural pressure on students and faculty to pass as nondisabled, and the exhaustion this produces.

Dolmage pays attention to how disability intersects with race, class, gender, and immigration status. He links eugenic history to current patterns. Students of color are overrepresented in some disability categories and underrepresented in others. He argues that any serious response to ableism in higher education must address these intersections. It should not treat disability as a single, separate category.

The book closes by asking what it would mean to design higher education differently. Dolmage offers less a program than a set of commitments. Center disabled people in decisions about them. Treat access as a shared and continuing duty rather than the job of one office. Examine the institution's own history honestly. And resist the urge to declare the problem solved. The University of Michigan Press published the book open access, a choice the author presents as consistent with its argument. It has become a standard reference in disability studies and in conversations about inclusive campuses.
mainPoints: Higher education has long been organized around excluding disabled people, and the "steep steps" of old campuses symbolize that design.
Universities were central producers of eugenic science, and that legacy shapes present definitions of merit, intelligence, and rigor.
The "retrofit," an accommodation added after the fact, is the main institutional response, and it keeps disability at the margins.
Accommodation systems put the burden of documentation, disclosure, and negotiation on disabled people.
Universal design is a better approach, but it can be hollowed out into a checklist or marketed in ways that move disabled people away from the center.
Universal design should be treated as an ongoing process that is never finished, not as a product.
Admissions testing, talk of excellence, and campus architecture each carry assumptions about which bodies and minds belong.
Disabled faculty are rarely counted and are often pressured to pass as nondisabled.
Ableism intersects with racism, classism, and sexism. Disability categories have been used to sort and exclude people along these lines.
An honest look at institutional history is a precondition for real change.
relevance: This book is more theoretical and historical than others on this list. Its value for practitioners lies in its critical lens. Anyone who runs an accommodation process, in a school, agency, or workplace, will recognize Dolmage's description of the retrofit. His critique can prompt a review of where burdens fall on the people being served. It also offers a useful caution for organizations adopting the language of universal design: the rhetoric can run ahead of the substance. Readers should know that the book is written from a disability studies perspective and is sharply critical of institutions. Some will find its tone polemical, and it offers fewer concrete tools than texts focused on practice. It works well paired with a practical UDL guide.
questions: Dolmage describes accommodation as a retrofit that keeps disability at the margins. How does your organization's accommodation process look to the person requesting it?
What is your institution's own history with disability, and has it been examined honestly?
Dolmage warns that universal design can become a checklist that moves disabled people away from the center. How would you keep disabled people central as your organization adopts inclusive design?

review.authorDecisionReason: Middle name abbreviated in catalogue.

title: Disability Rights and Wrongs
overview: Disability Rights and Wrongs is a critical reassessment of disability studies by Tom Shakespeare. He is a British sociologist and bioethicist who has achondroplasia and has worked inside the disability movement for decades. The book gathers and sharpens a decade of his writing into one sustained argument. The British "social model" of disability, he argues, is politically powerful but has hardened into a dogma that no longer describes disabled people's lives well. Shakespeare proposes instead a relational account, in which disability comes from the interaction of bodies, minds, and environments. He then tests that account against hard questions in medicine, genetics, care, and end-of-life ethics.
summary: Shakespeare begins with history. The British social model was developed in the 1970s by the Union of the Physically Impaired Against Segregation and given theory by Michael Oliver and Vic Finkelstein. It drew a sharp line between impairment, a feature of the body, and disability, the exclusion society imposes. That distinction gave activists a clear target: change the barriers, not the person. Shakespeare credits the model with building a movement and giving disabled people a positive identity. He writes as an insider rather than an opponent.

The first part of the book then explains why he thinks the model has become a "wrong." Its strict separation of impairment from disability, he argues, does not hold up. Pain, fatigue, shortened life, and loss of function are real and would remain even in a world without barriers. Treating impairment as irrelevant pushes out of the conversation the people whose impairments do matter to them, including many with chronic illness. The model also implies a goal that cannot be reached, a world with no disabling barriers at all. And it tends to assume that all disabled people share the same interests, which Shakespeare doubts.

In place of the social model, he offers what he calls a critical realist, interactional approach. It draws on Nordic disability research and on the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. On this view, disability always comes from an interaction between two sets of factors. Individual factors include the nature and severity of impairment, personality, and attitudes. Contextual factors include the built environment, policy, culture, and relationships. Impairment and barriers both matter. In any given case, the question is how much of each is at work and what can be changed. He also argues that impairment is a universal human predicament rather than a minority condition, since most people will face limitation at some point in life.

The middle chapters turn to debates about identity and culture. Shakespeare questions whether disability is best understood as a minority identity like race or sexuality. He is skeptical of calls for a distinct disability culture, though he sees the value of pride and solidarity. He also argues that opposing medicalization should not mean rejecting treatment, rehabilitation, or research into cure. Disabled people often want both rights and better health.

The second half applies the interactional model to bioethics, Shakespeare's other field. He works through prenatal screening and selective termination. These practices send troubling messages, he argues, but a blanket ban is not justified, and both parents' choices and disabled people's rights can be respected. He considers genetic research and the "expressivist" objection that screening devalues disabled people who are alive now. He also weighs the charge that bioethics as a discipline has been hostile to disability. On assisted dying he takes a cautious position. He understands the fears of disability activists. But he does not think opposition to legal assisted suicide follows automatically from a disability rights stance.

The final chapters address care and independent living. Shakespeare defends the goal of independent living and the shift from institutional care to personal assistance. But he argues that the movement's language of "independence" and "control" can hide the reality of interdependence and the interests of care workers. Drawing on feminist ethics of care, he suggests that help, when properly organized, is not a threat to dignity.

The book ends with a plea for pluralism. In Shakespeare's view, disability studies should rest on evidence rather than slogans. It should include impairment in its account of disabled lives. And it should accept that different impairments and contexts call for different solutions. A revised and expanded edition, Disability Rights and Wrongs Revisited, appeared in 2014 and responds to critics of the first.
mainPoints: The British social model was a vital political tool, but it has been treated as a complete theory of disability, which it is not.
Impairment matters. Pain, fatigue, and functional limits would remain even in a fully accessible society, and a theory that ignores them leaves out many disabled people.
Disability is best understood as relational: the product of interaction between individual features and the environmental and social context.
Impairment is a near-universal part of human life, not only a minority experience. This affects how services and policies should be designed.
Disabled people are diverse. Identity politics that assume shared interests across all impairments can mislead.
Opposing medicalization should not mean rejecting medicine, rehabilitation, or research. Most disabled people want both access and health.
Prenatal screening and genetic research raise real concerns about the messages they send to disabled people, but Shakespeare does not support banning them.
Disability rights do not automatically require opposing assisted dying. The question deserves argument rather than reflexive positions.
Independent living is a worthy goal, but "independence" is better understood as interdependence, with the interests of care workers also in view.
relevance: For practitioners, the book corrects overly simple training messages. Many DEIA curricula present the social model as the correct view and the medical model as the wrong one. Shakespeare's interactional approach gives trainers, HR staff, and program designers a sounder framework. It still centers removing barriers while recognizing that impairment shapes needs. Direct-service and policy staff will find his chapters on care and independent living useful when designing personal assistance, aging-in-place, or supported decision-making programs. The book is contested. Many disability studies scholars and activists argue that Shakespeare understates how flexible the social model is. They also argue that his bioethics positions give too much ground to medical and parental choice. Readers should present it as one side of a live debate.
questions: Where do our disability policies assume that removing barriers is enough, and where do they need to address needs that come from impairment directly?
Does Shakespeare's claim that impairment is a universal predicament strengthen or weaken the case for disability as a protected identity in our setting?
How should an agency handle the tension he describes between the independence of service users and the working conditions of care staff?

title: Nothing About Us Without Us: Disability Oppression and Empowerment
editionNote: First published 1998 · University of California Press · 213 pages
overview: Nothing About Us Without Us is a study of how people with disabilities are oppressed around the world and how an international movement has organized to resist. James Charlton, a Chicago-based disability rights organizer, wrote it after a decade of travel and interviews with activists in Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. His core claim is that disability is not a medical misfortune but a form of systematic oppression. It is like racism, sexism, and colonialism in structure, though different in detail. And disabled people themselves must lead the fight against it. The book spread the slogan in its title widely.
summary: Charlton opens by explaining the title. He first heard "Nothing about us without us" from South African disability activists. They had heard it from an Eastern European activist at an international disability rights conference. He makes it the organizing principle of the book. No policy, program, or decision about disabled people should be made without their full participation. The phrase has since become the unofficial motto of disability rights movements worldwide and of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

The first half of the book is theoretical. Charlton defines disability oppression as the systematic disadvantage of people with disabilities, produced by political economy, culture, and ideology. Drawing on Marxist political economy, he argues that disabled people are pushed to the economic margins because capitalist labor markets have little use for bodies and minds that do not fit productivity norms. Most disabled people in the world are poor, and most poor disabled people have no access to services at all. Poverty causes impairment through malnutrition, war, and unsafe work. Impairment in turn deepens poverty.

Culture and belief systems form the second layer. Charlton examines how religions, folk traditions, and modern professional ideas all treat disability as deviance, misfortune, punishment, or a reason for pity. He is especially sharp about the dependency and paternalism that medical and rehabilitation professions repeat. Disabled people are cast as patients, clients, and charity cases who must be managed by experts. In his account, charity is not a neutral good. It is a system that profits from disabled people's dependence and reinforces the idea that they are inferior.

A central chapter deals with consciousness. Charlton argues that oppression works partly by being taken inside. Disabled people come to believe the stories told about them, accept isolation as natural, and defer to professionals. He calls this false consciousness or internalized oppression. He treats overcoming it as the first task of any movement. Empowerment begins when disabled people see their situation as political rather than personal.

The second half of the book draws on Charlton's interviews with activists and organizers. They include leaders in Disabled Peoples' International and in national organizations in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Brazil, Thailand, and elsewhere. Through their accounts he traces how disability rights organizations formed, often in the 1980s. He shows how they related to independence struggles and labor movements, and how they faced both state neglect and the paternalism of established charities. He describes a common arc. Individuals find each other, form self-help groups, develop a political analysis, and demand representation. The chapter on organizing offers practical lessons about leadership, coalitions, and the risk of being co-opted by governments and funders.

Charlton also compares disability oppression with other oppressions. He is careful to say the parallels are structural, not identical. Disabled people are found in every other group. That makes solidarity both necessary and difficult, and disability movements must reckon with race, gender, class, and nation within their own ranks.

The book ends on the back-and-forth between oppression and empowerment. Oppression creates the conditions for resistance. Resistance, in turn, changes consciousness and creates new organizations and demands. Charlton does not promise victory. He argues that progress should be measured by whether disabled people are speaking and deciding for themselves. He insists that the slogan in his title is both an ethic and a strategy.
mainPoints: Disability is a form of oppression produced by economic systems, culture, and ideology, not simply a medical condition.
Most of the world's disabled people are poor, and poverty and impairment reinforce each other.
Professional and charitable systems often create an ideology of dependency that keeps disabled people in the role of client or recipient.
Oppression is internalized. Disabled people may accept the limits placed on them until they develop a political consciousness.
Empowerment begins when disabled people see their situation as shared and political, usually through contact with others.
Disability rights movements worldwide grew out of self-help groups, often alongside independence and labor movements.
Comparisons with racism, sexism, and colonialism shed light on the structure of disability oppression, but they should not erase its specific features.
Disability crosses every other social category, so disability movements must deal with race, gender, and class within their own ranks.
Co-optation by governments, funders, and charities is a constant threat to a movement's independence.
"Nothing about us without us" is both an ethical principle and a practical test of whether any policy or program is legitimate.
relevance: This is the source most often cited when agencies adopt participatory principles in disability programs. It gives practitioners a vocabulary for why representation matters. HR, policy, and program staff can use it to review how decisions get made. Are disabled employees and service users at the table, with real authority, or consulted after the fact? Direct-service staff will find its critique of the dependency ideology uncomfortable but useful. It can guide a review of how intake, case management, and "client" language position people. The book's Marxist framing and its focus on physical and sensory disability in the 1980s and 1990s date it in places. Readers interested in psychiatric, intellectual, or chronic-illness perspectives will need other sources too. Its global scope is a strength for teams working with immigrant and refugee populations.
questions: Which decisions in our organization that affect disabled people are now made without disabled people taking part, and what would change if the slogan were applied literally?
Where does our service model repeat the dependency and paternalism Charlton describes, for example in language, eligibility rules, or who holds authority?
Charlton says oppression is partly internalized. How might that shape the way disabled employees or clients respond to new opportunities, and how should staff take it into account?

title: Make Them Go Away: Clint Eastwood, Christopher Reeve and the Case Against Disability Rights
editionNote: First published 2003 · Advocado Press · 296 pages · available to borrow
overview: Make Them Go Away is a journalist's account of the backlash against the Americans with Disabilities Act in the decade after it passed. Mary Johnson was the founding editor of the disability rights magazine The Disability Rag, later Ragged Edge. She uses two celebrities as case studies. Clint Eastwood fought an ADA lawsuit over his California hotel and lobbied Congress to weaken the law. Christopher Reeve, after his injury, campaigned for a cure and drew public sympathy that access advocates never received. Johnson's core claim is that most Americans never accepted disability as a civil rights issue. The law has been narrowed, she argues, because the public would rather disabled people be cured, cared for, or kept out of sight than accommodated.
summary: Johnson opens with the Eastwood story. In the late 1990s a disabled woman sued the actor's Mission Ranch resort in Carmel because it lacked accessible rooms and bathrooms. Eastwood fought the case. In May 2000, months before a jury largely cleared him, he testified before Congress for the ADA Notification Act. That bill would have required people to notify businesses and wait ninety days before suing. Johnson shows how the media framed the dispute as a decent man harassed by greedy lawyers. Coverage almost never asked why the resort was still inaccessible eight years after the ADA. The episode becomes her example of a larger pattern. The law depends on private lawsuits for enforcement, and that reliance was turned into proof that the law was unreasonable.

Reeve supplies the contrasting image. After his 1995 spinal cord injury, Reeve became the nation's most visible disabled person and used his platform for research toward a cure. Johnson does not attack him personally. She argues that his story was so welcome because it fit what the public already believed: that disability is a tragedy to be overcome through medicine. Ramps, access, and job protections are, by comparison, unglamorous demands that ask nondisabled people to change. Reeve sometimes made comments dismissing the idea of accepting disability, she notes, and these drew applause rather than scrutiny.

From these cases the book moves to the larger pattern. Johnson traces how the ADA passed in 1990 with support from both parties and little public debate. Then business groups, columnists, and later the courts recast it as a law about "special" treatment and frivolous lawsuits. She documents the Supreme Court decisions of 1999 and 2002, including the Sutton and Toyota cases. These narrowed the definition of disability so sharply that many people with serious conditions could not claim the law's protection. She also covers the Garrett decision limiting suits against states. The Court, she argues, reflected the general view that the ADA was never really a civil rights law.

Johnson spends several chapters on language and ideas. She examines how terms like "reasonable accommodation" and "undue hardship" invite businesses to see access as a cost that individuals impose, rather than a public good. She compares disability rights to earlier civil rights movements. That comparison is central to activists' thinking, she finds, but it never took hold with the public. Race discrimination came to be understood as a wrong done to people. Disability discrimination remained a matter of unfortunate biology. Charity and pity, she argues, were the only frames most people had.

A key argument concerns who benefits. Johnson insists that accessible design helps far more people than the narrow category of "the disabled." It helps parents with strollers, older people, delivery workers, and people with temporary injuries. By letting the ADA be seen as a law for a small special group, advocates lost the chance to present access as universal design, something everyone eventually needs.

The title sums up her diagnosis. Society's underlying preference is for disabled people to go away, whether through cure, institutions, inaccessible buildings, or legal definitions that exclude them. Johnson closes by arguing that the movement must make its case in public, not only in court. It must explain disability as a shared human condition and access as an ordinary civic expectation.
mainPoints: The ADA passed in 1990 with little public understanding of its purpose, which left it open to being redefined by opponents.
The Eastwood case and the ADA Notification Act show how the law's reliance on private lawsuits for enforcement was turned into an argument against the law itself.
Christopher Reeve's push for a cure was embraced because it matched the public's existing belief that disability is a medical tragedy.
Supreme Court rulings in the late 1990s and early 2000s narrowed the law's coverage in ways that reflected public doubt rather than the law's text.
Terms like "reasonable accommodation" and "undue hardship" frame access as a cost imposed by individuals rather than a public responsibility.
The civil rights comparison that drives the disability movement has never been widely accepted outside it.
Pity and charity remain the main public frames for disability, and they do not fit with a rights frame.
Accessible design helps most people at some point in life, and presenting it as a "special" need weakens support.
Many people eligible for ADA protection avoid identifying as disabled, which weakens the movement's public presence.
Lasting change requires winning the public argument, not only lawsuits and regulation.
relevance: Johnson's book explains the resistance practitioners meet when they raise accessibility. People often see it as special treatment, a lawsuit risk, or a cost rather than a civil right. HR and facilities staff can use the book to reframe accommodation conversations around universal design and shared benefit. Communications staff will find its media analysis useful when planning how to describe disability initiatives. Trainers should note where the book sits in history. It predates the ADA Amendments Act of 2008, which reversed much of the court-made narrowing Johnson describes, so its legal chapters need updating. The book is partisan in tone and written for a movement audience. Some readers will find its treatment of Eastwood and Reeve unfair, and a balanced session should say so.
questions: When accessibility comes up in our organization, is it framed as compliance, cost, charity, or civil rights, and what does that framing lead us to do?
How much of our disability work aims at cure, treatment, or care, and how much at removing barriers? Is the balance deliberate?
