The ADA Amendments Act restored much of the law's coverage. Has the public attitude Johnson describes changed, or only the legal text?

title: The Minority Body: A Theory of Disability
editionNote: First published 2016 · Oxford University Press · 160 pages · available to borrow
overview: The Minority Body is a work of analytic philosophy that defends a simple but contested thesis. Being physically disabled is a way of being a minority, not a way of being worse off. Elizabeth Barnes is a philosopher at the University of Virginia who writes from her own experience of disability. She argues that philosophers have assumed, without argument, that disability is a harm to be prevented or cured. She sets out to show that this assumption is not justified. Disabled people's own testimony about their lives, she argues, deserves the weight any other testimony would get. And a "mere-difference" view of disability can survive the standard objections.
summary: Barnes begins with definition. Earlier accounts, she argues, fall into two camps. Some treat disability as a biological defect, which slips in the very judgment she wants to question. Others treat it as purely socially constructed, which cannot explain what unites the people the disability rights movement speaks for. Her alternative is an account based on solidarity. A person is physically disabled if they have a bodily feature that the disability rights movement, through its rules for solidarity, counts among the conditions it seeks justice for. On this view, disability is a social category organized around shared political experience, but it tracks real features of bodies. She deliberately limits the book to physical disability. Cognitive and psychiatric disability, she says, raise further questions she does not address.

The central distinction is between "bad-difference" and "mere-difference" views. A bad-difference view holds that disability by itself makes a person worse off, even in a world without stigma or barriers. A mere-difference view holds that disability is a neutral feature, like being gay or belonging to a minority ethnic group. Such a feature can make particular things harder or easier, but it does not lower overall well-being. Barnes argues that most philosophical writing simply assumes bad-difference. That assumption, she says, rests on intuition rather than evidence.

She then develops what she calls the value-neutral model. Disability, she grants, can be locally bad. It can involve pain, exclusion, or lost options. But local bads do not make something globally bad. Many valuable parts of life, such as parenthood or demanding careers, carry costs and still add to a good life. Disability, she argues, is similar. It removes some goods and opens up others, including distinctive experiences, communities, and kinds of knowledge. Whether a particular person flourishes depends on the whole shape of their life, not on whether they have an impairment.

Much of the book answers objections. The strongest is adaptive preference. If disabled people say they are satisfied, perhaps they have simply lowered their expectations, as people in oppressive conditions often do. Barnes replies that this charge, applied only to disabled people, is a form of what she calls testimonial injustice, following Miranda Fricker. Nondisabled people's reports about their own lives are taken at face value, while disabled people's reports are explained away. She examines the research on well-being. She argues that the "disability paradox" is only a paradox if one assumes bad-difference in advance. That paradox is the finding that disabled people report a good quality of life despite outsiders' predictions.

A second objection concerns causing disability. If disability is merely a difference, is it acceptable to cause it, for example by choosing to have a deaf child? Barnes argues that the mere-difference view does not lead there. Causing an unconsented change to someone's body is wrong because it interferes with them, not because the resulting state is bad. The same reasoning explains why it would be wrong to make a disabled person nondisabled without consent. She also separates removing a disability from preventing one in a future person.

The final chapters take up disability pride and the role of testimony in philosophy. Barnes argues that pride movements are a rational response to stigma, not a form of denial. She closes by reflecting on how philosophy might change if it treated disabled people as knowers about their own condition rather than as cases to be assessed. The book is short and closely argued, and it is written so that nonspecialists can read it.
mainPoints: Philosophy has treated disability as an obvious harm, but that treatment rests on assumption rather than argument.
Barnes defines physical disability through solidarity: the bodily features the disability rights movement organizes around.
The key distinction is between bad-difference views (disability itself lowers well-being) and mere-difference views (it is a neutral feature with local costs and benefits).
Disability can be locally bad, through pain or exclusion, without being globally bad for a person's life as a whole.
Disabled people's testimony about their own well-being is routinely discounted, which Barnes treats as a form of testimonial injustice.
The adaptive preference objection, that disabled people have simply lowered their expectations, is applied selectively and is not supported by the evidence.
The "disability paradox" of good reported quality of life only looks like a paradox if one already assumes that disability is bad.
Holding that disability is a mere difference does not make it acceptable to cause disability in others without consent.
Disability pride is a reasonable response to stigma, like other minority pride movements.
The argument is limited to physical disability. Barnes does not claim it extends to cognitive or psychiatric conditions.
relevance: The book gives practitioners a rigorous basis for a claim they often make informally: that disability is a dimension of diversity rather than a deficit. Trainers can use the bad-difference/mere-difference distinction to bring hidden assumptions in a room to the surface. HR or policy staff can draw on the testimonial injustice argument when designing processes that take disabled employees' and clients' self-reports seriously, for example in accommodation reviews or program evaluation. Direct-service staff should note the stated limit to physical disability. Applying the argument to intellectual or psychiatric disability takes further work. The thesis is debated. Some philosophers and disabled writers argue that Barnes gives too little weight to suffering tied to impairment, or that her solidarity definition is circular. Others find her account the strongest one available. Present it as a position, not a settled consensus.
questions: Where in our policies or language do we assume that disability is a harm to be prevented, and would those assumptions survive Barnes's challenge?
When disabled clients or employees report satisfaction with their lives or choices, how does our organization respond? Do we ever explain their testimony away?
Barnes limits her claim to physical disability. Which of her arguments, if any, apply to the mental health and intellectual disability populations we serve?

title: Disabled Upon Arrival: Eugenics, Immigration, and the Construction of Race and Disability
editionNote: First published 2018 · Ohio State University Press · 190 pages
overview: Disabled Upon Arrival is a rhetorical history of how North American immigration control in the early twentieth century used disability to decide who could enter. Jay Dolmage is a disability studies scholar and professor of English at the University of Waterloo. He examines the inspection stations at Ellis Island and Canada's Pier 21, the eugenic science behind them, and the images and language that made exclusion seem natural. His core claim is that immigrants were not found to be disabled but were made disabled by the process. Disability served as a flexible code for racial undesirability, and the same logic lives on in border policy today.
summary: Dolmage frames the book around the idea of rhetorical space. These are physical places designed to produce particular arguments about the people who move through them. Ellis Island, he argues, was built to sort. Its stairways, lines, and inspection rooms forced arrivals to put their bodies on show for doctors. The doctors watched for limps, coughs, eye disease, and signs of "feeble-mindedness." Inspectors practiced what was called the snapshot diagnosis. They judged a person in seconds and marked suspected conditions in chalk on their clothing. Those marked were pulled aside for more examination and possible deportation. In Dolmage's reading, the station was a device for turning foreignness into defect.

The book follows the eugenics movement into this system. Dolmage traces how eugenic ideas about heredity, degeneracy, and national fitness gave immigration officials a scientific vocabulary. Laws in 1907 and 1917 widened the grounds for exclusion. The older bar on anyone "likely to become a public charge" let officials exclude people for poverty, appearance, or presumed mental deficiency. He argues that disability became the main way racial exclusion was carried out. Inspectors and lawmakers could not openly bar Southern and Eastern Europeans or Jews as races, but they could bar them as defectives. Race and disability were produced together, and each lent the other authority.

A chapter on visual rhetoric examines the photographs, charts, and reports used to document immigrants. Dolmage reads the eugenic photography of the period, including images that paired supposedly inferior faces with diagnostic labels. He shows how these images taught the public to see disability and racial inferiority as visible on the body. The same techniques, he notes, appear in intelligence testing and in photographs taken in asylums and schools for the "feeble-minded."

Dolmage also crosses the border to Pier 21 in Halifax, which operated from 1928 and is now a national museum. Canada's inspection system, he argues, drew on American eugenic practice and used similar medical exclusions. The chapter examines how the museum today celebrates Pier 21 as a welcoming gateway. Meanwhile, it leaves the history of deportation and medical rejection largely out of view. This becomes an argument about memory. Nations tell the story of immigration in ways that erase the bodies turned away.

The later chapters bring the argument into the present. Dolmage connects the history to current policies that screen migrants for health conditions, cost to public systems, and "inadmissibility." He also points to the continued use of disability as a reason to deny entry or residence in both countries. He argues that the rhetoric of the public charge, revived in recent U.S. policy debates, descends directly from the eugenic framework. Throughout, he insists that the point is not only historical. Ableism, he holds, is the underlying logic that makes racism, nativism, and other exclusions work. It supplies a standard that seems neutral, the normal body and mind, against which others can be measured.

The book ends with reflections on method and accessibility. Dolmage writes about the duty of scholars who work with archives of dehumanizing images. He chose to describe such images and explain their context rather than reproduce them uncritically. The book itself was produced with care for accessible design, in keeping with his broader work on accessible scholarship.
mainPoints: Immigration inspection stations such as Ellis Island were rhetorical spaces designed to produce judgments of defect, not neutral sites of medical screening.
The "snapshot diagnosis" and chalk-mark system turned quick visual impressions into official findings of disability.
Early twentieth-century immigration law, especially the public charge provision, gave officials broad freedom to exclude people on grounds of presumed disability.
Disability became the means of carrying out racial exclusion when open racial bars were politically harder to defend.
Eugenic science supplied the vocabulary and authority for these practices, linking heredity, race, and national fitness.
Photographs, charts, and government reports taught the public to read inferiority as visible on bodies and faces.
Canada's Pier 21 applied similar medical exclusions, and its current museum story largely leaves out the history of medical rejection.
Today's health-based inadmissibility rules and the revived public charge doctrine descend from the same framework.
Ableism is a basic logic that makes other forms of exclusion workable by supplying a norm of the fit body and mind.
Scholars and institutions handling eugenic archives are responsible for how dehumanizing images are reproduced and explained.
relevance: For agencies serving immigrants and refugees, the book directly shows how health, disability, and "burden" criteria have been used to exclude people. This can inform intake design, advocacy, and staff training on intersectionality. It is also a case study in how administrative tools that look neutral, from inspection checklists to cost thresholds, carry ideology. Policy analysts can apply that lesson to current eligibility rules. Trainers will find the Ellis Island material a vivid way to show race and disability as built together rather than as separate categories. Some cautions apply. The book is scholarly and rhetorical in method. It gives less attention to quantitative history or to immigrant voices than some readers will want. Its broad claim that ableism underlies all exclusion is a theoretical position that others in the field contest.
questions: Which of our eligibility, screening, or risk tools rely on judgments of "burden" or "capacity," and what histories might those criteria carry?
How do our public materials tell the story of who we serve? Whose exclusion is left out of that story?
Dolmage argues that race and disability are produced together. Where in our data or casework do we treat them as separate categories, and what is lost?

title: Ableism: The Causes and Consequences of Disability Prejudice
overview: Ableism is a research synthesis on disability prejudice written for students, researchers, and practitioners. Michelle Nario-Redmond is a social psychologist at Hiram College and a longtime member of the disability community. She brings the tools of prejudice research, long applied to race, gender, and sexuality, to bear on disability. Her core claim is that ableism is a distinct and measurable form of prejudice. It has identifiable origins, predictable stereotypes, and documented effects on disabled people. The interventions meant to reduce it can be tested rather than assumed to work. The book is part of Wiley's Contemporary Social Issues series.
summary: Nario-Redmond opens by defining ableism as prejudice and discrimination aimed at people because of disability. She explains why social psychology has neglected it. Disability, she notes, has usually been treated as a medical or rehabilitation topic, not as a group identity subject to bias between groups. She reviews how disability is defined and who counts. The group's boundary shifts and is open, since anyone can join it, and this sets it apart from other minority categories. The book also traces the roots of ableist ideas. These include evolutionary and existential explanations for why disability causes discomfort, and the ideologies and language used to justify exclusion.

The next section asks where ableism comes from. Nario-Redmond groups the explanations at several levels. Evolutionary and existential accounts hold that disability triggers responses meant to avoid disease. It also reminds observers of their own vulnerability and mortality, and terror management research suggests this leads people to keep their distance. Just-world beliefs lead people to assume disabled people somehow deserve their condition. Social and economic explanations stress how ableism helps justify unequal access to resources. She presents each account with its evidence and its limits rather than choosing one.

A core chapter examines stereotypes. Using the stereotype content model, Nario-Redmond shows that disabled people as a group are usually seen as warm but incompetent. This draws pity rather than respect or fear. She lists the common stereotypes: dependent, childlike, asexual, heroic, bitter, inspirational. Stereotypes vary by type of impairment. People with psychiatric disabilities, for instance, are more likely to be stereotyped as dangerous, and they meet avoidance and hostility rather than pity. The chapter on prejudice develops the distinction between hostile and benevolent ableism. Benevolent or paternalistic ableism shows up as unwanted help, condescension, and praise for ordinary activities. It is harder to recognize and resist than open hostility, and she argues it is the more common form.

Discrimination is treated at several levels. Nario-Redmond reviews evidence of discrimination between people in hiring, health care, education, and everyday life, including microaggressions. She also reviews institutional discrimination in law, policy, built environments, and media. She separates outcomes where disabled people are shut out from those where they are let in on paternalistic terms, such as sheltered employment or segregated classrooms.

A large part of the book takes the perspective of disabled people themselves. Drawing on social identity theory, Nario-Redmond examines how people respond to stigma. Some conceal their disability or distance themselves from other disabled people. Some cope on their own. Others develop a collective disability identity and become activists. She reviews research, including her own, on disability identity as a source of resilience and well-being. She also reviews how stereotype threat and internalized ableism undermine performance and health. The chapter is careful to note that not everyone identifies this way, and that many people with impairments do not consider themselves disabled.

The final chapters evaluate interventions. Nario-Redmond reviews education, contact, perspective-taking, and media campaigns, and she weighs each against the evidence. Her treatment of disability simulations is especially pointed. In these exercises, nondisabled people use a wheelchair or blindfold for a short time. Studies suggest they increase pity and anxiety rather than respect, because they mimic the moment of loss rather than the experience of living with disability. She recommends sustained contact on equal terms, programs led by disabled people, and structural changes over awareness exercises. The book closes with a call for more research that treats disabled people as a social group. It also calls for interventions to be evaluated with the same rigor applied to other forms of prejudice.
mainPoints: Ableism is a form of prejudice that can be studied with the same methods used for racism and sexism, and social psychology has neglected it.
Disability is an unusual group category because anyone can enter it, which shapes how nondisabled people react to it.
Ableism has several origins: disease avoidance and reminders of mortality, just-world beliefs, and the economic role of justifying inequality.
Disabled people are commonly stereotyped as warm but incompetent, which produces pity and paternalism rather than respect.
Stereotypes differ by impairment. People with psychiatric disabilities face stereotypes of danger and meet avoidance or hostility.
Benevolent ableism, shown through unwanted help and condescension, is more common and harder to challenge than hostile ableism.
Discrimination works between people, through microaggressions and biased decisions, and within institutions, through policy, design, and media.
Disabled people respond to stigma in varied ways. A collective disability identity is linked with resilience and activism.
Stereotype threat and internalized ableism can undermine performance and health.
Disability simulations tend to increase pity and anxiety and are not recommended. Sustained contact on equal terms and programs led by disabled people have better evidence.
relevance: This is the most directly usable book in this section for designing training, because it sorts interventions by evidence. HR and learning staff should take its findings on simulations seriously. They should rethink any "disability awareness day" exercises that rely on blindfolds or wheelchairs. The chapters on stereotypes and benevolent ableism give trainers concrete, research-based content on how paternalism shows up in workplaces and services. The identity chapter helps employee resource groups and peer programs understand why some employees embrace a disability identity while others avoid it. Program designers serving people with psychiatric disabilities should note their distinct stereotype profile. The book is long, dense, and academic in style, so most practitioners will use selected chapters rather than the whole.
questions: Which forms of benevolent ableism, such as unrequested help or praise for routine tasks, show up in our workplace or services, and how would we recognize them?
Does any of our current disability training rely on simulation exercises? What does the evidence Nario-Redmond reviews suggest we should do instead?
How do our programs support employees or clients who want to build a collective disability identity, and how do we respect those who do not?

title: Mad at School: Rhetorics of Mental Disability and Academic Life
editionNote: First published 2011 · University of Michigan Press · 279 pages
overview: Mad at School examines how American higher education treats people with mental disabilities. Margaret Price uses that term to cover psychiatric conditions, cognitive differences, and related experiences of madness. Price is a rhetoric and disability studies scholar who writes from her own experience of mental disability. She argues that academic life rests on an unspoken ideal of the able mind: rational, productive, present, and independent. Her core claim is that the ordinary practices and values of colleges, from classroom participation to hiring, are built around this ideal. As a result, they exclude, discipline, or make invisible those whose minds work differently.
summary: Price begins with language. She explains why she chose "mental disability" over "mental illness," "psychiatric disability," or "madness" alone. She wants a term broad enough to include people who identify as mad, mentally ill, neurodivergent, or simply as struggling. She also wants a term that signals a disability studies frame rather than a medical one. She notes that disability studies itself has tended to assume a disabled body with a nimble mind. Bringing the mind into the field means rethinking its core assumptions. A key borrowed concept is rhetoricity, the ability to be received as a reasonable speaker. Drawing on work by Catherine Prendergast, Price argues that being seen as mentally disabled means being denied rhetoricity. One's words are discounted in advance.

The first main chapter analyzes academic discourse through its key terms. Price examines how words such as participation, presence, productivity, collegiality, rationality, security, and independence are used in syllabi, tenure guidelines, and faculty handbooks. She shows that each one quietly measures people against an able-minded norm. A participation grade assumes a student who can speak in real time in a crowded room. Collegiality assumes an even temper. Productivity assumes steady output that depression or mania never interrupts. These terms are rarely defined, which makes them hard to challenge.

Price introduces the concept of kairotic space to describe the settings where these norms bite hardest. Kairotic spaces are less formal, real-time, in-person encounters with high stakes. Examples are classroom discussions, office hours, conference question periods, job interviews, and department meetings. They reward quick responses and social ease, and they offer few accommodations. That is because accommodation systems are built around formal, documented tasks like exams. Much of the book argues that these spaces, not lectures and papers, are where mental disability is most disabling.

A chapter on the classroom looks at syllabus language, attendance policies, and participation requirements. It proposes alternatives that keep rigor while widening who can succeed. These include several ways to participate, flexible attendance with clear expectations, and accessibility statements that invite rather than warn. Price draws on universal design for learning. But she is cautious about any approach that promises to remove the need for individual accommodation.

Price then turns to public rhetoric. She examines media coverage of the shootings at Virginia Tech in 2007 and Northern Illinois University in 2008. She shows how commentators looked back and cast the shooters as clearly mad, then called for campuses to identify and remove students like them. She argues that this link between mental disability and violence is not supported by the facts, and that it has real effects. It drives surveillance, mandatory leave policies, and a climate in which students hide their conditions rather than seek help.

Later chapters consider faculty and those hoping to become faculty. Price analyzes the academic job search as a kairotic gauntlet. She discusses the position of independent scholars, people who work outside institutional appointments, some of them because mental disability made the tenure track unworkable. She includes interview material and her own story. She also takes up the question of disclosure: when, whether, and to whom a mentally disabled academic should reveal their condition, given the cost of being denied rhetoricity.

The book ends with a call for an academic culture that treats access as a shared responsibility. Price offers practical suggestions, from how meetings are designed to how crises are handled. But her central recommendation is reflective. Institutions should examine the values built into their routine language and ask whom those values exclude.
mainPoints: Academic culture is organized around an unstated ideal of the able mind, and its routine practices measure everyone against it.
"Mental disability" is a deliberately broad term that brings madness, psychiatric conditions, and cognitive difference into disability studies.
Rhetoricity, the standing to be heard as reasonable, is routinely denied to people seen as mentally disabled.
Terms such as participation, presence, productivity, collegiality, and independence carry hidden assumptions and are rarely defined.
Kairotic spaces, meaning high-stakes, real-time, informal encounters, are where mental disability is most disabling and least accommodated.
Accommodation systems built around documented formal tasks miss the spaces that matter most.
Classrooms can widen access through several ways to participate and flexible, clearly stated policies without lowering standards.
Media coverage of campus shootings built a link between mental disability and violence that drives surveillance and concealment.
Faculty with mental disabilities face the same barriers in hiring, meetings, and tenure review, and disclosure carries serious risk.
Access to intellectual life should be treated as a shared responsibility rather than an individual request.
relevance: Although set in higher education, the book carries over directly to any workplace or service setting that values quick thinking, presence in meetings, and "fit." HR and management staff can use the analysis of kairotic spaces to review interviews, performance reviews, and team meetings. These often hold barriers that formal accommodation processes never reach. Trainers will find the chapter on key terms a ready-made exercise. They can ask a team to define "professionalism" or "collegiality" and then examine who is excluded. Program and policy staff in behavioral health or education should weigh Price's critique of threat-assessment and mandatory-leave practices. The book is theoretical and rhetorical in method, with limited empirical data. Some readers find that its broad definition of mental disability blurs distinctions that clinicians and service designers need to keep.
questions: Which of our evaluation criteria, such as "communicates well" or "works independently," assume an able mind, and how could they be defined more inclusively?
Where are our kairotic spaces, the high-stakes, real-time encounters that our accommodation process does not cover?
How do our crisis and safety policies affect whether employees or clients feel able to disclose a mental disability?

title: Black Disability Politics
overview: Black Disability Politics argues that Black activists in the United States have been doing disability politics for decades. But they have done it in forms that mainstream disability rights frameworks, which are mostly white, have failed to recognize. Sami Schalk is a professor of gender and women's studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who writes as a Black disabled scholar. She draws on archival research into the Black Panther Party and the National Black Women's Health Project. She also draws on interviews with Black disabled cultural workers today. Her core claim is that Black disability politics has its own distinct shape. It centers race, it is rooted in health and anti-violence work, and it often happens without the word "disability" appearing at all.
summary: Schalk opens by setting out the problem. Disability studies and disability rights groups have long been criticized for their whiteness. Black freedom movements, in turn, have often been read as ignoring disability or even as ableist. Schalk argues that both readings miss what was actually happening. Suppose one looks for disability politics only where people claim a disability identity and use the language of rights. Then one will not find Black disability politics, because it has usually been expressed through health, policing, poverty, and survival. She therefore proposes a method: read the archives of Black movements for how they engaged disability on their own terms.

From the archive she draws four qualities that define Black disability politics. First, it is intersectional but centered on race. It treats disability as bound up with anti-Black racism rather than as a stand-alone identity. Second, it is not necessarily grounded in disability identity. Participants may address disabling conditions without calling themselves disabled. Third, it is set in context and history. It pays attention to how slavery, medical experimentation, policing, and environmental harm produce disability in Black communities. Fourth, it is holistic. It approaches mind, body, and community together rather than isolating impairment. Schalk uses the term bodymind, borrowed from disability studies, to capture this refusal to separate physical and mental experience.

The first two chapters examine the Black Panther Party in the 1970s, using the party's newspaper. Schalk shows that the Panthers covered disability regularly. They supported the 1977 Section 504 sit-in in San Francisco with food and logistics and reported on it at length. They also linked accessibility to their broader survival programs. A shorter section treats the party's Oakland Community School as an often overlooked part of the same politics. The second chapter traces the party's long critique of psychiatric institutions, psychosurgery, forced medication, and medical experiments on Black prisoners and patients. Schalk reads this work as disability politics, even though the Panthers framed it as resistance to state violence and the medical-industrial complex. She introduces the idea of disabling violence to name how policing, incarceration, and medical abuse create disability.

Chapters three and four turn to the National Black Women's Health Project, a Black feminist health organization founded in the early 1980s. The project was not a disability rights group. Yet its self-help model and its focus on hypertension, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, substance use, and stress added up to a disability politics of chronic illness and well-being. Schalk highlights its HIV/AIDS work. It shows that health activism aimed at preventing conditions that can be disabling can still be anti-ableist. The project's holistic approach, she argues, anticipated the principles that the disability justice movement later put into words.

Between the archival chapters, Schalk places two "praxis interludes" addressed to organizers today. The first takes up language. It critiques how the Panthers' campaign against psychiatric abuse sometimes relied on ableist language and tropes. It then offers other ways to talk about and fight disabling violence. The second critiques the National Black Women's Health Project for mostly avoiding disability identity. It considers how Black movements can engage disability identity more openly. This interlude draws on her interviews with eleven Black disabled cultural workers about what inclusion would require.

The final chapter examines current activism, especially the Movement for Black Lives. Schalk analyzes its early platform statements. She finds disability largely missing, even though disability plays a central role in police killings. She recounts how Black disabled activists formed the Harriet Tubman Collective to demand inclusion. She argues that politics centered on race must not become a reason to put disability off. The book closes with a reflective "(Not a) Conclusion." Schalk wrote it during the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 uprisings, in which she took part as an organizer. The book was published open access.
mainPoints: Black activists have engaged disability for decades, but mainly through health, policing, and survival rather than disability identity or the language of rights.
Black disability politics has four qualities: intersectional but centered on race, not necessarily based on identity, set in historical context, and holistic.
The concept of bodymind captures a refusal to separate physical and mental experience that runs through Black health activism.
The Black Panther Party supported the 1977 Section 504 sit-in and treated accessibility as part of community survival.
The Panthers' critique of psychiatric abuse, psychosurgery, and medical experimentation was disability politics framed as resistance to state violence.
Disabling violence names how policing, incarceration, and medical harm produce disability in Black communities.
The National Black Women's Health Project's holistic self-help model was a disability politics of chronic illness, though it was never labeled that way.
Black activism against disabling violence has sometimes relied on ableist language and tropes. Anti-ableist alternatives can make the same case.
Black movements also gain from engaging disability identity openly, as the Harriet Tubman Collective's response to the Movement for Black Lives shows.
Disability justice principles have roots in Black feminist and Black radical organizing.
relevance: Schalk's book is useful for practitioners who find that disability programs reach few Black participants, or that racial equity programs do not name disability. Her four qualities offer a diagnostic tool. A health, violence-prevention, or reentry program may already be doing disability work that could be recognized and funded as such. Program designers can use the holistic model of the National Black Women's Health Project when designing chronic-illness and wellness services. HR and training staff can draw on the praxis interludes for anti-ableist ways to frame racial justice messages and to discuss disability identity. The book is an academic monograph grounded in archives and theory. It offers analysis rather than step-by-step guidance.
questions: Which of our programs address disabling conditions in Black communities without naming disability, and what would change if we recognized them as disability work?
How do our disability services and our racial equity efforts relate now? Do they share data, staff, or community partners?
Schalk critiques ableist language in some Black activism while still counting that work as disability politics. How do we handle disagreements about language across the communities we serve?

title: Deaf in America: Voices from a Culture
editionNote: First published 1988 · Harvard University Press · 134 pages
overview: Deaf in America is a short, influential account of Deaf people in the United States as a cultural and linguistic community, not a population defined by hearing loss. Carol Padden and Tom Humphries are both Deaf scholars who grew up in different circumstances: Padden in a Deaf family, Humphries in a hearing one. They write from inside the culture they describe. Their core claim is that Deaf people share a language, American Sign Language, along with a history, a set of stories and values, and a way of seeing the world. Understanding Deaf life means starting from that center rather than from the absence of sound.
summary: The authors begin with a distinction that the book did much to spread. "Deaf" with a lowercase d refers to the audiological condition of not hearing. "Deaf" with a capital D refers to membership in a cultural group that uses ASL and shares its traditions. The two overlap but are not the same: some people with profound hearing loss never join Deaf culture, and some hearing children of Deaf parents are raised within it. Padden and Humphries argue that most writing about deaf people has looked at the condition and ignored the culture, and they set out to correct the balance.

An early chapter, on learning to be Deaf, looks at how children enter the culture. Deaf children of Deaf parents learn ASL as a native language and learn the community's ways from the start. Deaf children of hearing parents, the large majority, often meet the language and culture only at residential schools, from peers and Deaf adults. The authors use childhood memories to show how Deaf children make sense of the hearing world. One story describes a Deaf child who assumed a hearing neighbor had something wrong with her because she could not sign. The point is that from within the culture, hearing is the unfamiliar condition.

The chapter on a different center develops this idea through language. In ASL, someone described as A-LITTLE HARD-OF-HEARING is only slightly different from Deaf, while in English "a little hard of hearing" means someone close to hearing. The same words sit at different points because the reference point differs. Deaf culture measures from Deafness as the norm. The authors use this and similar examples to argue that Deaf people are not simply hearing people minus hearing. They have a different orientation to the world, built around vision and sign.

Later chapters turn to the community's expressive life. Padden and Humphries describe the folklore, jokes, stories, and poetry of ASL, including stories passed down in residential schools and performed at Deaf clubs. They draw on accounts of old home movies and discuss how ASL art forms make use of the language's grammar: its use of space, rhythm, and facial expression. They also consider what sound means in Deaf life, as understood through vibration, hearing people's reactions, and cultural stories.

A historical chapter traces the suppression of sign language. In the late nineteenth century, oralist educators, encouraged by the 1880 Milan congress, pushed to ban signing in schools and to teach speech and lipreading instead. Deaf teachers were dismissed, and generations of Deaf children were taught by a method many found inaccessible. The authors show how the community kept ASL alive informally. Linguistic research from the 1960s onward then established ASL as a full language, and that recognition fed a changing sense among Deaf people of their own worth. The book's final chapter, on historically created lives, argues that Deaf culture is not a natural response to hearing loss. It is a historical achievement, made and remade by people over generations.

Throughout, the tone is descriptive rather than combative. Padden and Humphries do not argue against medical treatment or technology; instead, they ask that Deaf people's own understanding of their lives be taken as the starting point. The book appeared in the same year as the Deaf President Now protest at Gallaudet University and is often read alongside it.
mainPoints: "Deaf" (cultural identity, ASL users sharing a community) and "deaf" (audiological condition) are distinct, and the book made that distinction widely known.
Deaf culture has its own language, history, folklore, values, and institutions, and it should be studied as a culture rather than as a disability.
Most Deaf children have hearing parents and enter the culture through schools and peers, which makes residential schools central to passing on the culture.
From within the culture, Deafness is the reference point and hearing is the unfamiliar condition, as ASL vocabulary itself shows.
ASL is a full language whose grammar uses space, movement, and facial expression, and it supports literature, humor, and poetry.
Sound has cultural meaning in Deaf life even though it is not heard in the usual way.
Oralist education policies from the 1880s onward suppressed sign language and removed Deaf teachers, with lasting effects.
The community kept ASL alive informally, and later linguistic recognition of the language transformed how Deaf people understood themselves.
Deaf culture is a historical creation, built by Deaf people over time, not an inevitable result of hearing loss.
Respect for Deaf people begins with taking their own account of their lives as the starting point.
relevance: For practitioners, the book explains why many Deaf people reject being grouped under "disability." It also explains why language access, meaning qualified ASL interpreters and Deaf staff, is a cultural and civil rights matter and not only an accommodation. HR, training, and direct-service staff can use the different-center idea to ask whether their programs treat Deaf clients as hearing people with a deficit. Policy staff working on early intervention, education, or health care should note the history of oralism. They should also note the community's sensitivity to decisions made for Deaf children by hearing professionals. The book is from 1988 and predates the wide use of cochlear implants, and it focuses on the ASL-using community and says little about late-deafened or hard-of-hearing people who do not identify as Deaf. The authors' later book, Inside Deaf Culture, updates some of this.
questions: Do our intake forms, communications, and services treat Deaf people as a cultural and linguistic group or only as people with a hearing impairment, and what follows from each?
How do we make sure Deaf people, not only hearing professionals, shape decisions about services for Deaf children and adults?
Where might the "different center" idea apply to other communities we serve whose norms are measured against a majority standard?

title: Cultural Intelligence: Surviving and Thriving in the Global Village
authors: David C. Thomas and Kerr Inkson
overview: Cultural Intelligence is a practical guide to working well with people from other cultures. Its authors are David C. Thomas, a professor of international management, and Kerr Inkson, a scholar of careers and organizational behavior. The 2017 edition, subtitled Surviving and Thriving in the Global Village, is the third version of a book first published in 2004 as Cultural Intelligence: People Skills for Global Business. Its core claim is that no one can learn the customs of every culture. But anyone can develop a general capability, cultural intelligence, that carries across settings. It is built from knowledge, mindfulness, and skills for adapting.
summary: Thomas and Inkson open by describing the global village. In workplaces, cities, and supply chains, people of different cultural backgrounds interact all the time, often without seeing how much culture shapes their behavior. The authors show the costs of getting this wrong with short cases of misunderstanding in negotiation, management, and everyday work. The usual responses, they argue, fall short. Learning lists of do's and don'ts for particular countries is fragile and encourages stereotyping. Relying on good intentions and common sense fails because common sense is itself cultural.

The book's answer is cultural intelligence, which the authors define as the capability to interact effectively with people from different cultural backgrounds. Their model has three parts. Knowledge means understanding what culture is, how it varies, and how it affects behavior. Mindfulness means paying attention, in the moment, to cues from the situation and from one's own assumptions, rather than acting on autopilot. Behavioral skills mean having a range of actions and the ability to choose among them. That way one can adapt without giving up one's own identity. Cultural intelligence, they stress, is learned through experience and reflection. It grows through recognizable stages, from reacting out of one's own norms toward adjusting ahead of time.

A chapter on knowledge explains culture as shared patterns of values, assumptions, and practices. These patterns are learned, lie mostly below awareness, and shape what seems normal. Drawing on the cross-cultural research tradition of Geert Hofstede and others, the authors describe dimensions along which cultures vary. These include individualism versus collectivism, how far people accept unequal power, tolerance for uncertainty, views of time, and how much weight goes to achievement versus relationships. The authors present these as tendencies to be held lightly. Individuals vary within any culture, they note, and the dimensions describe averages, not persons.

The mindfulness chapter is the heart of the book's method. The authors describe practices for noticing one's own cultural reactions, holding off judgment, watching others' behavior for its deeper meaning, and checking interpretations before acting. They link mindfulness to the ability to see when a familiar script is not working. The same chapter then discusses how to build a wider range of behavior. This means trying new behaviors, asking for feedback, and learning from mistakes.

The remaining chapters apply the model to common work situations. The chapter on decision making examines how cultures differ in who decides, how much information is sought, and how risk is treated. The chapter on communication and negotiation covers direct and indirect styles, the role of silence, face, and the different meanings of agreement. The leadership chapter considers how expectations of leaders vary and why a style that works in one setting may fail in another. A chapter on multicultural teams discusses the extra friction such teams face. It also covers the conditions under which their diversity produces better results.

The authors discuss developing cultural understanding through exposure, reflection, mentoring and training. Their three-part approach differs from other published assessment models; the book also includes the authors' short-form assessment.
mainPoints: Culture shapes most people's behavior in ways they do not notice, and cross-cultural interaction is now routine in most workplaces.
Lists of customs for each country are fragile and promote stereotyping. A general capability is more useful.
Cultural intelligence is the capability to interact effectively across cultures. It is built from knowledge, mindfulness, and behavioral skill.
Knowledge includes understanding what culture is and the dimensions along which cultures tend to differ, held as tendencies rather than rules.
Mindfulness, meaning attention to one's own assumptions and to cues in the situation, is what turns knowledge into fitting action.
Behavioral skill means having a range of options and choosing among them without losing one's own identity.
Decision making, communication, negotiation, and leadership all vary by culture in predictable ways.
Multicultural teams face more friction but can outperform teams that are all alike when they are well managed.
Cultural intelligence develops in stages through experience, reflection, and feedback, and it can be built on purpose.
The authors' three-part approach is distinct from the separate four-factor model developed by Earley and Ang.
relevance: The book offers one perspective on intercultural practice for staff who serve diverse communities or work in diverse teams. Its emphasis on reflection can complement cultural humility. Its business-oriented examples and focus on national culture may overlook differences of race, class, religion and power within countries; consider them alongside accessibility, structural inequity and the experiences of people affected.
questions: Which of our interactions with the communities we serve run on cultural autopilot, and what would it take to bring mindfulness to them?
How can we teach cultural tendencies, such as differing expectations of authority or directness, without encouraging staff to stereotype?
Cultural intelligence focuses on individual skill. Where in our organization do structural barriers matter more than skill between individuals?

title: The Cultural Intelligence Difference: Master the One Skill You Can't Do Without in Today's Global Economy
editionNote: First published 2011 · AMACOM, American Management Association · 207 pages
overview: The Cultural Intelligence Difference is a practical guide by David Livermore to working across cultural differences. It presents one author's development model for managers, educators and service professionals. The wider program brings together multiple disciplines and perspectives.
summary: The author distinguishes his approach from general cultural awareness and discusses engaging with difference, learning, planning and adapting. The book was written for a general audience and includes a self-assessment; participation in this program does not require taking it or sharing results.

The author presents four linked areas: motivation, understanding cultural and social contexts, planning and reflection, and adapting behavior. They are one model among many, not the definition of this program.

The author discusses research on cross-cultural work and organizational outcomes. Interpret these claims in their research context; associations do not establish that training causes improvements, and individual assessments should not be used for hiring, ranking or performance decisions.

The book then offers ways to grow, several for each capability. For Drive, he suggests being honest about one's own biases and fears, linking intercultural work to personal goals, and seeking rewards that keep effort going. For Knowledge, he recommends learning a few core value dimensions deeply rather than memorizing lists of country facts. He also suggests studying how one's own culture looks from outside, and learning something of another language. For Strategy, he proposes planning encounters ahead of time, building in pauses, and asking better questions. For Action, he describes widening one's range of behaviors, adjusting how fast and how expressively one speaks, and practicing in low-risk settings before high-stakes ones. Each strategy is short and practical.

The author discusses the risk that generalizations can harden into stereotypes and describes how his approach can apply within a country as well as across national borders. This program uses community information to generate better questions, never to predict an individual's beliefs or needs.

The author describes development as ongoing and discusses reflection, feedback and motivation, drawing on stories from consulting and leadership. Readers can compare these ideas with other approaches and the experience of people affected.
mainPoints: The author describes working effectively across cultural differences as a capability that can be developed.
The book presents four related areas: motivation, understanding, planning and adapting.
The book discusses studies on intercultural work; interpret their findings and limitations in context.
The author argues that experience can be more useful when paired with reflection.
Learning a handful of cultural value dimensions well is more useful than memorizing etiquette country by country.
Generalizations about cultures should be held as starting guesses and revised in light of the individual.
Motivation is often what holds people back. Honestly admitting discomfort and bias is a first step.
Behavioral flexibility means adjusting how one speaks and acts without pretending to be someone else.
The book discusses differences within a country as well as across national borders.
Growth comes step by step and benefits from feedback, practice in low-risk settings, and clear personal goals.
relevance: This book is one practitioner perspective, written mainly for business and management. Public-service readers can compare its ideas with person-centered practice, accessibility, community knowledge and structural inequity. Do not use assessments or scores for hiring, ratings or promotion.
questions: What assumptions in a team practice are worth examining, and whose perspectives should inform a change?
How can an organization encourage generalizations as starting guesses without letting them become stereotypes in practice?
What might an individual-skills framework overlook in encounters shaped by unequal power or institutional barriers?

title: The Culture Map: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business
overview: The Culture Map is a field guide to how national cultures shape behavior at work. Its author, Erin Meyer, is a professor at the INSEAD business school who teaches executives from many countries. Meyer draws on her classroom, her consulting, and the comparative research of Edward Hall, Geert Hofstede, and Fons Trompenaars. From these she builds eight scales on which cultures can be plotted and compared. Her central claim is that most cross-cultural friction does not come from where a culture sits in absolute terms. It comes from where two cultures sit relative to each other.
summary: Meyer begins with stories of capable professionals who failed abroad because they assumed their own norms were universal. Her point is that these are not personality clashes. They are predictable collisions of cultural defaults. To make the defaults visible, she lays out a map with eight dimensions. Each is a continuum, with countries placed along it based on her research and that of earlier scholars.

The first scale, Communicating, runs from low-context to high-context, a distinction borrowed from Edward Hall. Low-context cultures such as the United States and Germany prize clear, literal messages. High-context cultures such as Japan and many Arab societies rely on shared background, implication, and reading between the lines. Meyer notes that multicultural teams generally work best when they default to low-context practices, since members cannot assume a common store of unspoken meaning. The second scale, Evaluating, concerns negative feedback. Some cultures deliver criticism directly and with strengthening words, while others wrap it in qualifiers. She warns that a culture can be low-context in communication yet indirect in evaluation, like the United States. Or it can be high-context yet direct in criticism, like France. This upsets simple assumptions.

Persuading contrasts two kinds of reasoning. Principles-first reasoning starts from theory and moves to application. Applications-first reasoning leads with examples and conclusions. She describes how a German or French audience may distrust a presentation that skips the conceptual grounding, while Americans grow impatient waiting for the point. Meyer adds that many Asian cultures use holistic thinking that does not fit neatly at either end. The fourth scale, Leading, runs from egalitarian to hierarchical. It covers how much distance is expected between boss and subordinate, who may speak to whom, and how status is signaled. The fifth, Deciding, asks whether decisions are made by consensus or from the top. She observes that this does not track leadership style. Japan is hierarchical but consensual, while the United States is egalitarian but top-down.

The Trusting scale separates task-based trust, built through reliable work, from relationship-based trust, built through shared meals and time. Meyer uses a memorable contrast between a peach and a coconut. The peach is soft outside with a hard core, and the coconut is hard outside with a soft center. The contrast describes how friendliness and real closeness are signaled differently. The seventh scale, Disagreeing, separates cultures that see open argument as healthy from those that see it as harmful to relationships. The eighth, Scheduling, runs from linear-time cultures, which value punctuality and sequence, to flexible-time cultures. The latter treat plans as adaptable and interruptions as normal.

A recurring theme is relativity. A Spaniard looks relationship-oriented to a German but task-oriented to a Saudi. The same person can be the blunt one in one room and the diplomatic one in another. Meyer advises leaders to map their own position and the positions of the people they work with. Then they should look at the gaps rather than the absolute placements. She also stresses cultural self-awareness as the first step, since one's own norms are usually invisible until set against others.

Throughout, Meyer offers practical tactics. These include explaining one's communication style openly, agreeing on team norms at the start, sending a low-context recap after meetings, adjusting how feedback is framed, and being open about how decisions get made. She closes by granting that individuals vary and that organizational, regional, and generational cultures also matter. Still, she holds that national patterns remain a useful starting point for anyone leading across borders.
mainPoints: Cross-cultural misunderstandings at work follow predictable patterns that can be mapped on eight dimensions.
The eight scales are Communicating, Evaluating, Persuading, Leading, Deciding, Trusting, Disagreeing, and Scheduling.
What matters is relative position: the gap between two cultures on a scale, not where either one sits in absolute terms.
Low-context versus high-context communication explains much confusion about what was "said" versus what was meant.
Directness in communication and directness in negative feedback are separate traits. A culture can be high on one and low on the other.
Hierarchy in leadership and top-down decision-making do not always go together.
Some cultures build trust through proven competence, and others through personal relationships.
Multicultural teams usually work best when they adopt clear, low-context practices and agree on norms up front.
Cultural self-awareness comes before understanding others. One's own defaults stay invisible until set against others.
National patterns are a starting guess, not a verdict on any individual.
relevance: The eight scales give trainers and managers a compact, nonjudgmental language for discussing communication, feedback, and decision norms in diverse teams. They adapt easily to workshops on team charters and feedback practices. Public-sector staff serving immigrant and refugee communities may find the Trusting and Communicating scales directly useful in service design. Some cautions apply. The book addresses national culture and business settings, not race, class, gender, or the experience of minorities within a country. It treats countries as fairly uniform units. Critics argue that the placements on the scales rest partly on anecdote, and that the approach can reinforce stereotypes if used carelessly. It works best paired with material on power, identity, and structural inequity.
questions: Where would you place your own organization's dominant culture on the Evaluating and Disagreeing scales, and who in your workplace is likely to find that placement uncomfortable?
How might the difference between task-based and relationship-based trust change how a public agency builds credibility with a community it has long underserved?
What are the risks of applying country-level maps to individuals, and what practices can keep the scales from becoming stereotypes?

title: Cultures and Organizations: Software of the Mind
authors: Geert Hofstede (later editions with Gert Jan Hofstede and Michael Minkov)
editionNote: First published 1991 · McGraw-Hill · 279 pages (available to borrow)
overview: Cultures and Organizations presents the best-known quantitative model of national culture. Its author, Geert Hofstede, was a Dutch social psychologist. In the late 1960s and early 1970s he analyzed employee attitude surveys collected inside IBM across dozens of countries. The book was revised in 2005 with his son Gert Jan Hofstede, and in 2010 with both Gert Jan Hofstede and the researcher Michael Minkov. It argues that people carry "mental programs" learned in childhood that shape their values, and that these programs cluster in national patterns that can be measured. Its core claim is that cultural differences are real, systematic, and important for how organizations, schools, families, and states function.
summary: Hofstede opens with the metaphor in the subtitle. Culture is software of the mind: a set of learned patterns of thinking, feeling, and acting that set one group apart from another. He separates culture from human nature, which is universal, and from personality, which is individual. Culture sits in the middle layer. He then describes culture as an onion. Symbols sit on the outside, followed by heroes and rituals, and together these make up visible practices. Values form the hidden core. They are learned early in life, which is why they change slowly. In his account, national culture is mainly about values, while organizational culture is mainly about practices.

The research base is the IBM study. Employees at one company in many countries were alike in most ways except nationality. So differences in their answers could be traced to national culture. Factor analysis of the answers produced four dimensions, each given a chapter. Power distance is how far the less powerful members of a society accept that power is shared unequally. Individualism versus collectivism concerns whether people see themselves mainly as individuals or as members of in-groups to which they owe loyalty. Masculinity versus femininity is the most debated label. It contrasts societies that stress achievement, assertiveness, and material reward with those that stress care, quality of life, and modesty. Uncertainty avoidance is how threatened a society feels by ambiguity, and how much it builds rules, rituals, and beliefs to cope.

Each dimension chapter follows a similar structure. Hofstede reports country scores and explains where the dimension came from statistically. Then he traces what it means for the family, the school, the workplace, the state, and religion or ideas. In high power distance societies, for example, children are expected to obey, and teachers are treated as gurus. Subordinates expect to be told what to do, and political systems lean toward central control. In societies with strong uncertainty avoidance, there are more laws, showing emotion is accepted, and people prefer specialist careers. He also offers tentative explanations for why countries ended up where they did, pointing to history, climate, and economics.

Two more dimensions came from later research. Long-term versus short-term orientation was already part of the 1991 edition. It came from a survey designed by Chinese scholars. It contrasts a focus on perseverance, thrift, and adapting with respect for tradition and quick results. Indulgence versus restraint was developed with Minkov from World Values Survey data. It contrasts societies that allow fairly free satisfaction of basic desires with those that control it through strict norms. A chapter on organizational culture reports a separate study of Dutch and Danish organizations. That study found six dimensions of practice, such as a focus on process versus results and on employees versus the job.

The closing chapters apply the model to encounters across cultures. Hofstede argues that ethnocentrism is the default. Stereotypes arise when people meet without understanding. Intercultural competence requires awareness, knowledge, and skills, in that order. He discusses how expatriates adjust, international negotiation, and the limits of carrying management theories from the United States to other settings. He is critical of the assumption that theories of motivation and leadership developed in one culture apply everywhere.

Hofstede states plainly that national scores describe averages and do not predict individuals. He also grants that nations are imperfect units that contain regional and ethnic variation. But he defends them as the units for which comparable data exist. The book ends by asking whether cultures grow more alike over time. He concludes that practices change faster than values and that deep differences remain.
mainPoints: Culture is learned mental programming that a group shares and that people acquire early. It is distinct from human nature and from individual personality.
Culture has visible layers (symbols, heroes, rituals) and a hidden core of values. Practices change faster than values.
The IBM data produced four dimensions of national culture: power distance, individualism/collectivism, masculinity/femininity, and uncertainty avoidance.
Later research added long-term/short-term orientation and indulgence/restraint.
Each dimension plays out in the same way across family, school, workplace, and politics within a society.
Organizational culture is mostly about shared practices rather than shared values, so it is easier to change.
Theories of management and motivation carry the cultural assumptions of the country where they were developed.
Country scores describe tendencies, not individuals. Using them to predict a person is the error the book warns against.
Intercultural competence moves from awareness to knowledge to skill.
Nations are an imperfect but practical unit of comparison, and regional and ethnic subcultures also matter.
relevance: The dimensions remain a standard vocabulary in diversity training, global HR, and policy work. The book is the main source behind many later tools, so practitioners gain from reading it directly rather than secondhand. Its analysis of how power distance and uncertainty avoidance shape expectations of authority and rules helps in designing services and workplaces for people from many backgrounds. The cautions are serious and widely discussed. Critics such as Brendan McSweeney argue that a survey of one company from decades ago cannot represent whole nations. They say the model treats cultures as fixed and uniform, and that the masculinity/femininity label is dated. Many DEIA practitioners also note that the framework says little about unequal power between groups within a country. It should add to equity-focused analysis, not replace it.
questions: How do differences in power distance show up in your organization between staff and the public you serve, and what does that mean for how you design feedback channels?
Hofstede claims that management theories carry the culture they came from. Which practices in your agency rest on assumptions that may not hold for all staff or clients?
What safeguards would you put around using national culture scores in training so they spark curiosity rather than stereotypes?
