The Khmer Rouge years, the Thai border camps and American resettlement form one connected story.
Policy and agency decisions shaped where families landed and what support they found.
Economic struggle became the main daily battle for many families after arrival.
Trauma, health and poverty were deeply intertwined in survivors' lives.
Gender roles and parent-child relationships changed under the pressures of a new country.
Discrimination and poverty were conditions people faced, not traits of the community.
Listening to both community leaders and public officials gives a fuller picture of resettlement.
relevance: Many Cambodian Minnesotans and their families carry the history Chan describes, and some first met public systems through the resettlement era she documents. Reading Survivors can help DSD staff understand why trust in agencies may be cautious and why paperwork and eligibility rules can feel heavy. It also shows why an older adult's disability or health needs may be bound up with a history the person may or may not wish to discuss. The book supports trauma-informed practice, careful interpreter planning, and partnership with Cambodian community organizations. It is a national study, not a Minnesota one. It was also written in the early 2000s, so it says less about today's children and grandchildren of survivors. Use it to ask better questions, never to assume a person's story.
questions: How might the resettlement experiences Chan describes shape how a Cambodian elder or family responds to our eligibility and assessment processes today?
Where in our work could we listen more closely to both community leaders and the frontline staff who serve Cambodian families?
What would trauma-informed practice look like in a first meeting with a Cambodian household, without asking anyone to retell their history?

title: Lucky Child: A Daughter of Cambodia Reunites with the Sister She Left Behind
overview: Loung Ung is a Cambodian American writer and activist who came to the United States in 1980 at the age of ten, after surviving the Khmer Rouge years she described in her first memoir, First They Killed My Father. Lucky Child is her second memoir and covers roughly 1980 to 2003. It alternates between two lives: Loung's own, growing up in Vermont with her eldest brother and his wife, and that of her older sister Chou, who stayed behind in rural Cambodia. The book asks what it means to be the one who left, and what was carried by the one who stayed.
summary: The book begins with separation. Eldest Brother chose Loung, the youngest and scrappiest, to travel with him to America, believing she had the best chance of making it. Loung and Chou, two years apart, had grown close after the deaths of their parents and sisters, and as the extended family gathered to say goodbye, neither imagined that fifteen years would pass before they met again. This decision, and the guilt and longing it left behind, shapes everything that follows in the memoir.

Loung's chapters, written in the first person, describe arriving in Vermont through a church sponsorship and learning a culture of peace while her memories remained shaped by war. She learns the everyday references her classmates take for granted and slowly unlearns survival habits, such as hiding food in her bed and flinching at holiday fireworks. Reviewers found these American chapters especially vivid, full of the small moments of a child trying to belong in a school and town that knew little about where she had come from.

Chou's chapters, written in the third person, follow her life in rural Cambodia as the Khmer Rouge continued to attack villages and Vietnamese troops fought them. Loung built these chapters from recorded conversations with her sister, translated into English. They show the ordinary work of rebuilding a household and family while violence and poverty continued, and some reviewers found this strand even more powerful than Loung's own. Set side by side, the two stories make readers feel the weight of chance and circumstance in each sister's life.

Neither life is presented as simply better. One sister gains schooling, safety and opportunity while carrying memory and distance; the other builds a life with fewer choices but deep ties to place and family. The memoir closes with Loung's return to Cambodia and her reunion with Chou and the family, a journey Ung has since made many times as an activist. The ending does not erase loss, but it shows how a refugee's story is often a family story spread across two countries.
mainPoints: Resettlement often begins with a family decision about who goes and who stays.
A child refugee may carry survival habits and memories long after reaching safety.
Belonging in a new country is built through many small, everyday adjustments.
Those who stay behind live their own full and difficult histories, not just a missing chapter.
Guilt and longing can follow the person who left for many years.
Refugee families often stretch across two countries and remain connected across distance.
Chance and circumstance, not merit, shaped which sibling gained which opportunities.
relevance: Lucky Child gives DSD staff a personal voice to set beside the history in Survivors. It helps explain why a Cambodian Minnesotan's family obligations, decisions and grief may reach across an ocean, and why a person who seems settled here may still be carrying responsibility for relatives in Cambodia. The book can deepen empathy for children who arrived young and grew up translating a new culture for themselves and others. It is one woman's story, set in Vermont rather than Minnesota, and it reflects the experience of a family that came early in the refugee era. Treat it as one voice among many, and let it prompt open questions about family, faith and home rather than assumptions about any person you serve.
questions: How might family ties across borders affect a person's choices about services, caregiving or living arrangements?
What did Loung need from her school and town to feel she belonged, and what parallels exist in our own service settings?
How can we make room for a person's history without asking them to explain or relive it?

title: Chinese in Minnesota
editionNote: First published 2004 · Minnesota Historical Society Press
overview: Chinese in Minnesota is part of the Minnesota Historical Society Press People of Minnesota series. Its author, Sherri Gebert Fuller, worked at the Minnesota Historical Society and co-curated its exhibit on Chinese American history. She has also written about early Chinese families in St. Paul. The book was published in 2004 with a foreword by Bill Holm. This short, illustrated book traces Chinese Minnesotans from the first settlers of the late 1870s to the new arrivals of the 1960s and after. Historian Iris Chang praised it as a rare look at Chinese immigrant lives and hopes in Minnesota.
summary: Fuller begins with Minnesota's first Chinese settlers, many of whom came east in the late 1870s to escape racial violence in California. They established scores of businesses, including laundries and restaurants, in Minneapolis, St. Paul and other towns. Local newspapers eagerly reported on their activities, including New Year celebrations, weddings and business openings. This shows how visible these small communities were. It also shows how much public curiosity surrounded them in their early years in the state.

A central part of the story is federal exclusion. Beginning in 1882, laws barred most Chinese immigration and denied citizenship to Chinese immigrants. Fuller shows how these laws put special pressure on Minnesota's community. They limited family life, shaped who could come and stay, and kept the population small for decades. Within those limits, Chinese Minnesotans built cultural and social organizations, businesses and family networks. These connected people across the state.

Library descriptions note that the book touches on immigration patterns, organizations, business, politics, education and family life. Together these give a rounded view of a community that was small but organized. Fuller then turns to change in the 1960s. A new wave of immigrants arrived, including students, business people and professionals from mainland China and Taiwan. They brought new energy and new issues to the community, and they helped ties between Minnesota and China flourish.

Like other books in the People of Minnesota series, it is short, has historical photographs and is written for a general reader. That makes it easy to share with a team. Its main story ends in the later twentieth century, so readers will need other sources for adoptees, recent students, newer professional families, Southeast Asian Chinese households and elders today. It works best as a foundation that helps staff ask better questions of current community partners.
mainPoints: Chinese Minnesotans have been part of the state since the late 1870s.
Many early settlers came to Minnesota to escape racial violence in California.
Federal exclusion laws from 1882 shaped and limited the community for decades.
Small businesses, organizations and family networks sustained early Chinese Minnesotans.
Immigration from mainland China and Taiwan from the 1960s on reshaped the community.
Chinese Minnesota is diverse in origin, language and occupation.
relevance: Chinese in Minnesota grounds the Chinese Minnesota brief in local history. It shows staff that Chinese Minnesotans are not only recent arrivals and that exclusion laws once shaped who could build a family here. That history can help staff understand caution toward government and why respectful, accurate service matters. The book also describes later immigration from mainland China and Taiwan. This supports the brief's reminder that people may identify with the People's Republic of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong or Southeast Asian Chinese communities, and that Cantonese is not Mandarin. It is a short book written in 2004, so it says little about adoptees, recent students, newer professionals or elders today. Pair it with current community partners.
questions: How might the history of exclusion laws inform how we think about trust and government among Chinese Minnesotans?
How do we confirm a person's preferred language, such as Cantonese or Mandarin, rather than writing Chinese on the request?
What parts of today's Chinese Minnesota community does this history not cover, and who could help us learn about them?

title: The Woman Warrior: Memoirs of a Girlhood Among Ghosts
editionNote: First published 1976 · Alfred A. Knopf · 209 pages
overview: Maxine Hong Kingston is a Chinese American writer who grew up in Stockton, California, the daughter of immigrants from southern China. The Woman Warrior, published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1976, blends memoir with the Chinese stories her mother told, which Kingston calls talk-stories. It won the National Book Critics Circle Award for nonfiction and was named one of Time's top nonfiction books of the 1970s. It became one of the most widely taught works of Asian American literature. It is also one of the most debated, especially over questions of authenticity and representation.
summary: The book has five sections. The first, No Name Woman, retells the story of an aunt in China whose name the family erased after she became pregnant outside marriage. Kingston imagines several versions of her aunt's life and concludes that the real question is why the family chose to forget her. The section raises questions about silence, shame and who gets remembered that run through the whole book. It also introduces the mother's talk-stories that Kingston both inherits and questions.

In White Tigers, Kingston retells the legend of Fa Mu Lan, a woman who fights in her father's place. She sets this heroic story against her own life as a young Chinese American woman, including her failure to stand up to a racist employer. Shaman turns to her mother, Brave Orchid, using her diplomas and photographs to tell of her years as a medical student and doctor in China. It shows the education and strength her mother brought to America, where her work and status changed sharply.

At the Western Palace follows Brave Orchid's sister, Moon Orchid, who arrives in America after thirty years apart from her husband. The sisters go to find him in Los Angeles. Moon Orchid's mental health declines in a country where she cannot find her footing, until she returns to her sister's home. The section is a sobering portrait of migration late in life and of how loss of language, role and family support can weigh on an older person.

The final section, A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe, explores language and voice: Kingston's struggle to speak, her conflicts with her mother, and a closing story of the poet Ts'ai Yen. The book won wide praise and became central to Asian American literature. But critics, most sharply the playwright Frank Chin, argued that it presented American stereotypes as Chinese culture. Others defended Kingston, who answered her critics in 1982, and the debate over authenticity remains part of the book's legacy.
mainPoints: Children of immigrants often grow up between their parents' stories and American life.
Family silences can carry shame, grief and protection all at once.
Immigrant parents may bring education and professional status that a new country does not recognize.
Language and finding one's voice are central to growing up Chinese American.
Mental health struggles can deepen when people lose the supports of their former lives.
Any single Chinese American story will be contested as representative of the whole.
relevance: The Woman Warrior offers DSD staff a lived voice to place beside Minnesota history. It portrays a mother whose professional training did not carry over and an aunt whose mental health declined after migration. These portraits can deepen understanding of the stresses older immigrants may face. They also show the ways families talk, or do not talk, about mental illness and disability. It also illustrates the brief's warning against treating Chinese as one culture or one language. The book is set in California in the mid-twentieth century and includes a passage reflecting attitudes toward disability common in its era. Its authenticity has long been debated within Chinese American letters, so read it as one artist's story and discuss those critiques as a team.
questions: How might a family's way of speaking, or not speaking, about mental illness shape how they approach our services?
What does Brave Orchid's experience suggest about the skills and status older immigrants may have lost in moving here?
What can the debate over this book teach us about the risk of letting one story stand for a whole community?

title: The Making of Modern Colombia: A Nation in Spite of Itself
editionNote: First published 1993 · University of California Press · 334 pages
overview: David Bushnell (1923–2010) was a U.S. historian often called the father of Colombian studies in the United States. Its publisher presented The Making of Modern Colombia as the first history of Colombia written in English. Reviewers called it the basic English-language text on the country. It traces Colombia from its Indigenous and Spanish colonial past through independence, nineteenth-century reform and civil conflict. It goes on through coffee, the Violencia, the National Front and the late twentieth century. Bushnell argues that Colombia often defied Latin American patterns.
summary: Bushnell begins by noting that Colombia was, in his words, among the least studied of the major Latin American countries. He sets out to give English-language readers a balanced overview. His first chapters cover Indigenous peoples and Spanish colonization, and then the long break with Spain from the 1780s to 1819. He shows how the country's mountains divided it into strong regions. This theme returns throughout the book and helps explain why Colombians identify so strongly with places such as Antioquia, the Caribbean coast or Bogotá.

The next chapters follow the short-lived union of Gran Colombia and the founding of New Granada as what Bushnell calls a nation-state that was not yet a nation. He describes the nineteenth-century liberal revolution and the rise of two lasting political parties, Liberals and Conservatives, who fought frequent civil wars. A conservative period known as the Regeneration began in 1885. It reshaped the constitution and the role of the church, and it ended with war and the loss of Panama.

Bushnell then turns to the early twentieth century, an age he associates with relative peace and the growth of coffee exports. Coffee brought new wealth and connected the country to world markets. It also created new tensions over land and labor. The chapters on the Liberal Republic from 1930 to 1946 describe reforms in labor, education and the role of the state, and the hopes and conflicts they raised. Bushnell organizes these chapters by period, an approach reviewers found clear and balanced. He keeps returning to how national change played out differently from region to region.

The book gives careful attention to the Violencia. This was a period of bloodshed between the parties, from roughly 1946 to 1957. It killed many thousands of people, especially in rural areas. Bushnell then explains the National Front, the agreement under which Liberals and Conservatives took turns in power from 1958. He weighs its success in ending the party wars against its failures, since it shut out other voices and left room for guerrilla movements to grow. For readers who know Colombia only through news headlines, these chapters show how much of the later conflict grew from earlier political choices.

The final chapter covers the years after 1978, which Bushnell describes as confounding predictions. He discusses drug trafficking and guerrilla conflict alongside steady economic growth and a democratic system that rarely gave way to military rule. His central argument is that Colombia has broken common Latin American patterns. It has had few military dictators, no lasting populist movement and a weak political left. Because the book was published in 1993, it does not cover the decades of conflict, peace negotiation and migration that followed.
mainPoints: Colombia's mountainous geography created strong regions and regional identities that still matter today.
Indigenous peoples, Spanish colonization and African enslavement all shaped the country's population and history.
Two long-lived parties, Liberals and Conservatives, dominated Colombian politics and fought repeated civil wars.
Coffee became the backbone of the economy in the early twentieth century and tied Colombia to world markets.
The Violencia of the mid-twentieth century left deep scars, especially in rural areas.
The National Front ended partisan war but narrowed political participation, with lasting consequences.
Colombia has often defied Latin American patterns, with little military rule and a durable electoral system despite serious violence.
relevance: This history helps DSD staff see Colombian Minnesotans as members of a distinct nation with strong regional identities, not as part of a single Latino group. It can explain why people from different regions may describe themselves differently. It shows why long histories of conflict may make some families cautious with institutions, and why it is a mistake to reduce Colombia to stereotypes about drugs. The limits are real. A U.S. historian wrote the book, and it focuses on politics and the state more than on everyday life. It ends in the early 1990s, before the 2016 peace accord and recent migration. Pair it with a Colombian author's voice and with community partners.
questions: Bushnell shows how strongly regional identities shape Colombian life. How do we ask people about their own identity instead of assigning a category?
Colombia is often reduced to stereotypes in the U.S. media. Where might those stereotypes show up in our work, even unintentionally?
How might a history of conflict and displacement affect a family's trust in government services, and how can we earn that trust?

title: The Man Who Could Move Clouds: A Memoir
overview: Ingrid Rojas Contreras is a Colombian-born writer whose first book, the novel Fruit of the Drunken Tree, was set during Colombia's years of violence. The Man Who Could Move Clouds is a memoir about memory, family and inheritance. It begins with a bicycle accident that leaves the author with temporary amnesia and becomes a journey into her family's history, including her grandfather, a curandero known for healing and other gifts. It was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.
summary: The memoir opens in Chicago, where a bicycle accident leaves the author with temporary amnesia. The loss of memory echoes an event in her mother's childhood: as a girl in Ocaña, Colombia, her mother fell into a well and lost her memory, and when she recovered, the family believed she had returned with new abilities, such as seeing spirits. The family recognized these as gifts like those of her grandfather, Nono. The author's own recovery, by contrast, brings no obvious powers, and she begins to wonder what she has inherited instead.

Nono, the author's maternal grandfather, is at the center of the family's stories. He was a curandero who, as relatives tell it, could heal the sick, see the future and change the weather, including moving clouds. The memoir explores how the family both treasured and feared these gifts, how they were passed on and hidden, and how they fit within Colombian traditions that mix Indigenous, Spanish and Catholic practice. The author writes about these beliefs with respect, without trying to prove or disprove them.

As she recovers, the author feels a strong urge to write about her family. Her mother objects fiercely to sharing family secrets and threatens to stop speaking to her if she does. That conflict between a daughter's need to tell and a mother's need to protect runs through the book. The family distinguishes between stories that begin with once upon a time and those that begin with once, in real life, and the author asks what it means to tell the truth when a family has good reasons to keep some things unsaid.

Several family members report dreams in which Nono asks to be disinterred. The family decides to return to Colombia to unbury and rebury him, and the trip becomes the memoir's frame. Along the way, the author moves between the present and Colombia's colonial past, its myths and its history, showing how a family story can hold histories that official records leave out. Reviewers praised the depth of her research and the lyric quality of her writing.

The book refuses the label of magical realism. Rather than treating her family's beliefs as decoration, the author asks readers to widen their sense of what is real and to take seriously ways of knowing that come from Indigenous and mestizo traditions. Some readers find its structure, which loops between times and voices, demanding. Others see that form as true to how memory works. The memoir ends less with answers than with a deeper understanding of inheritance, silence and the stories families choose to keep.
mainPoints: Memory, loss and inheritance can shape a family across generations in ways that are hard to name.
Curanderos and other traditional healers hold real meaning in many Colombian families' understanding of health and care.
Colombian traditions often blend Indigenous, Spanish and Catholic beliefs and practices.
Families may protect secrets for good reasons, and telling them can feel like betrayal to some members.
Dreams and spiritual experiences can carry weight in family decisions.
Family stories can preserve histories, including colonial and Indigenous histories, that official records leave out.
Respecting other ways of knowing does not require proving or disproving them.
relevance: This memoir helps DSD staff appreciate how some Colombian families understand health, healing, memory and the spiritual world. When a person's care plan involves traditional healers, prayer or family spiritual practice, staff who have read this book may be more likely to listen with respect and ask open questions instead of dismissing what they hear. The memoir's account of memory loss also offers a personal entry into conversations about brain injury and cognition. It is one family's story, shaped by the author's own region and ancestry, and it should never be used to predict what any Colombian family believes. Some readers find its looping structure demanding.
questions: The author's family valued a curandero's gifts. How do we ask about traditional or spiritual healing in a way that invites honesty rather than judgment?
The mother and daughter disagree about sharing family secrets. How do we respect a family's privacy while still gathering the information services require?
What might this memoir teach us about how memory loss feels from the inside, and how could that shape our support for people with brain injuries?

title: Cuba: An American History
overview: Ada Ferrer is a Cuban-born historian, born in 1962, whose family left for the United States soon after her birth. She taught for many years at New York University and has done research in Cuba since the 1990s. Cuba: An American History won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for History. It tells the story of Cuba from Spanish colonization to 2020, with close attention to the island's long and tangled ties to the United States. The title signals her argument: Cuba's history is also part of American history.
summary: Ferrer frames the book around the bond across the Florida Straits, the short stretch of water that has linked Cuba and the United States for centuries. She begins with Columbus and Spanish colonization. She shows how geography, including the currents that made Havana a key port, tied the island to the wider Atlantic world. She writes in an engaging, personal voice, at times bringing in her own family's history and her experience as a historian working on the island.

A major section covers slavery and sugar. Ferrer shows how Cuba became one of the world's great sugar producers on the labor of enslaved Africans, and how slaveholding interests in Cuba and the U.S. South were closely linked. The movement to end slavery, she argues, was bound up with fears and hopes about independence. Reviewers singled out this part of the book for praise, and it helps explain why race and nation are so closely joined in Cuban history.

The book then follows the long struggle for independence from Spain. Ferrer describes how Cuban fighters were close to victory when the United States intervened in 1898, turning the conflict into the Spanish-American War. The republic proclaimed in 1902 had limited sovereignty: the Platt Amendment gave the United States the right to intervene, a say over Cuban foreign relations, and a naval base at Guantánamo. This period, she argues, shaped Cuban views of the United States for generations.

Ferrer next traces the twentieth-century republic. This includes Fulgencio Batista's rise in the 1930s, the 1940 constitution drafted with broad public input, and Batista's 1952 coup. She explains how the movement led by Fidel Castro began by calling for that constitution to be restored. She frames the 1959 revolution in part as a response to long dependence on the United States. Some reviewers, including a human rights advocate writing for a Harvard journal, argued that she is too gentle with the revolutionary government and gives too little space to dissidents.

The final chapters cover the decades after 1959: waves of emigration to the United States, the economic crisis of the 1990s, civic movements in the 2000s, and shifting U.S. policy, ending with the 2020 election. Ferrer shows how migration and exile became central to both countries' stories. Readers come away understanding why different generations of Cubans and Cuban Americans hold very different views about the island, the revolution and the United States.
mainPoints: Cuba and the United States have been deeply connected for centuries by geography, trade, politics and migration.
Sugar wealth in Cuba was built on the labor of enslaved Africans, and slavery shaped Cuban debates about independence.
U.S. intervention in 1898 and the Platt Amendment limited Cuban sovereignty and shaped Cuban views of the United States.
The 1940 constitution and Batista's 1952 coup are key to understanding the movement that led to 1959.
The revolution reshaped Cuban society and set off waves of emigration that continue to the present.
Different generations and waves of Cuban migrants hold very different experiences and views.
Historians and readers disagree about how to judge the revolution, and those disagreements are part of the story.
relevance: This book gives DSD staff a clear, well-told history. It explains why Cuban Minnesotans may hold strong and differing views about politics, migration and government. It also explains why waves of arrival, from the 1960s to recent years, brought people with very different experiences. That understanding helps staff avoid treating Cuban families as one group with one story or one political view. It also clarifies that Cuban and Puerto Rican histories with the United States are different, with different legal consequences. Some reviewers criticize Ferrer's treatment of the revolution and of dissidents, so staff should hold the book as one respected view. It is long, focuses on national history rather than daily life, and does not address disability.
questions: Ferrer shows that Cuban arrivals came in very different waves. How do we avoid assuming one migration story for every Cuban family?
The book's history is contested, and families may hold strong views about it. How do we stay respectful and neutral when politics come up in service conversations?
What does Ferrer's framing of Cuba as part of American history change about how we think of the Cuban Minnesotans we serve?

title: The Prince of Los Cocuyos: A Miami Childhood
overview: Richard Blanco is a poet who, in 2013, became the first Latino and openly gay poet to read at a U.S. presidential inauguration. The Prince of Los Cocuyos is his memoir of growing up in Miami as the son of Cuban exiles, caught between his family's nostalgic memories of 1950s Cuba and the America he saw on television. Warm and often funny, it traces how he came to understand his cultural identity and accept himself as a gay man. It won the 2015 Lambda Literary Award for Gay Memoir.
summary: Blanco was born in Madrid shortly before his family moved on to the United States, part of a generation of Cubans displaced by the revolution. The family settles in Miami, where his parents work long hours and hold tightly to Cuban food, customs and memories. Young Richard lives between two imagined worlds: his parents' Cuba of the 1950s, which he has never seen, and the America of television reruns, which seems just as distant and just as appealing.

Many of the early stories are about the gap between those worlds. Richard longs for the foods his American classmates eat and tries to bring American traditions into his home, including a Thanksgiving dinner that the family remakes with Cuban touches. His grandfather plants a garden of tropical fruit trees that recalls the lost island. The memoir is told in loosely connected episodes, each one a small window into a household working out what it means to be Cuban in the United States.

Blanco's grandmother is one of the book's most vivid figures. She runs a small illegal numbers business, hides her money in secret places that only Richard knows, and gives her pennies to the church poor box. She is fierce and funny, but she is also harshly homophobic. She punishes Richard's interest in activities she considers unmanly and works to steer him toward a narrow idea of what a boy should be. Her love and her cruelty exist side by side.

As adolescence brings feelings he must hide, Richard is sent to work at a family bodega. There he befriends a Cuban man who is quietly gay and who confides in him about a forbidden relationship. The friendship is a turning point, opening Richard to the possibility of accepting himself. It also helps him begin to make peace with what reviewers called the ghosts of Cuba that haunt his family and shape his own sense of belonging.

The memoir ends as Blanco begins to find his voice as an artist and to accept his sexuality, while still feeling, in his words, a little from everywhere. He presents his story as both singular and widely shared: a child of immigrants learning that identity is built from memory, family stories and choice. Reviewers praised its humor and tenderness, and its honest look at how love and prejudice can live in the same home.
mainPoints: Children of exiles often grow up with a homeland they know mainly through their parents' memories.
Food, gardens and holidays help families keep a lost home alive and adapt it to a new place.
Immigrant children may feel caught between their family's culture and the culture around them.
Love and prejudice can exist together in one family, especially around gender and sexuality.
A single trusted adult outside the family can help a young person accept who they are.
Cultural identity is shaped over time by memory, story and choice, not fixed at birth.
Humor is a powerful way to tell difficult family truths.
relevance: This memoir helps DSD staff understand the experience of Cuban American families shaped by exile, nostalgia and life between cultures, especially for those raised in the United States. It also offers insight into the experience of LGBTQ+ people in close-knit families, which can support staff in honoring a person's identity while respecting family relationships. It reminds staff that a U.S.-born Cuban American may relate to Cuba very differently from a recent arrival. Blanco's story is set in Miami's large Cuban community, which differs from Minnesota's smaller one, and his family's experience reflects one wave of exile. The book does not address disability.
questions: Blanco grew up loving a Cuba he had never seen. How might a person's connection to a homeland differ by generation, and how do we ask about it?
The grandmother's love and homophobia exist together. How do we support a person's identity while working respectfully with their family?
Blanco found support from a trusted adult outside his family. Who plays that role for the people we serve, and do we include them in planning?

title: From Cuenca to Queens: An Anthropological Story of Transnational Migration
editionNote: First published 2004 · University of Texas Press · 229 pages
overview: Ann Miles is an anthropologist at Western Michigan University who has done long-term research in Cuenca, the major city of Ecuador's southern highlands. From Cuenca to Queens follows one family, the Quitasacas, whom she has known since 1989. In 1995 the eldest son, Vicente, left Cuenca to live and work without papers in New York City. Through chapters on each family member, the book shows what migration means for those who leave and those who stay. It also places one family's story within the economic and historical forces behind Ecuadorian migration.
summary: Miles opens by introducing the Quitasaca family and the idea of transnational lives, in which people stay deeply tied to two places at once. She explains that migration is often discussed through numbers and economics. She sets out to show the human side of those statistics. Because she had known the family for years before Vicente left, she can describe their lives before and after his departure and trace what led the eldest son to make a dangerous trip north as an undocumented migrant.

The second chapter steps back to examine the economies and identities that shape migration from Ecuador. Miles describes the historical and structural conditions that push people to leave, especially from the southern highlands. These include economic crisis, inequality and racism within Ecuador. She shows how migration became woven into local life, so that leaving for the United States came to feel like one of the few paths open to poor families seeking a future.

A chapter on family life describes the Quitasacas as a household and the obligations that bind its members to one another. Miles then devotes chapters to individual family members, including Rosa and Lucho and the children, before turning to Vicente himself. Each chapter explores how that person sees social inequality and racism in Ecuador, and how he or she responded to Vicente's departure. The family members do not agree, and the book gives each perspective room.

Through these accounts, Miles shows that migration carries many meanings at once. For some family members it represents hope and promise; for others it marks failure, loss or resignation to an economy that offered few choices. Money sent home helps, but it does not erase the strain of separation or the risks Vicente faces in New York. The chapter on Vicente describes his life and work in Queens and his continuing ties to his family in Cuenca.

The closing chapter reflects on lives and stories, and on what one family can teach about a much larger movement of people. Miles argues that personal accounts reveal the costs and hopes behind migration in ways surveys cannot. The book is written for students and general readers as well as scholars, and it includes a timeline of key events. It was published in 2004 and focuses on New York, but its picture of family obligation across borders remains widely relevant.
mainPoints: Migration is a family decision and a family experience, not only an individual choice.
Economic crisis, inequality and racism within Ecuador push many people from the southern highlands to migrate.
Family members can hold very different views of the same migration, from hope to grief to resignation.
People who migrate often stay deeply tied to their home communities through money, calls and obligations.
Undocumented migration carries serious risks for the person who leaves and worries for those who stay.
Personal stories reveal the human meaning of migration that statistics alone miss.
Transnational families live in two places at once, and decisions in one place affect the other.
relevance: This book helps DSD staff understand the family duties and ties across borders (transnational ties) that may shape Ecuadorian Minnesotans' lives. These include supporting relatives abroad, making decisions together with family in Ecuador, or carrying worry about people back home. It can inform person-centered planning. It reminds staff that a person's circle of support may extend across borders. Money, time and decisions may be shared in ways that do not fit standard assumptions. Its limits: it centers on one family and on New York rather than Minnesota. It was written by a U.S. anthropologist and dates from 2004. It does not address disability or Indigenous Kichwa experience in depth.
questions: The Quitasaca family members saw Vicente's migration very differently. How do we make room for different views within one family during planning meetings?
How might obligations to relatives in another country affect a person's time, money or decisions, and how can our planning respect that?
Who belongs in a person's circle of support when important family members live outside the United States?

title: The Undocumented Americans
overview: Karla Cornejo Villavicencio came to the United States from Ecuador as a small child, and she and her parents lived without legal status for decades. She was a doctoral student protected by DACA when, after the 2016 election, she decided to write about being undocumented under her own name. The Undocumented Americans mixes memoir, reporting and a small amount of imagined narrative to portray undocumented people across the country as full human beings. It was a finalist for the National Book Award.
summary: Cornejo Villavicencio begins with her decision to write the book. After the 2016 election, she wrote her immigration lawyer's phone number on her hand and set out to report on the lives of undocumented people in different cities. She explains that she wanted to look beyond the border and beyond the well-known image of the activist student, toward people often reduced in the news to political symbols or nameless workers. She also states plainly that she did not write the book to be liked.

In New York, she meets undocumented workers who were recruited into the federally funded cleanup of Ground Zero after the September 11 attacks and who later lived with serious health problems. She also imagines the final hours of a day laborer who drowned in his basement apartment during Hurricane Sandy, a passage reviewers singled out as one of the book's most striking. These chapters show how people whose labor rebuilt the city were often left without protection or care.

In Miami, she visits botánicas, shops that sell herbs and remedies, and shows how many undocumented people turn to them because their status blocks access to other health care. In Flint, Michigan, she reports on how demands for state identification kept some immigrants from getting clean water during the water crisis. In Cleveland and in Connecticut, she spends time with families facing detention and deportation, including two teenage girls whose father has taken sanctuary in a church.

Woven through the reporting is the author's own story. She writes about her parents' decades of work and sacrifice, her uncle's work ethic, her brother, and the pressure on children of immigrants to repay their parents through endless gratitude, which she argues can harm their mental health. She speaks openly about her own depression, a psychiatric hospitalization and medication. These passages connect the political subject of immigration status to the private experience of fear and exhaustion.

The book's style is blunt, profane and often funny, and reviewers compared its voice to a sledgehammer. Cornejo Villavicencio refuses to present undocumented people as saints or as stories of inspiration. Instead she shows them with humor, love, heartbreak and flaws. The book is short but intense, and some readers find its frankness uncomfortable. Its central claim is that undocumented people are Americans in every way that counts, and that their lives deserve to be seen whole.
mainPoints: Immigration status shapes daily life, health, work and family well beyond the border.
Undocumented people are often seen only as workers or political symbols rather than as whole people.
Status can block access to health care, leading people to turn to other sources of care such as botánicas.
ID requirements can keep people from basic services, even in a public health emergency.
Children of immigrants may carry heavy expectations of gratitude that can harm their mental health.
Fear of detention and deportation affects entire families, including citizens and young people.
Telling these stories honestly includes humor, anger and flaws, not only struggle or inspiration.
relevance: This book speaks directly to access. It shows how ID requirements, fear of immigration enforcement and lack of health coverage can keep people from services they need, which is useful for DSD staff reviewing forms, intake processes and outreach. It encourages staff to ask only what a program truly requires, to explain clearly how information will be used, and to understand why families with mixed status may hesitate. It also opens conversation about mental health in immigrant families. It is not specific to Ecuadorian Minnesotans or to Minnesota, it uses strong language, and it includes some imagined scenes. Use it to examine systems, not to guess anyone's immigration status.
questions: The book shows ID demands blocking access to clean water. Which of our requirements might keep eligible people from applying, and are they all truly necessary?
How do we explain what happens to the information people share with us, so that families with mixed status can make informed choices?
The author describes the weight of gratitude on children of immigrants. How might that pressure affect young adults who are also caregivers?

title: A History of Modern Ethiopia, 1855–1991
overview: A History of Modern Ethiopia is the standard general history of the country. It was written by Bahru Zewde, a historian born in Addis Ababa in 1947. He taught for decades at Addis Ababa University and directed its Institute of Ethiopian Studies. The first edition, published in 1991, covered 1855 to 1974. This second edition adds a chapter on the revolution and its aftermath, bringing the story to 1991. A reviewer of later Ethiopian scholarship called it key reading for any student of Ethiopian history, at home or abroad.
summary: Bahru explains in his preface that Ethiopia lacked a general history for specialists, teachers and general readers. He wrote this book to fill that gap. After an introduction and a chapter on the background, the history proper begins in 1855 with the rise of the emperor Tewodros. The book follows the lives and policies of the country's last and most important monarchs, Tewodros, Yohannes, Menilek and Haile Selassie, as the frame for the modern period.

The chapter on unification and independence, from 1855 to 1896, describes the rebuilding of central power and the growth of the state. It ends with the victory over Italy at Adwa that preserved Ethiopian independence. The next chapter, from Adwa to Maychew, covers 1896 to 1935, including the consolidation of a modern state and the rise of Haile Selassie. For readers in Minnesota, this period matters because the expansion of the empire brought many peoples, including Oromo and southern communities, under a single state.

A chapter on the Italian occupation of 1936 to 1941 describes conquest, resistance and liberation. The following chapter, from liberation to revolution, covers 1941 to 1974. It describes the restored imperial government, attempts at reform and growing opposition from students and the public. It also covers the crises of drought and famine that weakened the emperor. These decades set the stage for the upheaval that followed. Bahru shows how the restored monarchy struggled to answer new demands from a changing society, and how the gap between promise and reform grew wider over time.

The new chapter, titled Revolution and its Sequel, covers the 1974 revolution, the rule of the military committee known as the Derg, and its fall in 1991. A reviewer praised this account as nuanced and worth attention in its own right. Bahru had personal knowledge of this era: a recent review of his autobiography notes that he was imprisoned for five years under the Derg after returning from graduate study in London.

The book closes with a conclusion that reflects on the long arc of state building, war and change. It is compact and clear, with maps and illustrations. As a history of the state, it centers rulers and the central government. Readers who want the perspectives of peoples brought into that state, such as the Oromo, or events after 1991, will need to read further. Even with those limits, it remains a clear and trusted starting point.
mainPoints: Modern Ethiopian history is often told through its last emperors, Tewodros, Yohannes, Menilek and Haile Selassie.
Victory at Adwa in 1896 preserved Ethiopian independence and remains a source of pride for many.
The expansion of the empire brought many distinct peoples under one state, with lasting consequences.
The Italian occupation of 1936 to 1941 was met with resistance and ended in liberation.
Reform failed to keep pace with student and popular demands and with famine in the 1970s.
The 1974 revolution and the Derg era caused widespread violence and drove many Ethiopians abroad.
Ethiopia is a multiethnic, multilingual country, and Ethiopian is a national label, not a single people.
relevance: For DSD staff, this book explains the national history behind the many families who may be recorded as Ethiopian. It shows why some families left in the 1970s and 1980s and why the Derg era still shapes memories of government. It also shows why the expansion of the empire left lasting tensions between peoples. That context supports the guidance in this brief to let each household name its own people and language, whether Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, Gurage or another. It can also help staff recognize pride in Ethiopian independence without assuming every family shares the same view of national history. Limits: it is a history of the state, written mainly from Addis Ababa. It ends in 1991, and it does not address disability. Pair it with Oromo and other community histories, and with current Minnesota voices.
questions: Many Ethiopian Minnesotans left during or after the Derg era. How might that history shape a family's comfort with home visits, records or questions about relatives?
How do we make sure that an Ethiopian label in our records does not stand in for a family's actual people and language?
Where might different views of Ethiopian history among Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan and other families matter in group settings we organize?

title: Held at a Distance: My Rediscovery of Ethiopia
overview: Held at a Distance is a memoir by Rebecca G. Haile, an Ethiopian American lawyer whose family fled Ethiopia when she was eleven and settled in central Minnesota. Her father, Getatchew Haile, was a scholar of ancient Ethiopian manuscripts and later a MacArthur Fellow. He had served in parliament after the fall of Emperor Haile Selassie, and the new military government persecuted him. The book is built around her return to Ethiopia twenty-five years later, a four-week journey to see relatives and the historic north, and around the questions of identity and belonging that the trip raised.
summary: The memoir opens with the family's departure. In the mid-1970s, after the revolution, her father's political role made him a target of the military government, and the family was forced to leave. They rebuilt their lives in the United States, in central Minnesota. Haile grew up there before attending Williams College and Harvard Law School and working as a lawyer. A prologue sets up the central question of the book: what it means to return to a homeland one left as a child.

The first part of the book centers on extended family. Haile describes reunions with relatives who stayed in Ethiopia through the Derg years and after, including her grandmother and an aunt. A reviewer highlighted her portrait of an uncle, an engineer who kept building bridges throughout the Derg era. He argued that economic change would lead to political change and that local institutions needed strengthening. Through these portraits she shows how people endured a repressive period and what they hoped for afterward.

The second part follows her travels through the historic north of the country, with its ancient churches and sites of early Ethiopian civilization. Here Haile writes about Ethiopia's long history alongside its recent past. She connects her own family's experience to a much older story and weighs what she sees against what she remembers and was told. The journey becomes a way to place her own family inside a much longer national story, and to test childhood memory against the country as it is now.

The third part reflects on the intersections of a globalized life. Haile, who traveled with her husband, writes about living between two worlds: a public American professional life and a private connection to Ethiopia, family and history. A reviewer described the book's themes as dislocation, rediscovery, the strength of family, and the healing that time can bring to the trauma of exile. This section speaks to many children of immigrants who feel at home in two places and fully at home in neither.

The book also serves as a record of life under the Derg, and one reviewer saw it as part of a wider effort to help Ethiopians speak about state violence that many had kept silent about. The same reviewer noted that it covers only the north of the country. It reflects the experience of one educated family with deep roots in Ethiopian scholarship and the Orthodox Church, and it is written for a general reader.
mainPoints: Political persecution after the 1974 revolution forced many Ethiopian families into exile.
Some Ethiopian families built their new lives in Greater Minnesota, not only the Twin Cities.
Returning after decades can bring joy, grief and new questions about where one belongs.
Relatives who stayed carry their own histories of endurance and their own hopes for the country.
Many Ethiopian Americans live between a public American identity and private ties to family and history.
Speaking openly about state violence can be part of healing for individuals and communities.
Ethiopia's ancient history and its recent past are both part of how families understand themselves.
relevance: This memoir offers DSD staff a Minnesota-connected Ethiopian voice on exile, family and identity. It can help staff understand why some families keep a careful silence about the revolutionary years and why relatives abroad remain central to family decisions. It also shows why a person may feel fully American and fully tied to Ethiopia at once. For planning and engagement, it suggests asking about the people who matter to a family, including those overseas. It also suggests recognizing that experiences of state violence may affect trust in public systems. Limits: Haile writes from a highly educated, professionally successful family with close ties to scholarship and the Orthodox Church; her trip covers only the north; and the book does not address disability. It reflects one family, not Ethiopian Minnesotans as a whole. Use it to inform questions.
questions: Haile describes living between two worlds. How might that shape how an Ethiopian American adult wants their own family involved in their supports?
How could our team be more aware of experiences of state violence without asking families to retell them?
How might relatives overseas be part of a family's decisions, and how do our processes make room for that?

title: Empire of Care: Nursing and Migration in Filipino American History
editionNote: First published 2003 · Duke University Press · 272 pages
overview: Catherine Ceniza Choy is a historian of Filipino American and Asian American life who teaches ethnic studies at the University of California, Berkeley. Empire of Care, published by Duke University Press in 2003, asks why the Philippines sends so many nurses abroad, especially to the United States. Choy draws on interviews with Filipino nurses and on Philippine and American government and health records. She traces this migration to the Americanized nurse training system built under United States colonial rule. The book won the 2005 Association for Asian American Studies Book Award.
summary: Choy's introduction sets out her central argument. Economic reasons alone, such as higher wages abroad, cannot explain how many Filipino nurses have moved to the United States. The roots of this migration lie in the early twentieth century. At that time the United States ruled the Philippines and built a hospital and nursing school system on an American pattern. To make this case she uses interviews with Filipino nurses in New York City and elsewhere. She pairs them with government and health records from both countries.

The first part, Nurturing Empire, examines nursing under United States colonialism. Choy shows how nursing became a respected profession for Filipino women within the colonial project. American-style training, English-language teaching and professional standards prepared nurses who could later move into United States hospitals with relative ease. She does not treat this as a natural fit. She treats it as the result of deliberate colonial choices about health, education and the role of women.

The second part, Caring Unbound, follows nurses who came to the United States through the Exchange Visitor Program after World War II. In this program, a nursing cap became a kind of passport. Choy traces how many nurses moved from temporary exchange status to permanent residence. She argues that Philippine independence in 1946 and the 1965 immigration reforms did not start this flow of professional migration. They built on it, since colonial institutions had already set it firmly in place.

The third part looks at the harder side of this history. Choy examines how Filipino nurses were made scapegoats in a well-known criminal case. She also looks at the lack of solidarity between Filipino and American nurses, and at the exploitation of foreign-trained nurses on temporary work visas. She also describes how Filipino nurses organized to defend their rights and professional standing. An epilogue considers ongoing nurse migration and its costs for the Philippines, which needs trained health workers of its own.
mainPoints: Filipino nurse migration has roots in United States colonial rule of the Philippines.
Economic incentives alone do not explain why so many Filipino nurses work abroad.
American-style training and English instruction shaped a workforce ready for United States hospitals.
Temporary visa programs created pathways to permanent residence, and also exploitation.
Filipino nurses have faced scapegoating and discrimination in American workplaces.
Filipino nurses organized collectively to defend their rights and standing.
The migration of care workers has real costs for the sending country.
relevance: Filipino Minnesotans include many health care and direct care professionals. Some of them work in the disability service system that DSD funds and oversees. Empire of Care helps staff understand that history and the colonial ties between the Philippines and the United States. It also honors the skill and commitment Filipino care workers bring. It can inform workforce planning and the recognition of foreign-trained credentials. It can also guide respectful partnership with Filipino professional and community organizations. It supports the brief's point that staff should not assume everyone is fluent in English. It also notes that the colonial history here is Spanish and then American. The book focuses on nurses on the coasts, not Minnesota. It was published in 2003, so it says less about today's direct care workforce.
questions: How does the colonial history Choy describes change the way we think about Filipino workers in Minnesota's disability services workforce?
Where might foreign-trained care professionals face barriers or unfair treatment in the systems we oversee?
How can we partner with Filipino professional and community organizations in workforce planning?

title: Dear America: Notes of an Undocumented Citizen
overview: Jose Antonio Vargas is a Filipino American journalist who shared a Pulitzer Prize as a reporter at the Washington Post and later founded the nonprofit Define American. He was sent from the Philippines to live with his grandparents in California at the age of twelve, and learned at sixteen that he was undocumented. Dear America, published by Dey Street Books in 2018, is his memoir of that life. He describes it less as a book about immigration policy than as an account of the strain of living undocumented: the lying it requires, the work of passing, and the struggle to hold a family together.
summary: The memoir opens with separation. In 1993 Vargas's mother sent him from Manila to Mountain View, California, to live with his grandparents, whom he calls Lolo and Lola. She promised to follow but could not, and mother and son have not seen each other since. In school he struggled with English and tried to work out where Filipinos fit among the racial groups around him. He describes the immigrant Mountain View of crowded homes and families who followed news from the Philippines on Filipino television.

At sixteen, trying to get a driver's license, he learned that his green card was fake. His grandfather admitted that the family had brought him in on false papers, hoping he would one day find a lawful path to stay. Vargas describes how this discovery changed everything: he began a life of careful secrecy, deciding whom to tell and constantly calculating risk. He also came out as gay in high school, which led to a painful rift with his devout grandfather that was only healed shortly before Lolo's death in 2011.

Mentors carried him forward. A teacher encouraged him toward journalism, and a principal, a school superintendent and other supporters helped him find a scholarship and attend San Francisco State University. He went on to internships and then a reporting career at the Washington Post, covering major national stories, all while hiding his status. He describes how even professional success, including the Pulitzer, brought fear that he would be exposed, and how the burden of deception shaped his relationships and sense of self.

In 2011 he decided he could no longer live in hiding and revealed his status in an essay in the New York Times Magazine. He then founded Define American to change how immigrants are portrayed in the media. He describes both the support and the threats that followed, as well as criticism from some advocates who felt he was not representative of most undocumented people. In 2014 he was detained by Border Patrol in McAllen, Texas, and held briefly with young Central American refugees before his release.

Throughout, the separation from his mother remains the book's emotional center, and Vargas reflects honestly on what her sacrifice has cost them both. Reviewers described the memoir as mournful, personal and generous, blending memoir with commentary on what it means to belong. A young readers' edition is also available, which makes the story easy to share with colleagues and families alike. As its title suggests, the whole book reads as a letter addressed to the country he calls home.
mainPoints: Immigration status can shape every part of daily life, from school to work to relationships.
Many immigrant families are separated across countries for years or decades.
Grandparents often play a central role in raising children in Filipino families.
Secrecy and fear of exposure carry a heavy psychological toll.
Mentors and community supporters can open doors for young people without the usual safety nets.
Belonging and citizenship can be understood through participation and contribution, not only papers.
No single person can represent the full range of experiences in an immigrant community.
relevance: Dear America gives DSD staff a Filipino American voice on family, faith, identity and belonging. It helps explain why some people may be cautious about sharing information with public agencies, why mixed-status households may weigh every form carefully, and why fear of exposure can keep people from seeking services they are entitled to. It also shows the central place of grandparents and extended family in many Filipino households, which can matter in caregiving and service planning. Vargas is one prominent person whose path, by his own account, differs from that of most undocumented immigrants, and his story is set in California. Use it to build empathy and to ask better questions, never to assume anything about a person's status.
questions: How might fear of exposure or concern about immigration status affect whether a family seeks the disability services they need?
What does the role of Vargas's grandparents suggest about who may be part of care decisions in Filipino households?
How can we make our intake and forms feel safer for families who are cautious about sharing information?

title: Silence on the Mountain: Stories of Terror, Betrayal, and Forgetting in Guatemala
overview: Daniel Wilkinson is a human rights investigator who later served as managing director of the Americas Division at Human Rights Watch. Silence on the Mountain grew out of his work in Guatemala in the 1990s, near the end of a thirty-six-year internal war in which some 200,000 people died, most at the hands of the U.S.-backed military government. Part history and part detective story, the book uses one coffee plantation to explain how land, labor, race and fear shaped modern Guatemala, and why so many survivors stayed silent.
summary: The book begins in 1993, when Wilkinson, then a young human rights worker, sets out to learn why guerrillas had burned the manor house of a coffee plantation. The people he asks will not talk, or answer around his questions. That silence becomes his subject. Following it, he moves outward from a single act of arson to the history of the estate, the families who worked it, and the national conflict that reached even remote mountain communities.

A long section explains the coffee economy. Wilkinson describes how coffee built the nineteenth-century Guatemalan state and how it relied on Maya labor. Planters settled Maya families on the estates through loans and the right to use small plots, tying workers to the land through debt and dependence. He shows how a planter family's story of its own fairness could sit alongside a racial order that placed light-skinned owners above Maya and mestizo workers, and how some workers experienced the arrangement as protection.

The heart of the book is the land reform of the early 1950s. Workers on the plantation organized a union and received parcels of land under the reform. When the government that sponsored it was overthrown in 1954 in a U.S.-backed intervention, the reform was reversed, union members were jailed or expelled, and the land returned to the owners. Wilkinson treats this as the buried turning point that explains much of what followed, including the reluctance of older people to discuss it decades later.

Later chapters turn to the guerrilla movements and the army's counterinsurgency in the 1970s and 1980s. Wilkinson describes how army reprisals turned some villagers against the guerrillas and how violence came from more than one direction, including a guerrilla killing of unarmed neighbors that he recounts in detail. Throughout, he shows how terror worked as a tool of politics: it did not only kill people but taught survivors that speaking could be dangerous.

The book ends after the 1996 peace accords. Wilkinson helps gather testimony for the truth commission, sees the army keep much of its influence, and watches a younger generation leave the countryside for Guatemala City and the United States. His final chapters ask what it means for a society to remember, and who pays the price of speaking. Critics praised the reporting and narrative, while the anthropologist David Stoll argued that the book leans toward a sympathetic view of the guerrillas.
mainPoints: Guatemala's internal war lasted thirty-six years and killed some 200,000 people, most of them at the hands of state forces.
Coffee wealth was built on Maya labor bound to plantations through debt, dependence and racial hierarchy.
The land reform of the early 1950s and its reversal after 1954 are a key to understanding later conflict.
Terror teaches silence, and silence can be a reasonable survival strategy rather than a lack of trust in any one person.
Violence in the war came from more than one direction, and communities lived with pressure from several sides.
The peace accords did not end the army's influence or the poverty that pushes young people to migrate.
Recovering memory through testimony and truth commissions carries real risks for the people who speak.
relevance: For DSD staff, this book offers historical literacy that explains why some Guatemalan elders and families may be guarded with government agencies, may decline to share history, or may answer questions indirectly. It reframes reluctance as learned caution, which can guide trauma-informed engagement, careful consent practices and patient relationship building. It also helps staff see that many Guatemalan Minnesotans are Maya, with languages and histories distinct from Spanish-speaking Latin America. Limits matter: the author is a U.S. human rights worker rather than a Guatemalan, some scholars find his treatment of the guerrillas too generous, and the book focuses on one region. Pair it with a Maya author's voice.
questions: Wilkinson shows that silence can be a survival strategy. How might our questions or forms feel to someone who learned that speaking to officials was dangerous?
The book traces present conditions back to land and labor history. What history might help us understand the families we serve in our own region?
How can we build trust slowly with communities that have reason to be wary, without making assumptions about any one family's past?

title: Voices from Exile: Violence and Survival in Modern Maya History
editionNote: First published 1999 · University of Oklahoma Press · 287 pages
overview: Victor Montejo is a Jakaltek (Popti') Maya writer and anthropologist from the highlands of western Guatemala. He was a schoolteacher during the war. When violence reached his community in the early 1980s, he fled to Mexico. He later earned a doctorate in anthropology in the United States and taught at the University of California, Davis. Voices from Exile tells the story of Maya families from the Kuchumatan highlands who fled into Mexico. It combines his own experience with history, political analysis and the testimony of refugees. It won a political science award for scholarship on race and ethnicity.
summary: Montejo builds the book around the idea of elilal, a Maya word for exile. He describes exile as the condition of thousands of Maya who left their homelands to escape repression and death at the hands of their own government. The book's purpose, in his telling, is to give voice to people who had long struggled in silence. Because Montejo was himself a refugee, he writes as both a participant and a scholar. Reviewers saw that double position as a source of the book's depth.

A historical thread places the violence of the 1980s in a longer story. Montejo connects the army's campaigns in the highlands to centuries of forced labor, land loss and racism toward Indigenous people. These began with the Spanish conquest and continued after independence. He presents state terror not as a sudden break but as an extreme form of older patterns. He also examines how the army's war against the guerrillas (the counterinsurgency) targeted Maya communities and reshaped village life.

The core of the book draws on fieldwork in refugee camps in Chiapas, Mexico. Montejo lived and worked there with Maya families in the 1980s, and he returned in the early 1990s. He records how people fled across the border and how they organized life in the camps. He shows how they coped with grief, uncertainty and dependence on outside aid. The testimonies he gathers describe loss, but also humor, faith, community decision-making and stubborn hope.

A central theme is how refugees reaffirmed and celebrated their Maya identity in exile. Montejo shows people keeping languages, ceremonies, stories and ways of organizing community life alive far from home. He treats this cultural survival as a form of resistance. Reviewers noted that the book follows displaced Maya into Mexico and the United States. It takes seriously how people rebuild a sense of who they are when the places that held their identity have been taken.

The book also considers return. Some refugees eventually went back to Guatemala through negotiated processes, often to find land occupied and danger not fully gone. Montejo treats return as fragile and incomplete rather than a happy ending. In later years he served in Guatemala's Congress and in government work on peace and reparations. The book can be read as an early statement of his lifelong argument: Maya people must speak for themselves in their own history.
mainPoints: Exile, elilal, is a shared condition for many Maya families who fled Guatemala's highlands during the war.
State violence against Maya communities grew from long histories of forced labor, land loss and racism.
Refugee testimony can recover histories that fear kept silent for years.
Maya refugees kept their languages, ceremonies and community life alive as a form of survival and resistance.
Displacement often extends across more than one border, into Mexico and then the United States.
Return after exile is fragile, and homes and land may not be waiting.
Maya people writing their own history changes what the history says and who it serves.
relevance: Many Guatemalan Minnesotans are Maya. This book helps staff understand why a Spanish interpreter may not be the right match and why community and family decision-making can matter so much. It also shows why experiences of displacement may shape how people respond to government systems. It supports trauma-informed and culturally grounded practice. That includes asking about preferred language rather than assuming Spanish, and partnering with Maya-led organizations. Montejo's community is Jakaltek Maya, and other Maya peoples, such as K'iche', Mam and Q'eqchi', have their own languages and histories. The book is scholarly and was published in 1999. It centers on refugee camp life rather than life in the United States.
questions: Montejo shows Maya refugees keeping language and community life alive in exile. How do our services make room for languages other than Spanish and English?
Displacement can stretch across years and borders. How might that history affect a family's comfort with paperwork, appointments or home visits?
What Maya-led or Guatemalan community organizations could help us learn, and how would we make that partnership fair to them?

title: From Seven Rivers to Ten Thousand Lakes: Minnesota's Indian American Community
editionNote: First published 2019 · Minnesota Historical Society Press · 144 pages
overview: From Seven Rivers to Ten Thousand Lakes is an illustrated history of Minnesota's Indian American community. The Minnesota Historical Society Press published it in 2019 with a foreword by community leader S. K. Dash. Its author, Preeti Mathur, is a longtime member of that community. She is a founding member of the School of India for Languages and Culture and a past board member of the India Association of Minnesota. Using interviews, archival research and her own experience, she traces more than fifty years of migration from the Indian subcontinent to Minnesota.
summary: Mathur begins with the history and conditions that led people from the Indian subcontinent to Minnesota. She describes how immigration grew over more than half a century as students, professionals and families arrived and stayed. This opening helps readers understand that Indian Minnesota did not appear all at once. It grew through particular laws, opportunities and personal choices. Its members came from many regions, languages and religious traditions across India and its diaspora.

The book then turns to the experience of settling in Minnesota and building a community. Mathur describes how newcomers created organizations, places of worship, language schools and cultural groups. These helped them and their children keep ties to their heritage. The India Association of Minnesota and the Minnesota Historical Society have worked together for a long time. Their partnership has gathered oral histories since the 1990s, and it gives important background for this work. In this way the opening frames the rest of the book as a story of many journeys rather than one.

A central section covers professional, political and economic contributions. Indian Minnesotans work as engineers, doctors, teachers, entrepreneurs, artists and chefs. The book includes both permanent residents and those who came for a time. Mathur shows the many ways community members have shaped Minnesota's workplaces, civic life and economy. She also shows that no single profession defines the community. This work also reflects a community that has taken care to record its own history. The oral history projects have documented first-generation immigrants, their children, families in Greater Minnesota, and many cultural and religious organizations.

Mathur gives special attention to the pursuit and celebration of cultural and religious traditions. The book describes festivals, music, dance and faith communities that reflect the many traditions present in Indian Minnesota. These pages help readers see that Indian heritage is not one culture, one language or one religion. Celebrations and practices vary widely among households. By showing this range, Mathur makes clear that an Indian Minnesotan's work does not tell you about their language, faith or family life. The community also includes people at many different stages of settling in.

The book closes with profiles of notable people, businesses and organizations. A foreword looks toward the community's future. It is richly illustrated with about one hundred photographs and includes a bibliography and index. Historian Erika Lee praised it as informative and beautifully illustrated. As a community history, it tends to celebrate success. Readers may need other sources on struggles, inequality and newer arrivals. For readers new to the community, these chapters offer a respectful and wide-ranging introduction to the many ways Indian heritage is lived in Minnesota.
mainPoints: People from the Indian subcontinent have been coming to Minnesota for more than fifty years.
Indian Minnesota includes many regions, languages and religions, not one shared culture.
Community members built organizations, places of worship and language schools to keep their heritage alive.
Indian Minnesotans contribute across many fields, from medicine and engineering to the arts and food.
Festivals, music, dance and faith communities are central to community life.
Long-standing oral history work with the Minnesota Historical Society has helped document this community.
Both permanent and temporary residents are part of the community's story.
relevance: From Seven Rivers to Ten Thousand Lakes gives the Indian (Asian Indian) Minnesota brief a local, community-written history. It supports the brief's reminder that Indian Minnesotans speak many languages and practice many religions. Staff should ask about language and identity rather than guess. It can help staff identify community organizations, faith groups and cultural institutions that may be partners in outreach and engagement. It also reminds staff that this is a community of Asian Indian heritage, distinct from American Indian and Tribal Nation communities. The word Indian alone should not decide which resources to use. As a community history that celebrates, it says less about disability, poverty, family caregiving or recent arrivals. It should not lead staff to assume that every household has plenty of resources. Pair it with current partners and personal voices.
questions: How do we confirm a person's preferred language and religious or cultural practices rather than assuming from the word Indian?
Which Indian Minnesotan organizations or faith communities could help us reach families who may need disability services?
What might a celebratory community history leave out, and how could we learn about those parts of the community's experience?

title: Good Talk: A Memoir in Conversations
overview: Good Talk is a graphic memoir by Mira Jacob, an Indian American writer and illustrator. Her earlier book was the novel The Sleepwalker's Guide to Dancing. Published by One World in 2019, it is built around conversations, many of them with her young biracial son, whose father is white and Jewish.
