Drawn figures set against photographs and other images carry the story. It moves from Jacob's childhood in New Mexico, as the daughter of parents from India, to raising a brown child in the United States during and after the 2016 election.
summary: The book opens with questions from Jacob's six-year-old son, who is fascinated by Michael Jackson and wonders why the singer's skin changed color. His questions soon widen to how white people see brown people, whether his own father might be afraid of him, and whether Indians can be racist. These conversations frame the book and show how children notice race long before adults are ready to talk about it. Jacob answers as honestly as she can.

Jacob then moves back in time to her own childhood in New Mexico, growing up with parents who came from India. She writes about family expectations, cultural pressures and the experience of being a dark-skinned Indian girl in the United States. These scenes help readers see how immigrant families carry both their own traditions and the pressures of a new country, and how children learn early what is expected of them inside and outside the home.

A further thread follows her early years as a writer in New York. It includes relatives' efforts to arrange a match and a painful episode in which a possible partner's family judged her appearance. Reviewers noted that this story exposes colorism, the preference for lighter skin, as something present within families and communities as well as in the wider society. Jacob also writes about being a woman of color in publishing.

Jacob's marriage to a white Jewish man brings her into close relationship with in-laws who support Donald Trump. After the 2016 election, conversations with them, and with her son about what he hears in the news, become harder. She writes honestly about love and disagreement inside one family, and about the limits of explaining oneself to people who may not realize what they do not understand. These chapters show how political events can enter the most private parts of family life.

The art is unusual. The characters' faces stay much the same from page to page while the conversations grow more emotional, which asks readers to pay close attention to the words. Reviewers praised the book's humor, honesty and vulnerability, and its insistence that hard conversations are worth having even when they do not end in answers. Some readers may find the political conversations painful, but the book treats every person in it with complexity rather than contempt.
mainPoints: Children notice and ask about race much earlier than many adults expect.
Indian American identity is shaped both by family traditions and by American ideas about race.
Colorism can operate within families and communities as well as in the wider society.
Mixed families may hold deep love and deep disagreement at the same time.
Microaggressions add up over time and can cause real harm.
Hard conversations can be valuable even when they do not end in agreement or answers.
People of color should not be expected to educate others at the cost of their own safety.
relevance: Good Talk gives the Indian (Asian Indian) Minnesota brief a contemporary, personal voice that sits alongside community history. It helps staff understand that an Indian American family may be multiracial, multilingual or multifaith. Identity can be shaped by experiences of race, colorism and political climate as much as by heritage. Staff can use it to practice listening without assuming and to reflect on how everyday comments can land differently for people of color. It also shows the work families do to talk with children about race, which can inform how staff engage with parents and caregivers. It is one family's story, set mostly in New Mexico and New York rather than Minnesota, and it focuses on race and family more than on services. Pair it with local history and community partners.
questions: How might everyday comments or questions from staff feel different to a family of color, especially in a tense political climate?
How do we respect the many ways a family may describe its identity, including multiracial, multilingual or multifaith households?
What can we learn from Jacob about staying in a hard conversation without expecting the other person to educate us?

title: Enmity and Empathy: Japanese Americans in Minnesota during World War II
editionNote: First published 2025 · Minnesota Historical Society Press · 400 pages
overview: Ka F. Wong is a professor of Asian Studies at St. Olaf College in Northfield. He is also the producer, director and writer of the documentary Beyond the Barbed Wire: Japanese Americans in Minnesota. Enmity and Empathy was published by the Minnesota Historical Society Press in May 2025. It tells how the Japanese American population of Minnesota grew from fifty-one people in 1940 to several thousand by the end of World War II. Using personal interviews, archival sources and earlier scholarship, Wong follows people who left the incarceration camps and rebuilt their lives here. The book won the 2026 Minnesota Book Award for Minnesota nonfiction.
summary: The book begins with the wider national story. After Pearl Harbor, Executive Order 9066 led to the forced removal and confinement of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. Roughly two-thirds of them were United States citizens. The publisher calls this one of the worst civil rights violations of the twentieth century. Minnesota had no camps, yet the camps changed it. National policy, military needs and local advocacy brought Japanese Americans to the state in growing numbers during and after the war.

Wong then follows several paths that led people to Minnesota. College students left the camps to pursue higher education at Minnesota schools, often with support from educators and religious groups who became their allies. Young men and women trained as linguists at the Military Intelligence Service Language School, first at Camp Savage and then at Fort Snelling. Members of the US Cadet Nurse Corps served in Rochester hospitals. Each path depended on both the courage of the resettlers and the willingness of institutions to open their doors.

Another strand follows families and individuals who started businesses in the Twin Cities and beyond. They built businesses and households while facing suspicion and hostility in a state still at war with Japan. Wong describes the hardship of starting over with little, far from former homes and communities. He shows the persistence it took to find housing, work and acceptance. These stories show resettlement as a long process of rebuilding, not a single move from one place to another.

Throughout, Wong gives attention to the allies who stood with the resettlers: educators, religious groups, military personnel, nonprofit volunteers and ordinary people who spoke up. He frames this as empathy growing alongside the enmity stirred up by war hysteria. He says the book's central message is that unity can overcome division. The project grew from years of research with St. Olaf students. It also grew from interviews with people who were incarcerated or served in the war. Several of them have since died, which gives the book a sense of urgency.

Reviewers have praised the accounts of individual resettlers as the book's strongest passages. One review in the Japanese American press noted that its overall arc follows patterns familiar from other histories of wartime incarceration. Its value for Minnesota readers lies in placing that national history in specific local towns, campuses, hospitals and neighborhoods. The book also draws on the same interviews and research that shaped Wong's documentary, so readers who want to go further can pair it with the film.
mainPoints: Minnesota had no incarceration camps, but its Japanese American community grew because of them.
The state's Japanese American population rose from fifty-one people in 1940 to several thousand by war's end.
College study, the Military Intelligence Service Language School and the Cadet Nurse Corps were key paths to Minnesota.
Resettlers rebuilt lives while facing hostility and suspicion during wartime.
Allies in education, faith communities, the military and civic life helped open doors.
Empathy and solidarity grew alongside the fear and prejudice of war.
Oral histories preserve stories that are at risk of being lost as elders pass away.
relevance: Enmity and Empathy is the Minnesota history behind the Japanese Minnesota brief, which names Camp Savage, Fort Snelling and internment as background every staff member should know. The book helps DSD staff understand that some Japanese American families arrived here directly from incarceration. Public institutions harmed them, and through individual allies, also helped them rebuild. That double history can inform how staff think about trust, records and government questions. It also honors the brief's advice not to open a conversation with internment. Its attention to allies offers a clear example of what partnership with a community can look like. The book focuses on the war years, so it says less about later descendants, mixed families, company transferees or newcomers from Japan today.
questions: What does the role of allies in this history suggest about how public servants can stand with a community today?
How might a family's history of resettlement shape how they respond to government forms, records or questions about loyalty and status?
How do we hold this Minnesota history as background knowledge without making it the subject of a family's meeting?

title: They Called Us Enemy
authors: George Takei, Justin Eisinger, Steven Scott, and Harmony Becker
editionNote: First published 2019 · Top Shelf Productions · 208 pages
overview: George Takei, the actor and civil rights advocate, was four years old when his family was forced from their Los Angeles home and imprisoned in American concentration camps during World War II. They Called Us Enemy is his graphic memoir of those years. He wrote it with Justin Eisinger and Steven Scott, Harmony Becker illustrated it, and Top Shelf Productions published it in 2019. It became a New York Times bestseller and won the Eisner Award for Best Reality-Based Work and an American Book Award. It moves between childhood memories, history and Takei's adult reflections.
summary: The book opens with the 1942 order that removed every person of Japanese descent from the West Coast. Takei's family is forced from their home and held first at the Santa Anita racetrack, then sent by train to the Rohwer camp in Arkansas. Seen through a small child's eyes, the experience is sometimes strange and even playful, while the adults around him carry fear, loss and humiliation. That gap between a child's view and an adult's understanding gives the book much of its power.

Takei describes how his parents responded to injustice. His mother made hard choices to protect the family, and his father held on to faith in democracy even as the government imprisoned them. Later the family was moved to Tule Lake, a higher-security segregation camp for people the government labeled disloyal. This shows how questions of loyalty were used to sort and punish Japanese Americans. Throughout, Takei sets his memories alongside the history of the period and the decisions that made the camps possible.

The adult Takei appears throughout, including in remembered kitchen-table conversations with his father about what the family had lived through. These scenes tie the camp years to his later work in theater and politics, and to the questions the book keeps asking: what it means to be American, and who gets to decide. The publisher describes a childhood shaped by legalized racism, and the book shows how those years planted the seeds of a lifelong commitment to equal rights.

Reviewers praised the book's power and its blend of humor and sorrow. Common Sense Media noted that the illustrations lend buoyancy to a sometimes grim story, and Kirkus called it a powerful reminder of a history. Some critics, including in the New York Times, felt its frequent shifts between past and present can feel disjointed. The graphic form makes the book accessible to many readers, and it has been widely taught in schools, even as it has also been challenged in some.
mainPoints: The incarceration of Japanese Americans in World War II was a government policy of legalized racism.
Children and adults experienced the camps very differently.
Families made hard choices to protect one another under injustice.
Questions of loyalty were used to divide and punish Japanese Americans.
The memory of incarceration has shaped Japanese American civic life and activism.
One person's memory can become a lifelong commitment to civil rights.
relevance: They Called Us Enemy gives DSD staff a personal, readable account of the history the Japanese Minnesota brief calls literacy for the desk. It helps staff understand why government programs, eligibility questions and records may feel weighty to some Japanese American elders and families, and why the brief warns against opening with internment. The graphic form makes it a strong choice for team discussion. Takei's family was from California, not Minnesota, and the book is one family's story. Most Japanese Minnesotans today are later descendants, mixed families, company transferees or newcomers with other histories. Use it as background that helps staff listen well, never as a script for a conversation.
questions: How might the history of incarceration shape how some Japanese American families experience government questions about loyalty, records or eligibility?
Why does the brief advise against opening with internment, and how do we hold that knowledge respectfully?
What does Takei's father's faith in democracy, despite injustice, teach us about the trust people place in public systems?

title: Unbowed: A Memoir
overview: Unbowed is the memoir of Wangari Maathai, the Kenyan biologist, organizer and public servant. She founded the Green Belt Movement in 1977 and later received the Nobel Peace Prize. Born in 1940 near Nyeri in the central highlands, she tells her own story, which begins with a rural Kikuyu childhood under British rule, moves through study in the United States, and covers decades of environmental and democratic organizing in Kenya. Her life runs alongside the country's history from late colonialism to the early 2000s. So the book works both as a personal account and as an accessible introduction to modern Kenya, told by one of its best-known daughters.
summary: The early chapters describe childhood in a farming community in the shadow of Mount Kenya. There, land, streams and trees carried spiritual and practical meaning. Maathai shows how missionaries and British settlers reshaped that world as they moved people off land, pushed cash crops and changed how families lived and worshiped. She also describes the Mau Mau period and the mass detentions of the 1950s, which touched her own family and community. These pages give readers a grounded picture of how colonial rule reached into ordinary households. They also show why land and dignity remain such deep themes for many Kenyans today.

Maathai was one of relatively few girls of her generation to stay in school, and education runs as a thread through the whole book. In 1960 she traveled to Kansas through a scholarship effort often called the Kennedy Airlift. She later began graduate study at the University of Pittsburgh. She writes about seeing American segregation and the civil rights movement up close, and she credits those years with shaping her sense of what ordinary people can demand of their governments. For Minnesota readers, this section is a reminder that Kenyan ties to the United States go back several generations.

Returning to Kenya, Maathai joined the University of Nairobi, where she became a pioneering woman scientist and faculty member. She describes her marriage to a politician and the painful public divorce that followed, after which she lost her academic post and her housing. She is frank about how gender expectations limited what an educated woman could do in independent Kenya. She also shows how quickly a woman's standing could be challenged in court and in the press.

The heart of the book is the Green Belt Movement. In this grassroots effort, rural women planted trees to fight erosion, lack of firewood, poor water and failing soil. Maathai explains how the work grew from practical household needs into a broader movement. It came to be about civic voice, women's leadership and the link between a damaged environment and deepening poverty. Over time the movement planted tens of millions of trees. Still, she makes clear that it was never only about trees; it was about women gaining the confidence to speak in public and hold leaders to account.

In the later chapters, environmental work becomes openly political. Maathai describes opposing illegal land transfers under President Daniel arap Moi and organizing alongside opposition leaders. She spoke against ethnic violence in the Rift Valley and was arrested and beaten more than once. She closes with the democratic transition of 2002 and her election to Parliament, after which she served as a junior minister for the environment. Finally, she tells of the Nobel Peace Prize, news she learned while traveling on a rural road.
mainPoints: Colonial land policy and the Mau Mau era left lasting marks on Kikuyu families and on Kenya as a whole.
For many Kenyan families, education has long been a central hope and a serious investment.
Women's daily work with water, firewood and food can be the starting point for real public leadership.
Environmental harm, poverty and conflict are linked, and practical local solutions can address all three.
Kenyan ties to the United States, including study in America, go back to the early 1960s.
Standing up to an authoritarian government carried real personal costs, including arrest and violence.
One person's story can open Kenyan history, but Kenya holds many peoples and many different histories.
relevance: For DSD staff, Unbowed offers a respectful way into the history many Kenyan Minnesotans carry. That history touches land, schooling, women's leadership and a guarded relationship with government. The book can help staff understand why some families want clear explanations of rights, written records and a real role in decisions before they trust a public program. The Green Belt Movement is also a useful example of community-led partnership that starts from what households actually need. Keep its limits in mind. This is the story of one Kikuyu woman. It should not be read as a description of Luo, Luhya, Kalenjin, Kamba, Somali or other Kenyan communities. A Brookings review by Susan Rice found the later chapters emotionally guarded and less revealing about Maathai's private life. Use the book to ask better questions, and let each family tell you which language, faith and history are theirs.
questions: Maathai's movement began with women's daily needs for water and firewood. What are the everyday needs our services touch first, and how could we start from those when we engage Kenyan families?
How might a history of land loss, detention and government pressure shape the way some families respond to forms, home visits or eligibility rules?
Kenya holds many peoples and languages. How do we make sure we ask each household about its own language and community instead of assuming a single Kenyan story?

title: One Day I Will Write About This Place: A Memoir
overview: Binyavanga Wainaina was a Kenyan writer, born in Nakuru, who won the Caine Prize for African Writing in 2002 and founded the Nairobi literary magazine Kwani?. He was also known for the satirical essay "How to Write About Africa," which mocked the tired clichés outsiders use to describe the continent. This memoir, published by Minneapolis-based Graywolf Press and named a New York Times notable book, follows his middle-class Kenyan childhood, his unsettled years as a student in South Africa, and his return to a changing Kenya. It is funny, restless and deeply attentive to language, and it offers a contemporary, urban Kenyan voice.
summary: The book opens in childhood, in a home where Wainaina often felt slightly out of step with the world around him. His father held a long career as a senior manager at the Kenya Pyrethrum Board, and his mother, who was Ugandan, ran a hair salon. Wainaina captures the sounds, music, school routines and family rhythms of a professional Kenyan household in the decades after independence. Reviewers note that this kind of ordinary, educated, salaried African family life is rarely shown in books written for American readers, which is part of what makes the memoir valuable.

Language runs through every chapter. Wainaina moves among English, Kiswahili, Gikuyu, the Nairobi street language Sheng and other tongues, and he pays close attention to who speaks what, where and why. He shows how a shift into Gikuyu in an office can signal ethnic belonging, and how a matatu tout switches languages to suit each passenger. He treats Kiswahili as a shared national language that helps Kenyans live together across many communities.

As a young man, Wainaina went to South Africa to study commerce as apartheid was ending. The memoir describes that period as drifting and unhappy, marked by heavy drinking, quiet guilt about his parents' expectations, and the strangeness of watching a country remake itself. Political events of those years appear through his personal experience rather than as a history lesson. He is candid about feeling lost during these years and about how hard it was to tell his family that the plan was not working. The section reads as a portrait of a young person far from home, unsure of his direction and quietly carrying the weight of others' hopes.

The book also follows a family reunion in Uganda, his mother's home country, and journeys across Kenya that widen his sense of the country's many regions and peoples. These travels, along with his growing work as a writer, help him understand his own mixed inheritance and the variety of lives Kenyans lead. Reviewers describe the multicultural, multiethnic world these chapters reveal, in which belonging can cross national borders as easily as it crosses languages. These journeys feed his sense that no single story can capture what it means to be Kenyan, and that the country's variety is a strength as much as a source of strain.

In the later chapters Wainaina returns to Kenya as its politics shift, touching on the rigged 1997 election, the long rule of Daniel arap Moi, and later the 2007 post-election violence. Reviewers note that he treats these events as struggles for power in a modern state, not as ancient tribal hatreds, and that he handles them lightly rather than in depth. Throughout, he reflects on how he learned to write about his own place in his own terms, rather than for the expectations of outside judges.
mainPoints: Kenyan family life includes many educated, salaried, urban households whose stories are seldom told abroad.
Many Kenyans move among several languages in a single day, and each language can carry a different relationship.
Kiswahili often works as a shared national language that bridges many ethnic communities.
Mixed family heritage across East African borders is common and can shape a person's sense of identity.
Political violence in Kenya is better understood as a contest for power than as ancient tribal hatred.
Africans want to describe their own lives without the clichés outsiders often bring.
A young person can carry heavy family expectations about education and success while privately struggling.
relevance: This memoir helps DSD staff meet Kenyan Minnesotans as people with full, modern and varied lives, not as a single story of hardship. Its close attention to language is directly useful: a household may speak English with a provider, Kiswahili with neighbors and Gikuyu, Luo or another language with elders, so staff should ask which language each person wants for each conversation and book interpreters accordingly. The book also shows how family expectations and private struggles can sit side by side, which matters when a young adult with a disability, or a caregiver, may not want to disappoint relatives. Keep its limits in mind. It is one writer's Kikuyu and Ugandan, middle-class story, the tone is playful and digressive, and reviewers note that major political events are treated lightly. Use it to widen your picture, then let each person define their own story.
questions: Wainaina shows people choosing different languages for different relationships. How do we ask families which language they want for which kind of conversation, and do our interpreter practices allow for that?
Where might our materials or habits rely on the same clichés about Africa that this book pushes against, and how could we change them?
How might strong family expectations about education and success shape the way a Kenyan young adult or caregiver talks with us about disability and support?

title: Koreans in Minnesota
editionNote: First published 2019 · Minnesota Historical Society Press · 112 pages
overview: Koreans in Minnesota is part of the Minnesota Historical Society Press People of Minnesota series. Its author, Sooh-Rhee Ryu, is an associate professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-River Falls. Drawing on interviews with community members and on archival research, this short, illustrated book traces Korean Minnesotans from the first arrivals of the mid-twentieth century to the students, professionals and family networks that followed. It treats immigrant Korean households and Korean adoptees as two parts of one Minnesota story. It also notes that adoptees have a deeper tie to Minnesota than to any other state.
summary: Ryu opens with the early history of Korean arrival in Minnesota, in the years around the Korean War. A small number of early settlers, students and spouses laid the groundwork for a community that grew slowly at first. The book includes a personal account from Soon Ja Lee, who came to Minnesota in 1953 and, with her husband, helped build many of the community's first institutions. Her story gives readers a human way into a history that is often told only in numbers.

The book then follows the community's growth after immigration law changed, as students, professionals and relatives joined earlier arrivals. Ryu describes where Korean Minnesotans settled, how they found work, and how family networks shaped who came and when. This section shows that Korean Minnesota is not one wave but several. Each has its own reasons for coming, its own tie to Korea and its own experience of building a life in the Upper Midwest.

A central part of the story is community life. Ryu shows how churches and other religious groups became gathering places for worship, language, mutual aid and celebration. She describes social and cultural groups, including the Korean American Association of Minnesota. She also describes the schools and groups that teach Korean language and culture to younger generations. These institutions show how a fairly small community kept its traditions and supported newcomers. They also created spaces where Korean was spoken and honored.

The book gives special attention to two groups that matter for public service. It profiles the Korean Service Center, which supports elderly Koreans, many of whom rely on Korean for health care and daily life. It also describes AK Connection, a network for adult Korean adoptees. Ryu places adoptees inside the Korean Minnesota story rather than outside it, and in doing so she affirms that adoptees are part of the state's history. Their experience is different from that of immigrant families, but connected to it.

Like other books in the series, it is short and easy to read, with photographs and a brief list of further resources. One reader noted that the later chapters read somewhat like a directory of community families and organizations. Still, those stories are worth knowing. Readers who want a deeper account of adoption history, or of adoptees' own voices, will need to pair it with memoir and scholarship by adoptees. Its value lies in gathering many local names and places in one accessible place.
mainPoints: Korean Minnesotans have been part of the state since the years around the Korean War.
The community grew through several streams, including early settlers, students, professionals and family networks.
Churches and religious groups have been central to Korean community life in Minnesota.
Language and culture schools help younger generations keep ties to Korean language and heritage.
Organizations such as the Korean Service Center support Korean-speaking elders.
Korean adoptees are part of Minnesota's Korean history and have built their own networks, such as AK Connection.
Immigrant households and adoptee households share a heritage but often live very different experiences.
Community interviews and personal accounts, such as Soon Ja Lee's, ground the history in real lives.
relevance: Koreans in Minnesota gives the Korean Minnesota brief a local, historical foundation. It supports the brief's central point: two different kinds of households share this heritage. One is immigrant families, including elders who may need Korean in the lobby. The other is Korean adoptees, many raised in white Minnesota families. Staff can use the book to learn which community groups already serve elders and adoptees. That helps when planning outreach, interpretation and partnership. The book also reminds staff not to assume that an English-dominant person has no Korean identity. Nor should staff ask any one person to speak for the community. It is a short survey written for a general audience. So it offers less depth on adoption policy, adoptee experience or current needs. Pair it with adoptee voices and with current community partners.
questions: How do we make sure our services meet the needs of Korean-speaking elders as well as English-dominant Korean adoptees?
What assumptions might we make about a person's culture or language based on their name, their family or the language they use with us?
Which Minnesota Korean organizations could help us understand current needs, and how would we build that relationship respectfully?

title: The Language of Blood: A Memoir
editionNote: First published 2003 · Borealis Books (Minnesota Historical Society Press)
overview: The Language of Blood is a memoir by Jane Jeong Trenka, who was born in Seoul in 1972 and adopted as an infant, with her sister, by a family in rural northern Minnesota. First published in 2003 by Borealis Books, an imprint of the Minnesota Historical Society Press, and later by Graywolf Press, it won the Minnesota Book Award for Autobiography and Memoir and the award for New Voice. Trenka tells her story through an inventive mix of forms, following her from a Minnesota childhood to a reunion with her Korean birth mother.
summary: The memoir begins on her adoptive family's farm in rural Minnesota, in a conservative Christian household. Trenka describes a childhood in which she tried hard to please and to belong, while carrying a quiet sense of being split between two mothers and two lives. Her account gives readers a close view of what it can mean to grow up as a Korean child in a small, mostly white Minnesota community, where questions about origins are rarely asked out loud.

As she grows into adolescence and young adulthood, Trenka begins to question the story she was given about her adoption and her identity. She writes about longing for wholeness and about the distance between how others saw her and how she understood herself. This part of the book shows how identity for an adoptee is not settled in childhood, and how questions about race, family and belonging can grow sharper with time.

In college, Trenka is stalked by an acquaintance who is fixated on her Asian heritage. She uses this frightening experience to examine how Asian women are made exotic and how that can lead to harm. Reviewers noted that she handles this difficult material with care and without cliché. The episode is hard to read, but it helps readers understand how racialized attention can follow a person into places that seem safe.

The final part of the memoir follows her return to Korea and her reunion with her birth mother. Trenka writes about language, loss and the effort to connect across years of separation and a language she did not grow up speaking. The reunion does not resolve every question, but it transforms how she understands her family and herself. The book's title points to this search for a shared language that blood alone cannot supply.

Throughout, Trenka breaks from a straight narrative. She includes passages written as a play or screenplay, crossword puzzles, myths and dream sequences. Publishers Weekly praised the prose as original and beautiful, while noting that the path of the story is winding. Trenka later moved to Korea, wrote a second memoir, Fugitive Visions, and became an advocate for transparent adoption practices and the rights of adult adoptees. Her later work grew out of the questions this first book raised about adoption, truth and belonging.
mainPoints: Korean adoptees raised in Minnesota carry a heritage that is real even when it is not visible in their household.
An adoptee may feel connected to, and divided between, two families and two countries.
Questions of identity for adoptees often deepen in adolescence and adulthood rather than fading.
Racialized and exoticizing attention toward Asian women can lead to real harm.
Reunion with a birth family can bring connection and grief at the same time.
Language can be both a bridge and a barrier for adoptees who return to Korea.
Unusual literary forms can express experiences that a simple, straight story cannot.
relevance: The Language of Blood gives a personal, Minnesota-grounded voice to the adoptee side of the Korean Minnesota brief. It helps staff understand why an adult adoptee may be English-dominant, raised in a white family and still carry questions of heritage, loss and belonging that matter in care and planning. It also cautions against assuming that adoption is a simple or settled story, or that every adoptee feels the same way about Korea, their adoptive family or their birth family. Staff can use it to listen more carefully and to ask, rather than assume, how a person describes their identity and family. It is one adoptee's story, with painful content including stalking, and it should not be read as speaking for all adoptees. Pair it with Koreans in Minnesota and with adoptee-led organizations.
questions: How might our intake questions about family, heritage or language feel to an adult adoptee, and how could we ask them more respectfully?
What do we lose when we assume a person has no cultural connection because they were raised by a white Minnesota family?
How can we learn from adoptee-led organizations without asking any one person to represent all adoptees?

title: A History of Laos
editionNote: First published 1997 · Cambridge University Press · 253 pages
overview: Martin Stuart-Fox is an emeritus professor of history at the University of Queensland and a longtime scholar of Laos. He wrote A History of Laos as a concise English-language account of the country, from its royal past to the one-party state of the 1990s. Reviewers welcomed it as one of the first general histories of Laos in English. It traces the old kingdom of Lan Xang, French colonial rule, independence, the long war years, and the period after the Pathet Lao took power in 1975. It gives readers the Lao national story on its own terms, rather than as a side note to the war in Vietnam.
summary: The book is organized in four broad parts. The first covers early history and the kingdom of Lan Xang, whose territory was far larger than modern Laos. Stuart-Fox explains how Siamese and Vietnamese interventions in the eighteenth century, and the borders drawn in 1893, left many ethnic Lao living in what is now northeast Thailand. This history helps explain why Lao identity, language and culture stretch across today's borders, and why neighboring states have long pressed claims on Laos.

The second part examines French rule. As reviewers summarize it, Stuart-Fox describes a colonial government that ruled with few officials and imposed taxes that sparked rebellions, and it relied on a small number of ruling families and a narrow educated elite. The French encouraged Vietnamese and Chinese migration into towns and filled many clerical posts with Vietnamese staff. This limited Lao advancement in government and the professions, and it shaped tensions that would surface again after independence.

The third part follows independence, won in 1953, and the decades of conflict that followed. Stuart-Fox traces the rise of the communist movement and its close ties to Vietnam, as well as the heavy American intervention of the war years. He argues that foreign involvement corroded Lao political life and encouraged corruption, including aid used for political ends rather than for development. Throughout, he stresses the country's complex and shifting alliances. That theme helps readers see Laos as a nation with its own politics, not a sideshow to its neighbors' wars.

The final part covers the years after 1975, when the Pathet Lao set up the Lao People's Democratic Republic. Fast, authoritarian policies brought economic hardship, mistrust and large-scale emigration, the departure that brought many Lao families to Minnesota and elsewhere. Stuart-Fox also describes the stability of the party leadership and argues that Laos was slowly returning to a traditional role as a neutral state. The book is mainly a political history of elites and governments, so readers who want village life, religion or family experience will need other sources.
mainPoints: Modern Laos is a smaller successor to the historic kingdom of Lan Xang.
Many ethnic Lao live across the border in northeast Thailand because of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century history.
French colonial rule was thin, and it limited Lao advancement in government and the professions.
Laos has a national history of its own, not only a role in the war in Vietnam.
Foreign intervention during the war years shaped Lao politics in lasting ways.
The changes after 1975 led to hardship and large-scale emigration, including to Minnesota.
Shifting alliances with powerful neighbors are a constant theme in Lao history.
relevance: The Lao Minnesota brief asks staff to see Lao people as a people of Laos with their own state history. They are not a footnote to the Secret War, and they are not interchangeable with Hmong neighbors. Stuart-Fox's history gives that grounding. It can help staff understand why a Lao family's departure after 1975 shaped their relationship with government. It also shows why language and identity link Lao communities with northeast Thailand. Reviewers note honest limits. The book is largely political and focused on elites, and it was written in the 1990s. One reviewer felt it judged foreign powers more sharply than the post-1975 government. Pair it with community voices and with Lao-led organizations in Minnesota. Use it to frame questions rather than to explain any individual.
questions: How does knowing the history of Lan Xang and the post-1975 period change how we think about Lao identity as distinct from Hmong, Thai or Vietnamese identity?
What might a family's experience of government after 1975 mean for how they approach our assessments and forms?
Which Lao community partners could help us fill the gaps a political history leaves out?

title: How to Pronounce Knife: Stories
editionNote: First published 2020 · McClelland & Stewart (Canada) and Little, Brown (United States)
overview: Souvankham Thammavongsa was born in the Lao refugee camp at Nong Khai, Thailand, and raised in Toronto. A poet before she was a fiction writer, she published How to Pronounce Knife, her first book of stories, in 2020. It won the Scotiabank Giller Prize, Canada's leading fiction award, and the Trillium Book Award, and it was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award. The fourteen stories center on working-class Lao immigrants and their children in North America, written in spare, precise prose that reviewers called both brutal and tender.
summary: The title story grows out of the author's own childhood. A young girl asks her father how to say the word knife, follows his answer, and is corrected and mocked in front of her class. Kirkus noted how the collection treats knowledge itself as a form of privilege: the child who does not know the expected answer pays a price, even when her family has given her everything they have. The story shows how children of immigrants often protect their parents from the small humiliations of a new country.

Many stories take place at work. In one, a woman who plucks chickens in a factory dreams of a different face and a different job, then watches an office position go to a recent graduate whose father works in the front office. In another, a former boxer works at his sister's nail salon and becomes fixed on a client's hands. These stories make visible the low-wage labor that many immigrants and refugees do, and the dignity, longing and humor people bring to it.

Other stories turn to family and love. A mother and daughter harvest earthworms in the middle of the night; a housewife devoted to country music abandons her family for a fantasy; a girl's love for her father carries across the language between them. The publisher describes lives lived amid isolation and severed history, yet the book is also full of joy, humor, resilience and wonder. Because many narrators are children, the stories often explore the vulnerability of not knowing how things work.

Thammavongsa conveys a great deal in a few carefully chosen words, so the stories are quick to read and slow to forget. Reviewers praised the spare, distant tone that still moves the reader, and the jury that awarded the Giller Prize described the collection as a clear-eyed exploration of immigrant lives. Kirkus also noted a limit: some stories lean on stereotypes, especially of wealthier characters, to make their point. The settings are unnamed North American cities rather than Minnesota.
mainPoints: Children of immigrants often carry and shield their parents' struggles in a new country.
Knowledge of unwritten rules functions as a kind of privilege.
Low-wage work is a central setting of immigrant life, full of dignity and longing.
Language barriers can coexist with deep love inside families.
Humor and resilience live alongside isolation and loss.
A spare, careful voice can carry a whole history without stating it.
relevance: How to Pronounce Knife offers DSD staff a contemporary Lao voice that is neither a war story nor a history lesson. It brings into focus the working lives, family roles and quiet pressures that many Lao Minnesotans and their children may know, including the role of a child who interprets the world for a parent. That insight supports the brief's call to book a qualified Lao interpreter rather than relying on family members, and to explain systems without making people feel they should already know the rules. The author is Lao Canadian and the stories are fiction set in unnamed cities, so they are not a portrait of Minnesota's community. Read them to sharpen empathy and to ask better questions.
questions: Where in our processes might a person feel like the child in the title story, expected to know an answer no one taught them?
How can we avoid placing children or relatives in the role of interpreter for a family member?
What do these stories suggest about the connection between work, disability and dignity for the people we serve?

title: Inventing Home: Emigration, Gender, and the Middle Class in Lebanon, 1870-1920
editionNote: First published 2001 · University of California Press
overview: Inventing Home is a history by Akram Fouad Khater, a historian of the Middle East at North Carolina State University and a leading scholar of the Lebanese diaspora. It studies the decades between the 1860 conflicts in Mount Lebanon and the French mandate of 1920. In those years, more than a third of the peasants of Mount Lebanon left their villages, most for the Americas. Khater follows these emigrants abroad and back home. He shows how migration, returning migrants and new ideas about women and family helped create a new Lebanese middle class. It is the history behind the first Lebanese families who settled in places like Minnesota.
summary: The opening chapter, A Departure from the Ordinary, sets the scene in the villages of Mount Lebanon in the late nineteenth century. Khater describes peasant households, their ties to land and to local notables, and the economic pressures that made the old ways of life harder to keep up. He explains why, between 1890 and 1920, so many villagers decided to try their fortunes across the ocean. This chapter gives readers a clear picture of the world the emigrants were leaving, and of the hopes and pressures that shaped their choice.

As its title suggests, a chapter called Factory Girls turns to young village women who worked in the mountain's factories. Khater uses their experience to examine shifting gender roles and ideas about family and respectability. He shows that women took an active part in the economic changes of the period. The chapter shows that the changes in family life that came with migration had roots in the mountain itself. The story of Lebanese emigration cannot be told only through men's journeys.

The chapters on Emigration and on the Mahjar, the Arabic word for the diaspora, follow villagers on their journeys and into new lives in the Americas. Khater shows how life abroad, and the ties emigrants kept with family and village, brought new money and new ideas about home and comfort. They also brought new expectations of men and women. In Khater's account, emigrants did not cut ties with home; they lived in ongoing connection with family in the mountain. This two-way connection is central to his argument about how a new middle class took shape.

In Back to the Mountain, Khater turns to the many migrants who returned. They brought savings, new tastes and new ideas back to their villages. Khater traces how these returns reshaped family life and social standing. The book shows that migration was often a circle rather than a one-way trip. This return movement, Khater argues, mattered as much as the departure in changing Lebanese society. Returnees brought back expectations about comfort, family life and respectability that set them apart from neighbors who had stayed. These differences helped shape new social classes in the villages.

The chapter A Woman's Boundaries and an epilogue on the making of a middle class pull these threads together. Khater argues that Lebanese villagers did not simply copy Western ways. Instead, they created their own local form of modern life. It was shaped by migration, by debates over women's roles, and by a growing sense of middle-class respectability that still echoes in Lebanese families today. For readers now, the argument offers a way to understand the pride, ambition and family loyalty that run through many Lebanese family histories.
mainPoints: Large-scale Lebanese migration to the Americas began in the late nineteenth century, so many Lebanese American families have roots going back generations.
Economic pressure in the villages of Mount Lebanon, not only conflict, pushed many people to emigrate.
Emigrants kept close ties with family and home villages across great distances.
Many emigrants returned home, and migration moved people, money and ideas in both directions.
Debates about women's work, family honor and respectability were central to how Lebanese families changed.
Lebanese communities created their own form of modern life rather than simply adopting Western ways.
Connections between diaspora families and home villages have long shaped Lebanese identity.
relevance: For DSD staff, Khater's history explains why the Lebanese Minnesota community is both historic and recent. Some families have been in Minnesota for several generations and may be English-dominant, while others arrived more recently. The book covers the long history of village networks, family enterprise, return visits and strong ideas about family standing. Knowing that history can help staff appreciate the role of extended family and community reputation when someone discusses disability, care or services. Keep its limits in mind. This is a scholarly history written for an academic audience, so it can be dense. It focuses on Mount Lebanon from 1870 to 1920. It does not cover the civil war, later migrations or the variety of Lebanese communities by faith and region. Pair it with a personal voice, and always ask each family about its own history, language and faith.
questions: Some Lebanese Minnesotan families have been here for generations and may prefer English. How do we avoid defaulting to an Arabic interpreter or other assumptions based on a surname?
Khater shows how important family standing and respectability were to Lebanese households. How might those values shape the way a family talks with us about disability?
Migration often moved in both directions, with ongoing ties to home villages. How could transnational family ties affect planning, decision-making or who a person wants involved?

title: House of Stone: A Memoir of Home, Family, and a Lost Middle East
overview: Anthony Shadid was a Lebanese American journalist, born and raised in Oklahoma City, who won the Pulitzer Prize for his reporting from the Middle East. House of Stone, a finalist for the National Book Award, is his memoir of taking a year away from journalism to rebuild his great-grandfather's house in Marjayoun, in southern Lebanon, after it was damaged in the 2006 war. Shadid died while on assignment in Syria shortly before the book was published. It weaves together his family's emigration to America, the history of the town and the region, and his own search for home.
summary: The memoir begins with Shadid covering the 2006 war in Lebanon and finding his family's ancestral house in Marjayoun, long abandoned and struck by a rocket. The house had been built by his great-grandfather, and his grandmother had lived there for her first twelve years before the family left for America. Worn down by years of covering war and going through a painful divorce, Shadid decides to restore the house as a way to restore himself.

Much of the book follows the slow, often comic work of rebuilding: getting permits, finding stonemasons and other craftsmen, arguing over materials and timelines, and negotiating with relatives about who has a say in the family home. The local characters have strong personalities, and the project becomes a way to understand small-town life and the patience it requires. Shadid writes about these frustrations with humor and affection. The rebuilding becomes a lesson in local ways of working, where relationships, reputation and patience matter as much as plans and money.

Alongside the rebuilding, Shadid traces the history of two family lines, the Samaras and the Shadids, who came together in Marjayoun in the late nineteenth century. As the Ottoman Empire collapsed after World War I, upheaval pushed many families to emigrate, including his own, who eventually built new lives in Oklahoma. He writes movingly of what emigrants carried with them and what they left behind. These family stories give the book its depth, linking a single house to the larger history of migration from the eastern Mediterranean to the Americas.

Shadid also describes the community around him in Marjayoun, a place of Christians, Muslims and others, marked by loss and division but also held together by close customs, food, hospitality and shared memory. He reconnects with the rhythms of Arabic and with the textures of daily life he had rarely seen as a war correspondent. Kirkus describes the narrative as a gentle unfolding of observation and insight. Shadid documents a way of life he sees disappearing, along with the habits and memories of neighbors who have lived through war and loss.

The book closes with reflections on home as both a physical place and a feeling of belonging, and on a region whose older ways of living together he feared were vanishing. The final pages, written after a frightening period of detention in Libya, describe his return to the house and his daughter's first visit. The book is also, quietly, about a father and a daughter, and about passing a sense of home to the next generation. Because Shadid died before publication, many readers experience these last pages with added poignancy.
mainPoints: Many Lebanese American families trace their roots to villages they left a century or more ago.
The family home and village of origin can carry deep meaning across generations.
Lebanese communities include Christians, Muslims and others, with histories of both coexistence and conflict.
Hospitality, food and shared memory are central to Lebanese community life.
War and displacement have touched many Lebanese families, including those settled abroad for generations.
Lebanese Americans may hold a strong sense of heritage while having grown up fully in the United States.
Restoring a sense of home can be part of healing after loss.
relevance: For DSD staff, House of Stone offers a warm way to understand Lebanese Minnesotans whose families may have lived in the United States for generations yet still feel close ties to an ancestral village, extended family and Lebanese food, faith and custom. It shows why a person might be fully American in language and daily life while their sense of family obligation, hospitality and home remains rooted in Lebanon. That can matter when staff talk with families about where someone will live, who helps decide and what home means to them. Keep its limits in mind. This is one family's story, written by an Oklahoma-raised journalist, and its tone is nostalgic, so it may romanticize the past. It does not speak for recent Lebanese arrivals or for every faith or region in Lebanon. Use it to open conversations, not to predict them.
questions: Shadid shows how a family home can carry meaning across generations. How do we learn what home means to each person when we plan housing or support?
How might a person be fully English-speaking and American in daily life yet hold strong Lebanese family values, and how do we avoid assuming either way?
Lebanese communities include many faiths and histories. What questions help us understand a particular family's background without relying on stereotypes?

title: The House at Sugar Beach: In Search of a Lost African Childhood
overview: Helene Cooper is a Liberian-born journalist and Pulitzer Prize winner who has reported for The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times. In this memoir she traces her family back to settlers who sailed from New York in 1820 to help found Monrovia, describes a privileged childhood in a large seaside house, and follows her family's flight after the 1980 military coup. The book blends personal story with Liberian history, from the founding of the republic through the coup and the wars that followed, and ends with her return to Liberia in search of the foster sister her family left behind.
summary: Cooper begins with Liberia's founding by freed and free-born Black Americans who settled on the West African coast in the nineteenth century. Her family descends from two of these settler lines, part of the group Liberians often call Congo or Americo-Liberian. She explains how this small settler class came to hold power, wealth and social standing over the many Indigenous peoples of the country for more than a century, a divide that shapes everything that follows.

Her childhood at Sugar Beach, outside Monrovia, was comfortable: a large house, servants, travel and private school. When she was eight, her family took in Eunice, a Bassa girl, as a foster child, a custom among elite families at the time. Eunice became known as Mrs. Cooper's daughter and a sister to Helene. Cooper writes about this bond with warmth, and the book slowly asks what that kind of arrangement meant across lines of class and ethnicity.

On April 12, 1980, soldiers led by Samuel Doe overthrew the government, killed President William Tolbert and executed members of his cabinet. Cooper's family was directly affected, and members of the settler class became targets of imprisonment and violence. After a terrifying attack on their home, Cooper, her mother and her sister fled to the United States. Eunice stayed behind. Cooper describes the shock of a comfortable childhood ending almost overnight, and the fear that followed for families like hers. This part of the book makes vivid how quickly status, safety and home could disappear for Liberians caught on the wrong side of a political upheaval.

In America, Cooper rebuilt her life, finished school and became a reporter, eventually covering many regions of the world for major newspapers while avoiding Liberia as it slid into years of civil war. She describes the distance she kept from her country, and the coping habit of focusing on small details after painful events. She writes honestly about the distance this created between her American career and her Liberian past, and about the guilt of having left Eunice behind. Readers see how a person can succeed in a new country while a part of their life stays unresolved in the old one, a pattern many immigrant families will recognize.

A near-death experience while reporting in Iraq in 2003 convinced Cooper she could no longer put off going home. The final part of the book follows her return to Liberia and her search for Eunice, who had lived through the years Cooper spent away. The reunion becomes a way to reckon with family, privilege, loss and the long road toward healing. Cooper presents her return as a story of grief, forgiveness and the long work of coming home. The meeting with Eunice also invites readers to think about how differently two girls raised in the same house could experience the same national history, depending on where each began.
mainPoints: Liberia was founded by Black American settlers, and its history ties directly to the United States.
For more than a century, a settler elite held power over the country's many Indigenous peoples, and that divide still matters.
The 1980 coup ended that order violently and opened decades of instability and war.
Many Liberian Minnesotans carry family histories of sudden flight, separation and loss.
Fostering and informal adoption have been part of Liberian family life, and they can cross lines of class and ethnicity.
Distance from a homeland can be a way of coping, and returning can reopen old grief.
Healing in a family or a nation often requires facing unequal histories honestly.
relevance: For DSD staff, Cooper's memoir explains Liberia's settler and Indigenous history, the 1980 coup and the long shadow of war, all of which can shape how Liberian Minnesotans relate to government, record keeping and family obligations. It is also a useful entry point for understanding fostering and extended family care, which may affect who a person considers family, who helps with decisions and who should be invited to a planning meeting. Keep its limits clearly in view. Cooper writes from the vantage of the former elite, and the experiences of Bassa, Kpelle, Gio, Mano, Kru, Vai and other Liberians were often very different; Eunice's story is a reminder of that gap. Publishers Weekly found the prose somewhat flat at times. Use the book to understand context, and let each family tell you where they come from and what the wars meant for them.
questions: The book shows a family that included a foster child as a daughter. How do our intake and planning practices make room for the people a family names as kin, even when there is no legal tie?
How might a family's experience of sudden flight and loss affect how they respond to urgent deadlines, home visits or requests for documents?
Cooper writes from one side of Liberia's social divide. How can we make sure we hear from Liberians whose history and standing were very different from hers?

title: The Dragons, the Giant, the Women: A Memoir
overview: Wayétu Moore is a Liberian American novelist, author of She Would Be King, who was born in Monrovia and raised largely in Texas. This memoir, published by Minneapolis-based Graywolf Press and a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award in autobiography, tells how her family fled the first Liberian civil war in 1990 when she was five, how her mother came back across borders to bring them out, and what it was like to grow up as a Black African immigrant girl in the United States. It is a contemporary, intimate voice that pairs well with a broader history of Liberia.
summary: The first part is told through the eyes of a five-year-old in Monrovia who mostly wants her mother, who is away studying and working in New York. When war breaks out, Moore's father, grandmother and sisters flee their home on foot. The child explains what she sees through the stories she knows: a leader becomes a dragon, gunfire becomes drumming, and the dead appear to be sleeping. The family walks and hides for about three weeks until they reach a village called Lai near the Sierra Leone border.

Reviewers note that this opening section gives little political background, which mirrors how a young child understands events only in part. It invites readers to learn more about the war on their own, though some may find the missing context frustrating. What it offers instead is a vivid sense of how families experienced the conflict day by day, and how children made sense of it. For readers in public service, the section is a reminder that children who lived through war may hold memories that are vivid yet incomplete, and that the full story may only come into focus years later, if ever.

The second part moves to the United States, where the family settles in Texas. Moore writes about racism, hostility and the steady stream of misconceptions she faced as an immigrant and a Black girl, including painful remarks about her hair from people close to her. She describes the bonds among African immigrants and the stereotypes they meet together. One reviewer stresses that the book refuses the idea that an immigrant's difficulties end once they arrive.

The third part shifts to her mother's point of view. In 1990, after communication from Liberia stopped, her mother flew to Sierra Leone to find her family. These chapters show her worry, courage and resourcefulness, and they tell the story of a teenage girl serving as a rebel soldier who risked her life to help smuggle the family across the border. This section fills in what the child could not see.

In the final chapters Moore returns to her own voice. The book's braided structure, child, adult and mother, makes a quiet argument: a family's story of war and migration is never only one story, and each person who lived it carries a different piece. Reviewers praised the lyrical prose and the way the shifting points of view work together. By the end, readers understand that the child's dragons, the adult's daily encounters with racism and the mother's journey across borders all belong to the same family history, and that each voice is needed to tell it fully.
mainPoints: Many Liberian Minnesotans, or their parents, lived through war as children and carry those memories in different ways.
Children often make sense of trauma through imagination and story, and adults may only learn later what they experienced.
Mothers and other women often carried families through war, sometimes at great personal risk.
Help sometimes came from unexpected people, including young people on the other side of the conflict.
Arriving in the United States did not end hardship; racism and misunderstanding became new challenges.
African immigrants and African Americans share some experiences of race in America, but their histories are distinct.
A family's history can only be understood by listening to several members, not just one.
relevance: This memoir can help DSD staff understand the layered experience of Liberian Minnesotans who came after the civil wars, especially those who were children at the time and now are parents, caregivers or people receiving services themselves. It shows why a family's account may differ depending on who is speaking, and why it helps to make room for more than one voice in planning. It also highlights the double weight of being both an immigrant and Black in America, which can affect trust in public systems. Approach it with care. The book describes war and does not explain Liberia's politics in depth, so pair it with a history such as The House at Sugar Beach. It is one family's story, and staff should never assume that any Liberian person shares these memories or wants to talk about the war.
questions: Moore's book tells the same events from a child's, an adult's and a mother's point of view. How do we make space for several family members' perspectives in person-centered planning?
What would trauma-informed practice look like for a Liberian family where the war is part of the background but may never be named?
How do we avoid treating Liberian Minnesotans and African American Minnesotans as one community while still recognizing shared experiences of race?

title: Mexicans in Minnesota
editionNote: First published 2005 · Minnesota Historical Society Press · 112 pages
overview: Dionicio Nodín Valdés is a historian of Mexican and Mexican American life in the Midwest. He taught at Michigan State University and wrote the longer studies Barrios Norteños and Al Norte. Mexicans in Minnesota is his short volume in the Minnesota Historical Society Press People of Minnesota series, with a foreword by the Minnesota writer Bill Holm. It traces Mexican and Mexican American Minnesotans from the early twentieth century to the start of the twenty-first. It argues that their story is above all a working-class story, rooted as much in rural towns as in St. Paul.
summary: Valdés opens with the point that frames the whole book: Mexicans first came to the Upper Midwest to work, not to settle. In the early decades of the twentieth century, railroads, heavy industry, meatpacking and the sugar beet fields recruited Mexican and Mexican American laborers. Many arrived expecting to stay only for a season. The publisher notes that, more than for most immigrant groups, the history of Mexicans in the Midwest is a history of working people. Valdés keeps labor at the center of his account throughout.

Farm labor gets special attention. Sugar beet production in the Red River Valley and elsewhere depended on families who traveled north for the growing and harvest seasons, often from Texas and Mexico. Valdés describes the struggles migrant workers faced in making Minnesota a home. The work was hard and poorly paid, and the housing was seasonal. The reception welcomed their labor while treating them as outsiders among a mostly Northern European population. This double message, wanted as workers but not fully as neighbors, runs through much of the book.

The book then follows the building of lasting communities. St. Paul's West Side became the best-known Mexican neighborhood in the state, home to churches, businesses, mutual aid and cultural groups. Valdés shows how families kept religious, social and cultural institutions going over generations. He also shows how Mexican foods and conjunto music became part of the wider Minnesota landscape. He treats these institutions as the community's own answer to exclusion, created by residents rather than handed to them.

A distinctive theme is the growth, late in the twentieth century, of barrios and colonias in towns outside the Twin Cities. Valdés presents this as something new in Minnesota history. Mexican and Mexican American families put down roots in rural and small-town communities tied to food processing, meatpacking and farming. That shift changed schools, congregations and local services across Greater Minnesota. It also set the pattern that current data still reflect, with a large share of Mexican Minnesotans living outside the metropolitan area.

Like other books in the series, this one is meant as an introduction rather than a full history, and it is short enough to read in an evening. Its value is perspective. It shows that Mexican Minnesota has a century of history and that much of it unfolded in the countryside. It also shows that community institutions have long carried the work of welcome and survival. Readers who want more depth can turn to Barrios Norteños, Valdés's longer study of St. Paul and Midwestern Mexican communities.
mainPoints: Mexican and Mexican American people have been part of Minnesota since the early twentieth century, not only in recent decades.
The community's history in the Midwest is above all a history of working people in railroads, industry, meatpacking and agriculture.
Many early arrivals came for seasonal work rather than permanent settlement, and that pattern shaped housing, schooling and belonging.
Minnesota welcomed Mexican labor while often treating Mexican families as outsiders, a tension that runs through the history.
St. Paul's West Side became a center of Mexican community life, with churches, businesses and cultural organizations built by residents.
Families sustained their own religious, social and cultural institutions across generations, including food traditions and conjunto music.
Late in the twentieth century, barrios and colonias grew in towns outside the Twin Cities, making Greater Minnesota central to the story.
relevance: This is the clearest short history for staff who serve Mexican Minnesotans, and it is grounded in this state. It explains why a large share of the community lives in Greater Minnesota. It shows why seasonal and farm work still shapes some families' schedules and housing. It also makes the case that long-standing community organizations deserve a place at the table when DSD plans outreach or engagement. And it helps staff resist the idea that Mexican Minnesota is a recent arrival story. The book is introductory and was published in 2005. So it predates current population figures, newer Indigenous Mexican communities, and recent policy changes. It says little about disability specifically, so pair it with current data and with conversations led by community partners.
questions: Valdés shows that many Mexican families first came to Minnesota for seasonal work. How might seasonal work, travel or housing patterns affect when and how a family can engage with our services?
The book highlights community-built institutions on the West Side and in rural towns. Which of these kinds of organizations are already partners in our region, and which have we never contacted?
If a large share of Mexican Minnesotans live in Greater Minnesota, does our outreach, interpreter access and provider network reflect that?

title: The Distance Between Us: A Memoir
overview: Reyna Grande is a Mexican-born novelist who came to the United States as an undocumented child and later became an award-winning writer. The Distance Between Us is her memoir of childhood and youth, told from the point of view of a child left behind when both parents went north to work. It follows her years in Mexico, her crossing at age nine, and her coming of age in a home shaped by her father's ambition and his drinking. Reviewers praised its honesty and its lack of self-pity.
summary: The first part of the memoir takes place in Mexico. Grande was a small child when her father left for the United States to earn money, and her mother later followed him, leaving Reyna and her two siblings in the care of a harsh grandmother. Grande describes poverty, the longing for absent parents, and the way children make sense of a separation that adults explain as temporary. The bond between Reyna and her older sister becomes one of the book's central threads, a source of protection when the adults around them are not.

The parents' absence stretches on for years, and the family changes while they are apart. Grande writes about the confusion of loving parents she barely remembers, about the hope attached to every phone call and money transfer, and about the small and large losses that come with a family divided by a border. Publishers Weekly described the book as the story of a family shattered by repeated separations and traumas, and the early chapters show how those separations accumulate.

When Grande was about nine, her father returned and reluctantly agreed to bring his children north. She entered the United States without papers, and the memoir describes the crossing briefly before turning to the harder subject of what came next. Life with her father was not what she had imagined. He insisted on education and pushed his children to succeed in school, but his alcoholism led to violence, abuse and chaos at home, and his new partner showed little interest in the children.

In the middle of this turmoil, Grande found refuge in library books and in writing, inspired in part by Latina writers whose work showed her that her own story could be told. School became both a burden and a way forward. The memoir is candid about the cost of living in a home where love and harm came from the same person, and about the push and pull between gratitude for opportunity and grief for what the family lost along the way.

The book closes as Grande leaves her father's house after a serious confrontation and finds her own path. She became the first in her family to graduate from college and later earned an MFA in creative writing. The ending is hopeful but not tidy. Grande does not present her story as proof that hardship pays off; she shows how separation, migration and family pain continue to shape a person long after the border is crossed.
mainPoints: Family separation across a border can last for years and leaves lasting marks on children and parents alike.
Children left behind often carry hope, anger, loyalty and confusion about absent parents all at once.
Siblings can become each other's main source of safety when adults are absent or unreliable.
Reunification brings its own difficulties, because the parent and the child have both changed.
A parent can hold high hopes for a child's education while also causing harm at home.
Libraries, books and writing can offer refuge and a path forward for young people in crisis.
Undocumented childhood shapes identity, belonging and opportunity well into adulthood.
relevance: This memoir helps staff understand, from the inside, what family separation and reunification can mean for children in Mexican immigrant families. That matters when DSD staff meet adults who were once separated children, or families in which a parent, grandparent or older sibling carries caregiving roles that do not match a standard household form. It can also deepen trauma-informed practice by showing how loyalty and fear can exist together in one family. Read it as one person's story, not a description of Mexican families in general. It describes domestic violence and alcoholism directly, so offer it with care, and note that it says little about disability or about Indigenous Mexican experience.
questions: Grande's family was divided for years before it was reunited. How do our intake forms and assessments account for caregivers and household members who have changed over time?
The book shows a parent who both supported and harmed his children. How do we stay open and respectful with families whose stories are complicated?
Books and a library offered Grande refuge. What trusted spaces, such as schools, libraries or congregations, could help us reach families who are wary of agencies?

title: A History of Nigeria
authors: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
overview: A History of Nigeria is a one-volume history by Toyin Falola and historian Matthew M. Heaton. Falola is a Nigerian-born historian and one of the leading scholars of the country. Published by Cambridge University Press, the book runs from the earliest human societies in the region, around 9000 BCE, to the elections of 2007. Reviewers note that this long view deliberately pushes back against accounts that begin at independence in 1960. The book covers politics and the economy, and it also gives real attention to religion, culture and social life. That makes it a clear, balanced introduction for readers who want context for Nigerian Minnesota.
summary: The opening chapters cover early states and societies from about 9000 BCE to 1500 CE. They then turn to slavery, state and society from about 1500 to 1800. Readers meet the long histories of kingdoms, city-states and communities in the regions that are now Nigeria, including Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo and many other peoples. These chapters make clear that Nigeria's peoples had deep, complex political and cultural traditions long before the colonial era. They also show how the Atlantic slave trade and regional trade networks reshaped those traditions.

The next chapters follow the political and economic changes of the nineteenth century, including shifts in religion, trade and political power. They then describe the British conquest between 1850 and 1903. The authors show how Britain joined very different regions into one colony, a decision that still shapes the country's politics and its regional and religious divides. They pay attention to how these regional differences, including the different paths of Islam and Christianity, shaped the communities that came under British rule. Their account helps readers see why region, religion and ethnicity remain so important in Nigerian public life and in diaspora communities today.

Chapters on colonial society to 1929 and on nationalist movements from 1929 to 1960 describe how Nigerians lived under British rule. Nigerians built schools, newspapers, unions and political parties, and they organized for independence. The authors pay attention to how ordinary people adapted, resisted and created new identities in a changing world. These chapters trace how new leaders, organizations and regional parties took shape on the road to independence. Readers can see how the hopes and divisions of this period carried straight into the first years of independent Nigeria. They can also see why the transition was both proud and fragile.

The post-independence chapters cover instability and civil war from 1960 to 1970, and oil, state and society from 1970 to 1983. They also cover civil society and the long transition back to democracy from 1984 to 2007. The civil war period, which many Igbo families remember through Biafra, is placed within the larger story of regional tension and military rule. The rise of oil wealth and its uneven effects get careful treatment. The authors show how these decades of coups, conflict and oil wealth shaped the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

A closing chapter considers Nigeria and Nigerians in world history, including the global reach of Nigerian people and culture. The book ends with remarks on corruption, efforts to fight it, and the 2007 elections. Throughout, it includes helpful aids such as a chronology, a glossary, a list of notable people and a map of major cities and ethnic groups.
