The appendices and maps make the book easy to use as a reference when a staff member wants to place a name, region or event in context. Reviewers noted that the book gives real space to culture and social history, including art, music, literature and drama, alongside politics and the economy.
mainPoints: Nigeria is made up of many peoples with long, distinct histories, not a single culture.
Deep precolonial traditions of government, trade, art and faith still shape Nigerian identity today.
British rule joined very different regions into one country, which helps explain lasting regional and religious tensions.
The civil war of 1967 to 1970 remains a significant memory, especially for many Igbo families.
Oil wealth brought great resources and also deepened inequality and political struggle.
Nigerians have built a strong civil society, including churches, mosques, unions, professional groups and media.
Nigerian people and culture have a large and growing presence around the world, including in Minnesota.
relevance: For DSD staff, this history gives the background needed to avoid treating Nigerian Minnesotans as one group. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo and other communities have different histories, languages and often different faiths. Knowing this helps staff ask the right questions about language access and community partners. Understanding the civil war, military rule and the long struggle over corruption can also help explain why some families value strong records and clear rules. It may also explain their trust in community institutions such as churches, mosques and hometown associations. Keep its limits in mind. It is a university-level survey written for students, so it can feel dense. It ends in 2007, before more recent events, and it does not describe life in the Nigerian diaspora in Minnesota. Pair it with a personal or current voice, and treat each family as the expert on its own history.
questions: Nigeria holds many peoples and languages. How do our intake and interpreter practices make sure we ask which language and community each family identifies with?
How might experiences of military rule and corruption shape the way some Nigerian families view paperwork, eligibility rules or promises from public agencies?
Which Nigerian community institutions in Minnesota, such as congregations or cultural associations, might be respectful partners for outreach, and how would we approach them?

title: Americanah
editionNote: First published 2013 · Alfred A. Knopf · 477 pages
overview: Americanah is a novel by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, one of the most widely read Nigerian writers of her generation. It won the 2013 National Book Critics Circle Award for fiction. The story follows Ifemelu, a young Nigerian woman who leaves Lagos to attend university in the United States, and Obinze, her secondary-school love, whose path takes him to London. Although it is fiction, the book is widely read as a sharp, contemporary portrait of Nigerian migration, of learning what race means in America, and of returning home changed. It offers the lived, present-day voice this brief pairs with a history of Nigeria.
summary: The novel opens with the bond between Ifemelu and Obinze as students in Lagos, in a Nigeria marked by military rule, strikes that close universities and a strong pull toward opportunities abroad. Adichie draws the warmth and humor of middle-class Nigerian family life, the importance of education and the pressure young people feel to succeed. These early chapters show the hopes and frustrations that lead many Nigerians to leave. Readers also see the friendships and family loyalties that will later pull Ifemelu home.

Ifemelu's arrival in the United States is hard. She struggles with money, work authorization, loneliness and the small daily humiliations of being new. Most strikingly, she discovers that in America she is seen first as Black, a category that had not defined her in Nigeria. The novel follows her as she learns the unwritten rules of American race, class and accent. She also faces pressure about her hair, her accent and how to present herself at work and in relationships. Adichie shows how newcomers learn to change parts of themselves to fit in, and how much that effort can cost over time, especially for a young woman without family nearby.

Ifemelu eventually becomes known for a popular blog about race in America, written from the viewpoint of a non-American Black person. Her observations, which appear throughout the novel, notice the relations between and within racial groups that many Americans take for granted, including differences between African immigrants and African Americans. Many readers find these sections the most memorable and the most useful for discussion. The blog gives Ifemelu a public voice and some success, but it also raises questions about who gets to speak about race and for whom. Adichie uses these passages to show the gap between how Americans talk about race in public and how people live it in private.

Obinze, hoping to join Ifemelu in the United States, is refused a visa after 9/11. He goes to London instead and lives there without legal status after his visa expires, working under someone else's name. His story shows the precarious, often hidden lives of undocumented migrants and the shame and fear that can come with them. Adichie draws the daily fear of discovery, the dependence on others' goodwill and the loss of dignity that can come with living without papers. Obinze's experience contrasts with Ifemelu's and shows that migration paths can diverge sharply depending on timing, policy and luck.

Years later, both return to Nigeria, now a democracy, and reconnect. Ifemelu has become an "Americanah," a returnee who sees her homeland with new eyes. The ending explores what it means to come home after many years away, and whether home has changed, the person has changed, or both. Adichie uses this homecoming to look honestly at contemporary Lagos and at how returnees are seen by those who stayed. The novel ends on a note of possibility rather than neat resolution, leaving readers to consider what home means after a long time away.
mainPoints: Many Nigerians migrate for education and opportunity, often carrying high family expectations.
Many African immigrants first learn what it means to be Black in America only after they arrive.
African immigrants and African Americans share some experiences of race but have distinct histories and cultures.
Immigration status, work authorization and visa rules can shape every part of a newcomer's life.
Undocumented life often brings fear, hidden work and shame that people may not speak about.
Accent, hair and appearance can become sites of daily judgment for African immigrants.
Returning home after years abroad can bring a sense of being between two places.
relevance: For DSD staff, Americanah opens a conversation about the everyday experience of Nigerian Minnesotans: high expectations around education and work, the stress of immigration rules, and learning American racial categories as an adult. It can help staff understand why a Nigerian family might not identify with African American experiences in the way a form assumes, and why accent or name can affect how people are treated in systems. Its portrait of undocumented life can also deepen empathy for people who are cautious about sharing information. Keep its limits clearly in view. It is a novel, not a guide, and it centers one educated, Igbo, Lagos-raised woman's experience, not Yoruba, Hausa or other perspectives. Some critics, including an NPR reviewer, found parts of the storytelling flat. Use it to prompt reflection, never to predict any individual's views.
questions: Ifemelu learns American ideas about race only after she arrives. How do our forms and practices about race and ethnicity work for people who see themselves first by nationality or ethnic group?
How might fear connected to immigration status affect a family's willingness to share information with us, and what reassurances can we honestly offer?
What judgments about accent, name or appearance might show up in our own interactions, and how would we notice them?

title: Puerto Rico: The Trials of the Oldest Colony in the World
editionNote: First published 1997 · Yale University Press · 228 pages
overview: José Trías Monge was a Puerto Rican jurist and scholar who served as chief justice of the Supreme Court of Puerto Rico and helped draft the 1952 constitution that created the Commonwealth. In this book, published by Yale University Press, he argues that despite that status Puerto Rico remained a colony of the United States. He traces Spanish rule, U.S. colonial policy after 1898, citizenship, the Commonwealth and the island's economic dependence, and he urges the United States to resolve the island's political status.
summary: Trías Monge begins with Spanish rule over Puerto Rico and the island's long efforts to gain greater self-government before 1898. He then describes the U.S. takeover at the end of the Spanish-American War and the colonial policies that followed. To show that Puerto Rico's situation was not unique, he compares U.S. policy there with American rule in the Pacific and with British, French and Dutch rule in the Caribbean, setting the island's story within a broader history of empire.

A central part of the book explains the legal framework created in the early twentieth century. A series of Supreme Court decisions known as the Insular Cases described Puerto Rico as belonging to, but not part of, the United States, in a phrase reviewers often quote, foreign in a domestic sense. These rulings allowed Congress to govern the island under its power over territories without making it a state. Trías Monge shows how this doctrine continues to limit the rights of people living on the island.

He explains that Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917, yet those living on the island have no voting representation in Congress beyond a nonvoting resident commissioner and cannot vote for president. He then turns to the creation of the Commonwealth in 1952, in which he took part. Its Spanish name, Estado Libre Asociado, suggested a free associated state, but Trías Monge argues that the arrangement left Congress's ultimate power over the island in place.

The book also addresses the economy. Trías Monge argues that large federal transfers to Puerto Rico had not produced lasting development and had instead deepened dependence, while a majority of families still lived below the poverty line at the time he wrote. He links economic weakness to political status, suggesting that the island could not plan its own future without real authority over its own affairs. In his view, money alone could not substitute for the power to make decisions, and dependence on federal transfers made the status question harder, not easier, to resolve.

In the final chapters, Trías Monge reviews the status options of independence, statehood and an enhanced commonwealth, and he criticizes Congress for saying it will respect the will of Puerto Ricans without saying which options it would accept. One reviewer found his own proposal frustratingly vague, while praising the book as a rich and succinct history. Because the book appeared in 1997, it does not cover later events such as the 2016 federal oversight law and Hurricane María in 2017.
mainPoints: Puerto Rico has been under colonial rule for more than five centuries, first by Spain and then by the United States.
The Insular Cases allowed the United States to govern Puerto Rico as a territory without making it a state.
Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917, but island residents lack voting representation in Congress and cannot vote for president.
The 1952 Commonwealth expanded self-government but, the author argues, left ultimate power with Congress.
Federal funding has not produced lasting development and has deepened economic dependence.
Political status and economic conditions on the island are closely linked.
Resolving status requires Congress to state clearly which options it would accept.
relevance: This book helps DSD staff understand why Puerto Rican Minnesotans are U.S. citizens by birth and should never be treated as immigrants, while also understanding the island's unequal political relationship with the United States. That history can explain mixed feelings about federal and state systems, the movement of families between the island and the mainland, and differences in benefits and services between Puerto Rico and the states. Written by a key figure in the Commonwealth's creation, the book carries both insider knowledge and a clear point of view. It is legal and political rather than personal, it predates major events after 1997, and it does not address disability.
questions: Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens by birth. Where might our forms or scripts mistakenly treat Puerto Rican families as immigrants?
The book shows that island residents have limited political voice. How might that history shape a family's trust in government systems?
Families often move between Puerto Rico and Minnesota. How can we make it easier for them to transfer services and records?

title: When I Was Puerto Rican
overview: Esmeralda Santiago is a Puerto Rican writer and filmmaker who grew up in rural Puerto Rico and moved to Brooklyn as a teenager. When I Was Puerto Rican is the first volume of her memoir trilogy. It recreates her childhood in a rural barrio, her family's unstable life as her parents separated and reunited, and her move to New York, where she had to learn a new language and new rules. The book follows her path from the countryside to New York's High School of Performing Arts.
summary: The memoir opens in rural Puerto Rico, where Santiago, the eldest of what would become eleven children, grows up in a house of corrugated metal surrounded by fruit trees and gardens. She describes the sights, sounds and tastes of country life with great detail, from tree frogs at night to the right way to eat a guava. The family is poor, but the children have room to play and a freedom that, as reviewers noted, she would never find again in later homes.

Her parents are not married, and their relationship is a constant source of tension. Mami is beautiful, ambitious and a force of nature; Papi is a gentle man and frustrated artist whose infidelities and refusal to marry wear on the family. Mami repeatedly moves the children to town, into rented rooms or relatives' homes, and then back again when the couple reconciles. Each move means new schools and new household routines, and Esmeralda, a good student, endures teasing from children raised in the city.

School brings its own lessons, including the clash between Puerto Rican and U.S. culture. Santiago describes being taught American customs in a Puerto Rican classroom, and the confusing messages children received about which culture was worth more. She also writes about the rural identity of the jíbaro, the country people whose ways her family lived, and about learning that others looked down on them. These passages show how questions of identity began long before she left the island.

When Mami takes one of the children to New York for medical treatment, she decides to move the whole family to Brooklyn. Esmeralda, now a teenager, must learn English, adapt to cold weather and crowded city housing, and take on adult responsibilities, including translating for her mother at the welfare office. The new home feels dangerous, and the contrast with the open country she left is sharp. Kirkus noted that in Brooklyn even snow could be dangerous, a small detail that captures how unfamiliar and unsafe the new surroundings felt to a girl raised among mango groves.

Determined to escape hardship, Esmeralda works hard in school and wins a place at the High School of Performing Arts, the first step toward her later education at Harvard. The book ends with her balancing two identities and wondering what remains of the girl she was. The title captures this feeling. She was Puerto Rican on the island; in New York she must figure out what that identity means. Reviewers praised the memoir as lyrical and clear-eyed.
mainPoints: Rural Puerto Rican life offered children closeness to land and family, even amid poverty.
Family instability and frequent moves can deeply shape a child's schooling and sense of security.
Puerto Rican children learned early that U.S. and Puerto Rican cultures were valued differently.
Jíbaro, or rural, identity carries pride and has also faced prejudice.
Moving to the mainland is a change of language and culture, not an immigration in legal terms.
Children of Spanish-speaking families often take on adult roles, such as interpreting at public offices.
Identity can feel divided or uncertain after a move, and people make sense of it over time.
relevance: This memoir helps DSD staff see the experience of Puerto Rican families who move to the mainland as U.S. citizens who still face a major change of language, climate and culture. Santiago's account of translating for her mother at a welfare office is a powerful reminder of why agencies must provide qualified interpreters and never rely on children. Her story also shows how frequent moves and family strain can affect a young person's stability. It is one family's experience from the 1950s and 1960s, set in New York rather than Minnesota, and many Puerto Rican Minnesotans today are English-dominant or born on the mainland. It does not address disability.
questions: Santiago translated for her mother at a welfare office. Where might our services still lean on children or family members to interpret, and how can we change that?
Puerto Rican families are citizens, yet moving to the mainland can still mean a major cultural change. How do we support that transition without treating people as immigrants?
Santiago's family moved often. How might frequent moves between Puerto Rico and Minnesota affect continuity of services, and what could we do to help?

title: Unforgetting: A Memoir of Family, Migration, Gangs, and Revolution in the Americas
overview: Roberto Lovato is a Salvadoran American journalist who grew up in San Francisco's Mission District as the son of Salvadoran parents. Unforgetting combines memoir and reporting. It connects his family's private silences with El Salvador's public history of massacre, civil war, migration and gang violence. The book moves between his father's childhood, his own youth and a reporting trip to El Salvador in 2015. Lovato argues that facing buried history, which he calls unforgetting, is necessary for families and nations trying to break cycles of violence.
summary: The memoir moves along three timelines. One follows Lovato's return to El Salvador in 2015 to report on the country's violence. A second traces his own path from a troubled youth in San Francisco to revolutionary activism, human rights work and journalism. The third rebuilds his father's childhood in rural El Salvador during the Depression. Reviewers noted that this structure lets Lovato tie one family's history to the history of a nation, and to the history of the United States' role in Central America.

Lovato's father grew up in deep rural poverty and learned to survive by working in the country's informal and black-market economies. For decades he would not talk about his early life, and his silences and anger weighed heavily on his son, and they included harsh physical discipline. Lovato finally asked him about La Matanza, the army's 1932 massacre of tens of thousands of mostly Indigenous Salvadorans. His father, who had been a child at the time, described what he had seen and broke down in tears. That moment anchors the book.

The San Francisco chapters describe Lovato's teenage years in the Mission District in the 1970s and 1980s. At that time, Salvadoran gangs, including the ones that later became notorious, were forming in California. He ran with a small crew and felt angry and confused about his heritage, but later he traded street life for political work. During El Salvador's civil war of 1980 to 1992, he joined the guerrilla movement for a short time. He treats that experience as one chapter in a longer search rather than as the center of his identity.

In the reporting chapters, Lovato looks into how El Salvador became so violent after the war. He befriends a man deported from the United States who is later killed, and he describes a standoff over a mass grave. He also goes back to bury his mother's ashes, only to be chased from the cemetery by gang members. He rejects common media portrayals that treat gangs as mysterious death cults and leaders as merely incompetent. Instead, he links present violence to war, deportation, poverty and policy decisions in both countries.

The book's theme is memory. Lovato suggests that his father's breakthrough, finally speaking about what he witnessed, offers a way forward for the country as well. Horror that is acknowledged may become something people can move beyond. He writes with open emotion rather than a reporter's distance, a choice reviewers saw as a strength. The result is a personal account that asks readers to see migration and gang violence as outcomes of a history that many people would prefer to forget.
mainPoints: Family silence about trauma can shape children's lives even when the children do not know what happened.
La Matanza of 1932, the army's massacre of mostly Indigenous Salvadorans, is a buried foundation of modern Salvadoran history.
The civil war of 1980 to 1992 drove migration and left lasting damage in families on both sides of the border.
Salvadoran gangs took shape partly in U.S. cities and spread through deportation, linking the two countries' histories.
Media portrayals of gangs as inexplicable evil hide the policies and histories that sustain violence.
Speaking about buried history, which Lovato calls unforgetting, can open a path out of cycles of violence.
A person's identity can include rebellion, activism and searching, not a single fixed story.
relevance: This book gives DSD staff historical background on El Salvador. It helps explain why some Salvadoran families may carry unspoken trauma across generations and why elders may not discuss the past. It also shows why deportation and gang violence touch many households without defining them. The book supports trauma-informed and family-centered practice. It can help staff avoid seeing Salvadoran youth or families through a lens of gang stereotypes. It is one man's story, told with strong political views, and it includes descriptions of violence. It does not address disability. Use it to build understanding, never to draw conclusions about a particular family's history or experiences.
questions: Lovato's father kept silent about his childhood for decades. How might unspoken family history show up in the way people respond to questions about their past or their health?
The book challenges stereotypes about Salvadoran gangs. Where might those stereotypes show up in how systems treat Salvadoran young people?
How can our team learn the history of a community without expecting individual families to explain or relive it for us?

title: Solito: A Memoir
overview: Javier Zamora is a Salvadoran poet, born in the fishing village of La Herradura, whose collection Unaccompanied was widely praised. Solito is his memoir of the journey he made in 1999, at nine years old, from El Salvador to the United States to rejoin his parents. Told in the voice of the child he was, it follows a trip that was supposed to last about two weeks and instead took nine, along with the strangers who became a family to him along the way.
summary: The book opens in La Herradura, where Javier lives with his grandparents and an aunt while his parents work in California. His father left when he was a toddler, and his mother went north several years later. Adults explain the separation through the war and the lack of work. Javier's days are full of school, the sea, and family affection, but also of the ache of missing parents he knows mostly through phone calls and photographs. The decision to send him north is made for him, with hope and fear in equal measure.

Javier leaves in the care of a smuggler, with a plan to travel through Guatemala and Mexico and cross near Tijuana, where his parents will meet him. On the road he joins a group of adults he does not know. A woman named Patricia and her daughter Carla are given papers listing them as his family, and they slowly become one, with Patricia caring for him as for her own child. A nineteen-year-old named Chino becomes an older-brother figure who, at one point, carries the exhausted boy on his back.

The plan falls apart: the smuggler disappears, the group is stopped by soldiers at gunpoint, and the route changes. Instead of crossing near Tijuana, the group attempts to cross the Sonoran Desert into Arizona on foot, more than once. Javier is detained, released and sent back to try again, and throughout he faces hunger, heat, fear of death and of being robbed or jailed, and constant uncertainty about whether the adults around him will stay.

Zamora writes with a poet's attention to detail and a child's way of seeing. Small things carry weight: trying to pass as Mexican, slipping when he uses a Salvadoran word instead of the Mexican one, naming desert plants, sharing a joke in a terrible moment. The book mixes Spanish and English and moves between grim and funny episodes. Reviewers noted his worry that no one would believe what happened, and they saw the memoir as an answer to that fear.

The journey ends at a safe house in Arizona, where his parents come for him. Zamora does not present the reunion as a simple happy ending, since the weeks of fear and the separation that came before them stay with him. The book's power lies in its insistence that a child migrant is a whole person, with humor, loyalty and inner life. It contains frank depictions of violence and danger to children, which some readers will find hard.
mainPoints: Many Salvadoran children grew up apart from parents who migrated for work and safety after the civil war.
Child migrants make dangerous journeys that can stretch far beyond what adults planned or promised.
Strangers on the road can become a lasting chosen family who protect and care for a child.
Small details of language, such as Salvadoran words and voseo, mark identity and can expose or protect a person.
Fear, hunger and detention leave lasting marks even when a journey ends in reunion.
Humor and imagination are part of how children survive extreme hardship.
Telling one's own story, and being believed, is a form of dignity and healing.
relevance: This memoir helps DSD staff understand experiences that some Salvadoran adults and young people carry from childhood: long separation from parents, dangerous migration and detention. It can deepen trauma-informed practice and remind staff that a person's family may include people who are not related by blood. It also shows why Salvadoran Spanish matters, and why an interpreter's dialect and a person's comfort with that interpreter can make a difference. Zamora's story is his own, and it should never be assumed for anyone else. The book describes violence and danger to children in detail, it predates more recent policy changes, and it does not focus on disability.
questions: Zamora's travel companions became family. How do our definitions of family and caregiver make room for chosen family?
The book shows how a single word can reveal where someone is from. How do we make sure interpreters and materials fit Salvadoran Spanish and the person's own preferences?
How can we invite people to share as much or as little of their past as they choose, without making them prove their story?

title: Thailand: A Short History
editionNote: First published 1984 · Yale University Press · 351 pages
overview: David K. Wyatt was a historian at Cornell University and one of the leading Western scholars of Thai history. Thailand: A Short History was first published by Yale University Press in 1984. For many years it was the standard English-language history of the country, and it was reviewed in major journals of Asian studies. Wyatt revised it for a second edition in 2003, adding material on social and economic change in the late twentieth century. The book traces the Tai peoples from their early history through the kingdoms of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, the Bangkok era, and modern Thailand.
summary: Wyatt begins with the early history of the Tai-speaking peoples and their movement into mainland Southeast Asia. He shows that the people who became Thai shared roots with Lao and other Tai groups. This helps explain the related languages and customs found across the region. At the same time, he traces how separate kingdoms and national histories grew from those shared roots. That distinction matters for anyone tempted to treat Thai and Lao communities as the same.

The middle chapters follow the rise of Thai kingdoms, including Sukhothai and the long era of Ayutthaya. Ayutthaya was a powerful trading and Buddhist kingdom that dealt with neighbors and distant traders alike. Wyatt describes how kingship, Theravada Buddhism and ties with neighboring states shaped political and cultural life over several centuries. He then explains how the fall of Ayutthaya and the founding of a new capital at Bangkok opened a new chapter in the country's history.

Later chapters cover the Bangkok kings and the era of Western colonial pressure. Reviewers praised Wyatt's account of how the Thai government changed over time. They also praised his account of how Siam stayed independent while its neighbors were colonized, partly through reform and diplomacy. This independence is central to Thai national identity. It sets Thai history apart from that of Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam and Myanmar. It also helps explain the pride, and the particular relationship to the monarchy, that many Thai people hold.

The final chapters address the twentieth century. They cover the end of absolute monarchy, the shifts between military and civilian governments, and rapid economic and social change. The second edition carries the story into the early 2000s. Reviewers described the book as concise, readable and educational. They noted how it clarifies the makeup of Thailand's population and its place among its neighbors. As a political and national history, it says less about everyday rural life or migration abroad, and it predates recent events in Thai politics.
mainPoints: Thai, Lao and other Tai peoples share deep roots but have distinct national histories.
Theravada Buddhism and kingship have been central to Thai political and cultural life.
Sukhothai, Ayutthaya and Bangkok mark major eras in the Thai story.
Thailand was never colonized, and that independence shapes national identity.
Reform and diplomacy helped Siam navigate Western colonial pressure.
Twentieth-century Thailand saw major shifts in government and rapid economic change.
relevance: The Thai Minnesota brief warns against filing a Thai household under Hmong, Lao or refugee-camp histories. Wyatt's history gives staff the background to see why that matters. Thailand has its own long state history, a monarchy, Theravada traditions and a sense of national independence that differ from its neighbors. Many Thai Minnesotans came as students, workers, spouses or family members rather than as refugees. Knowing this history helps staff approach them with fitting questions. The book is a national political history by a Western scholar, and its later chapters are now dated. It does not address Thai life in the United States. Pair it with Thai community voices, and use it as context, never as a description of any person.
questions: How does knowing that Thailand was never colonized change the assumptions we might bring to a Thai household?
What questions could we ask, instead of assuming, about how a Thai Minnesotan came to live here?
How might shared Tai roots with Lao culture lead to errors in interpreter booking, and how do we prevent them?

title: Sightseeing: Stories
overview: Rattawut Lapcharoensap was born in Chicago in 1979 and raised in Bangkok. Sightseeing, his first book, is a collection of seven stories set in contemporary Thailand, published by Grove Press in 2005. Publishers Weekly called it a stellar debut, and he was later named one of Granta's Best Young American Novelists. The stories are told mostly by young Thai narrators, and they look past the tourist image of Thailand to family bonds, class, violence, humor and the pressures of a society changing under Western influence.
summary: The opening story, Farangs, is narrated by the son of a beachside motel owner and an absent American soldier. He keeps falling for foreign tourist girls, hoping to mean more to them than a holiday romance. The story's comic and painful collision with a pompous American boyfriend, complete with flying mangoes and a pet pig, introduces the book's central contrast between visitors' fantasies of paradise and the lives of the people who live there. Like several later stories, it is told by a young Thai narrator who guides the reader.

Several stories explore class and power. In Draft Day, a boy whose parents bribed an official to rig the military draft lottery watches his friend, who has no such protection, get drafted, and his guilt grows. In At the Café Lovely, two brothers move from a celebratory meal at an American fast-food restaurant to a darker night out. Priscilla the Cambodian follows the narrator's friendship with a Cambodian refugee girl and the moment when local adults burn the refugees' shantytown, a story reviewers read as an account of prejudice within a small community.

The title story follows a young man about to leave for college and his fiercely independent mother on a holiday shaped by her coming loss of sight. It is a tender portrait of a parent and child facing disability and change together. The closing pieces shift perspective sharply. Cockfighter is told by a teenage girl watching her proud father's long struggle with a violent local family, and Don't Let Me Die in This Place follows an elderly American, paralyzed after a stroke, living with his son's Thai family and struggling to connect with his grandchildren.

Most reviewers praised the collection's range, warmth and humor, and the way it asks readers to look again at the prejudices that form their blind spots. Publishers Weekly called the tales richly nuanced, and Salon singled out the final story as the strongest. One review felt the American characters rarely moved beyond cliché. The book is fiction set in Thailand itself, not an account of Thai life in the United States, so it offers context and empathy rather than local knowledge.
mainPoints: Thailand's tourist image hides a much fuller, more complex everyday life.
Family loyalty, class and influence shape young people's chances.
Prejudice toward refugees and outsiders exists within Thai communities too.
Disability and aging appear as family experiences shared across generations of a household.
Living between cultures can bring both humor and painful displacement.
Children often see adult injustice clearly before they can name it.
relevance: Sightseeing gives DSD staff a Thai voice that complicates easy images of Thailand. Two stories touch disability directly: a mother losing her sight and a stroke survivor cared for within a family. They can open conversations about how Thai families may understand care, independence and obligation, always as questions rather than conclusions. The story of a Cambodian refugee girl also reinforces the brief's point that Thai, Khmer, Lao and Hmong histories are distinct, even where they meet. The stories are set in Thailand, not Minnesota, and they are fiction. Use them to build empathy and curiosity, and rely on Thai Minnesotans and community partners for how life is lived here.
questions: What does the title story suggest about how a family might experience a parent's disability together?
How do tourist images or stereotypes of a country show up, even subtly, in how we approach households from that country?
What can the story of the stroke survivor teach us about care, culture and living with a family in a new place?

title: The Gates of Europe: A History of Ukraine
overview: The Gates of Europe is a single-volume history of Ukraine by Serhii Plokhy, the Mykhailo Hrushevsky Professor of Ukrainian History at Harvard University. Published by Basic Books in 2015, it traces about two thousand years of history. It starts with the ancient peoples described by Greek writers and moves through medieval Kyiv, the empires that divided Ukrainian lands, the Soviet era and independence. It ends with Russia's annexation of Crimea and the war in eastern Ukraine. Plokhy explains how a distinct Ukrainian identity and state took shape, and why both have faced constant threats.
summary: Plokhy begins far back in time, with the peoples who lived on the northern shores of the Black Sea in the ancient world and the origins of the Slavs. He then describes the rise of medieval Kyiv and its ruling dynasty. Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all claim this period in different ways. By starting here, he helps readers see why questions about who owns this history remain so charged today.

Much of the book follows the centuries when Ukrainian lands were divided among larger powers. These included the Polish-Lithuanian state, the Ottoman world, the Russian Empire and the Habsburg Empire. Plokhy shows how these borders shaped religion, language and identity in different regions. This helps explain why Ukrainians in the west and east, or in cities and villages, may have different histories while still sharing a sense of peoplehood. These differences are part of a shared history rather than signs of division.

Plokhy traces the slow formation of a modern Ukrainian national identity, including the role of the Cossacks, writers and political movements. He shows how Ukrainian identity grew even under imperial rule and repeated efforts to suppress the language and culture. Reviewers noted that he gives fair weight to each phase of the story and keeps a measured, balanced tone. This part of the book shows that national identity was built over a long time by many hands. Language and culture were often at the center of the struggle to survive as a people.

The twentieth century brings revolution, short-lived independence, Soviet rule, famine, world war and Nazi occupation. Decades of Soviet control followed, and finally independence in 1991. Plokhy explains how these events shaped families and communities, and why memories of Soviet rule and its violence remain powerful. These chapters help readers understand the depth of experience behind Ukrainian attitudes toward Russia and toward state power. They also show how much loss is held in Ukrainian family stories, even when it is not spoken aloud.

Reviewers called the epilogue the book's strongest section. It places Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, and its support for separatists in eastern Ukraine, within a long pattern of Russian-Ukrainian relations. Reviewers praised the book as a welcome, readable introduction. One noted that the many names and places can be hard to follow. Another noted that readers seeking Ukraine's role in wider world history will need other sources. Later editions have been updated.
mainPoints: Ukraine has a long and distinct history that is not simply part of Russian history.
For centuries, Ukrainian lands were divided among larger empires, which shaped regional differences in language, religion and identity.
Ukrainian national identity grew despite repeated efforts to suppress its language and culture.
Soviet rule, famine and war left deep marks on Ukrainian families and memory.
Independence in 1991 opened a new chapter that has faced ongoing threats.
Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea fits a long pattern in Russian-Ukrainian relations.
Shared history in the region is often claimed in competing ways by different nations.
relevance: The Gates of Europe gives the Ukrainian Minnesota brief the historical depth behind its central point. Ukrainians are a people with their own country, language and history, not a branch of a Russian-speaking group. Staff can use the book to understand why booking a Russian interpreter for a Ukrainian household may feel hurtful. It also shows why regional and generational differences matter, and why recent arrivals and long-settled families may relate to history in different ways. It helps staff recognize the weight of war and loss that some families carry. The book is a dense political and national history. So it says little about everyday family life or about Ukrainian communities in Minnesota, and the first edition predates the 2022 full-scale invasion. Pair it with personal voices and with local Ukrainian community partners.
questions: How might a family's history with empire, repression or war affect how they experience a government agency today?
How do we make sure we ask about a person's preferred language, Ukrainian or Russian, instead of assuming?
How could we respectfully serve both recently arrived Ukrainian families and families whose roots in Minnesota go back generations?

title: The Rooster House: My Ukrainian Family Story
editionNote: First published 2023 · Abrams Press (US) and Virago (UK) · 304 pages
overview: The Rooster House is a family memoir by Victoria Belim, a journalist and writer born in Ukraine who grew up in Chicago and now lives in Brussels. Published in 2023, it begins in 2014, when Russia's annexation of Crimea and a family quarrel send her back to Ukraine to reconnect with her aging grandmother. There she finds a line in her great-grandfather's diary about a great-uncle who vanished in the 1930s, and her search for his fate leads to a mansion in Poltava that once housed the secret police. The book spans four generations.
summary: Belim begins with her own ties to Ukraine. She spent childhood summers in the village of Bereh, which she came to see as a second home, and her great-grandparents acted almost as a second set of parents. After moving to the United States, she longed for that place but rarely returned. In 2014, as Russia seized Crimea and war broke out in the east, an uncle's pro-Soviet views pushed her to go back and to ask what her family's history really was.

In Bereh, Belim spends time with her grandmother Valentina, helping in the cherry orchard and garden and cooking traditional meals. These scenes give the book its warmth and texture. Reviewers praised its rich detail of rural life and its portrait of Ukrainian women, and they noted how domestic life and family memory are woven together with the larger history of the country. The rhythms of village life, the work of the garden and the sharing of meals become a way for Belim to understand who her family is, and what they have carried through decades of upheaval.

The central thread is the search for Nikodim, her great-grandfather's brother, who disappeared during the political purges of the 1930s after being questioned at the secret police headquarters known as the Rooster House. Her grandmother refuses to talk about him, and Belim must turn to archives and official files to learn what happened. Her search shows how fear and silence can be passed down through families long after the events themselves.

Along the way, family memories touch on the hardships of Soviet rule, including the famine of the early 1930s known as the Holodomor, and on the bureaucratic absurdities that many Ukrainians inherited from the Soviet system. Belim reflects on the grief of losing a place and on what it means to belong to a country that others have tried to erase. These memories show how the history of a nation lives inside the history of one family, and how younger generations may inherit grief they were never told about.

Reviewers called the book honest, insightful and moving, and praised its picture of a nation beyond war headlines. One review noted its many characters and layered structure, which ask for sustained attention. Belim frames her great-uncle as someone who fought for a free Ukraine, and her effort to restore him to the family story becomes a way of reclaiming her own Ukrainian identity. For readers, it offers a rich sense of Ukrainian life and memory.
mainPoints: Family silence can carry fear and trauma across generations.
Soviet repression, including the purges and the famine of the 1930s, left lasting marks on Ukrainian families.
Daily life, food, gardens and village ties are central to many Ukrainians' sense of home.
Members of one family may hold very different views of the Soviet past and of Russia.
Recovering a hidden family history can be a way of reclaiming identity.
Ukrainian women often carry and protect family memory.
People in the diaspora may feel both deeply connected to and distant from Ukraine.
relevance: The Rooster House gives the Ukrainian Minnesota brief a personal, multigenerational voice that complements national history. It helps staff understand that Ukrainian families may carry silence, grief and divided views about the past, and that some topics may be painful or difficult to raise. It also shows the importance of home, land, food and family ties, which can inform how staff think about caregiving, elders and recent displacement. Staff can use it to remember that a person who seems settled in the United States may still be deeply affected by events in Ukraine. It is one family's story, told by a writer who grew up in Chicago and lives in Europe, not in Minnesota, and its main events take place before the 2022 full-scale invasion. Pair it with local Ukrainian community partners.
questions: How might family silence about past trauma affect what a person is ready to share with us?
How can we be sensitive to the ongoing effects of war in Ukraine on families who live in Minnesota?
What role do elders, land and family memory play in the families we serve, and how might that shape our planning?

title: The Best We Could Do: An Illustrated Memoir
overview: Thi Bui was born in Vietnam three months before the war ended and came to the United States in 1978 as part of the wave of refugees known as boat people. The Best We Could Do is her debut graphic memoir, published by Abrams ComicArts in 2017. It was a National Book Critics Circle finalist in autobiography and an Eisner Award finalist, received an American Book Award, and was chosen as UCLA's common book for 2017. Through drawings and spare text, Bui traces her parents' lives across a century of Vietnamese history and her own journey as a daughter who becomes a mother.
summary: The book opens with Bui becoming a parent herself, an experience that sends her back to her own parents' stories. She wants to understand the distance and hardness she felt growing up, and she begins asking her mother and father about their past. This frame makes the memoir both a family history and a reflection on what children inherit from parents who lived through war, and on how becoming a parent can change the way a person sees the people who raised them.

Bui then reaches back to her paternal great-grandfather and follows her family through French colonial rule, the Japanese occupation during World War II, the First Indochina War and the American war. Her father appears as a distant, chain-smoking man whose harsh parenting reflected the terror he experienced as a boy. Her mother appears as a fiery, independent student who resisted her French schooling by teaching herself to write Vietnamese. Through them, readers meet a century of Vietnamese history from inside one family.

The middle of the book describes the family's life after the fall of South Vietnam and their dangerous escape by boat in 1978 to a refugee camp in Malaysia, followed by asylum in the United States. Bui shows the choices her parents faced with honesty, including the costs of each choice and the small acts of care that sustained the children. The later chapters follow the family into American life and the strain that memory and hardship placed on relationships at home.

Bui reflects throughout on inherited trauma, grief, and the gap between what parents feel and what they can say. As she learns her parents' history, her guilt about her own daughterhood eases and her empathy grows. Reviewers praised the way the book moves across decades and continents, and the way its artwork carries emotion that words alone might not. It offers a personal entry point into Vietnamese history and the refugee experience, and shows how understanding a painful past can change what a family passes on.
mainPoints: Parents' wartime experiences can shape how they raise their children in ways children do not see.
Vietnamese history spans French colonialism, Japanese occupation and decades of war, not only the American war.
Refugee escape involved dangerous choices with real costs and acts of care.
Inherited trauma can be eased when families come to understand each other's histories.
Becoming a parent can open new empathy for one's own parents.
Silence in a family may carry grief rather than indifference.
relevance: Vietnamese Minnesota is a community built after 1975, and many families include parents and grandparents who lived the history Bui draws. Her memoir helps DSD staff understand why an elder may speak little about the past, why caregiving decisions may reflect deep family loyalty, and why adult children may move between two cultural worlds while supporting aging or disabled relatives. It supports trauma-informed and family-centered practice without asking anyone to share their story. Bui's family settled in California, and this is one family's experience, so it does not speak for Kinh, Hoa or other Vietnamese Minnesotans. The graphic form also makes it a strong choice for team discussion.
questions: How might a parent's or grandparent's history shape the way a Vietnamese family talks, or does not talk, about disability and care?
What does Bui's experience suggest about the needs of adult children supporting an aging parent?
How can we honor a family's history in planning without making it the subject of the conversation?

title: Sông I Sing
overview: Bao Phi was born in Saigon in 1975, and his family came to Minnesota that same year as part of the first wave of Vietnamese refugees. He grew up in the Phillips neighborhood of Minneapolis, became a two-time Minnesota Grand Slam poetry champion and a National Poetry Slam finalist, and worked for many years at the Loft Literary Center. Sông I Sing, his first poetry collection, was published by Minneapolis's Coffee House Press in 2011. The title plays on sông, the Vietnamese word for river. The poems explore immigration, race, class and community in a voice rooted in spoken word.
summary: The collection opens with a poem that names many identities and the insults attached to them, setting the tone for a book that speaks directly about racism and belonging. Phi's spoken-word background shows on the page in rhythm, breath and sharp wordplay, and reviewers noted his alliteration and sensory detail. Vietnamese language appears throughout, and the double meaning of sông links memories of rivers in Vietnam with life in the present, tying refugee memory to daily life in Minnesota.

Many poems confront racism and violence head on, including slurs, police violence and institutional racism. One poem is an elegy for Fong Lee, a Hmong American teenager killed by Minneapolis police, whose case ended in an acquittal; the poem connects Vietnamese and Hmong Minnesotans in shared grief and protest. Phi uses harsh language on purpose to show what racism sounds like to those who receive it, and he names perpetrators rather than speaking in generalities.

Phi also looks inward at Vietnamese America. A series of portraits of people named Nguyễn shows how varied Vietnamese American lives are, across class, gender, sexuality and degrees of connection to Vietnam; one poem follows two Nguyễns who fail to connect across class lines. Reviewers noted how the book challenges narrow ideas of who counts as authentically Vietnamese, and how it makes room for people who do not fit the community's own expectations.

Other poems rework Asian American history, including laws that once restricted Asian immigrants, and trace what New York Times critic Dana Jennings described as a kind of refugee geography. The closing poem, Race, had earlier been selected for Best American Poetry 2006. Reviewers described the book as strong and angry, and also hopeful, with deep faith in love and community. A diaCRITICS review called it a major contribution to Vietnamese American literature and praised how it brings poetry directly to the people.
mainPoints: Vietnamese Minnesotan history includes families who arrived here in 1975.
Racism in everyday speech and institutions shapes how people experience public life.
Vietnamese American identity is varied across class, gender, sexuality and connection to Vietnam.
Solidarity across Southeast Asian communities in Minnesota has deep roots.
Spoken-word poetry brings community voices directly to the people.
Anger at injustice can live alongside hope and love for community.
relevance: Sông I Sing is a Minnesota book by a Vietnamese Minnesotan, written from the neighborhoods many DSD staff serve. It helps staff hear how racism, class and refugee history feel from inside the community, and why trust in public institutions, including police and government, cannot be assumed. Its portraits of many different Nguyễns echo the brief's call to see diversity within the community and to ask rather than assume. The poems use strong language and direct anger, which some readers may find challenging, and they reflect one poet's perspective. Read them as an invitation to listen and to partner with Vietnamese Minnesotan artists and organizations, not as a summary of the community.
questions: What did these poems teach you about how public institutions may be experienced by Vietnamese Minnesotans?
How do the portraits of different Nguyễns challenge the idea of a single Vietnamese experience?
Which Minnesota artists or community organizations could help our team hear these perspectives directly?

title: Holding Our World Together: Ojibwe Women and the Survival of Community
editionNote: First published 2012 · Viking (Penguin Library of American Indian History) · 240 pages
overview: Holding Our World Together is a history of Ojibwe women by Brenda J. Child. She is a historian at the University of Minnesota and an enrolled member of the Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians. The book was published in the Penguin Library of American Indian History. Child argues that Native history has too often centered on male warriors and leaders. In fact, many Native communities were organized around women's work, the importance of mothers and the knowledge of women elders. Focusing on Ojibwe people of Lake Superior and the Mississippi River, Child follows women's influence from the fur trade era through reservation life and into the cities of the twentieth century.
summary: Child builds the book around an Ojibwe idea of the older woman as the one who holds things together. That role carried status, wisdom and authority, not simply age. From the start she explains a challenge she faced as a historian. Early written records rarely paid attention to women, and European observers often misread Ojibwe family life and labor. So she draws women's stories out of unexpected places, including family memories, interviews and the passing details of other people's accounts. She reads them with care.

One major thread is the seasonal economy. Child describes how women organized the yearly round of harvesting wild rice, gathering berries and making maple sugar. That work gave women real economic authority and shaped where families lived through the year. She shows that land loss, removal policy and outside control of resources disrupted this cycle. Women's authority over food was tied to the health of the whole community.

Another thread concerns kinship and diplomacy during the fur trade. Child highlights Madeleine Cadotte, an Ojibwe woman who served as an important link between her people and European traders. Through stories like hers, the book shows how marriage and family ties built alliances. It also shows how women helped their communities manage contact with outsiders on terms that protected Ojibwe interests. Child presents these women not as exceptions but as examples of the authority many women held within their families and villages.

The book then follows women into the reservation era, when federal policy pushed families toward an imposed idea of civilization. Child traces how women adapted, from work in tourism and service jobs to keeping traditions and family bonds alive under pressure. She also notes that a woman without children of her own often acted as a mother to nieces, nephews and others. Elders were honored rather than set aside. These points correct outside assumptions about Ojibwe family life.

In the twentieth century the story moves to the city. Child writes about Gertrude Buckanaga, whose community work in postwar Minneapolis helped many Native families out of poverty. She also writes about women's part in later activism, including the American Indian Movement. These chapters connect directly to the urban Native community in Minnesota today. Reviewers praised the book as a warm, people-centered history, though one noted that some stories could have been told at greater length.
mainPoints: Ojibwe communities were often organized around women's labor, mothers and the knowledge of women elders.
An older woman who holds things together is a position of authority and respect, not just a description of age.
Women's control of harvests such as wild rice and maple sugar gave them economic standing in community life.
Removal and land loss disrupted the seasonal round and, with it, women's authority and family well-being.
Kinship and marriage served as tools of diplomacy during the fur trade.
Caring for children was shared widely, so mothering roles reached beyond one's own children.
Many European records trivialized Native women, so careful reading of sources is needed to see their real roles.
Urban Ojibwe women in Minneapolis built organizations and networks that helped families move out of poverty.
relevance: This book helps DSD staff look past a single image of Native life. It asks them to notice who often holds families together: grandmothers, aunties and women elders who coordinate care, make decisions and connect people to resources. For case management and planning, it encourages staff to ask who the family's key decision makers and helpers are. Staff should not assume the person on the form is the only voice. Its account of urban Native organizing in Minneapolis is useful for partnership work. Many Native Minnesotans live in the Twin Cities and are served through community organizations as well as Tribal programs. Keep its limits in view. It centers Ojibwe history and does not speak for Dakota or other Native communities. Its evidence is also thinner in early periods because of the records available. It is a starting point for respectful curiosity, never a profile of any one family.
questions: When we plan with a Native person or family, how do we learn who the trusted decision makers and caregivers really are?
What urban Native organizations in our region already support families, and what would a respectful partnership with them look like?
How might our own records, like the historical records Child describes, overlook the work women do to hold a family together?

title: Inventing the Feeble Mind: A History of Intellectual Disability in the United States
editionNote: First published 1994 · University of California Press · 356 pages
overview: Inventing the Feeble Mind is a history of how the United States has named, served and confined people with intellectual disabilities. Its author, James W. Trent, is a professor of sociology and social work at Gordon College. It first appeared in 1994 and was fully revised for a 2016 Oxford University Press edition, which carries the subtitle A History of Intellectual Disability in the United States. Trent draws on institutional records, court documents, private letters and rare photographs. He argues that the economic vulnerability of disabled people and their families has shaped the services and policies built around them, more than any claim about their abilities.
summary: Trent opens in a time before institutions, when people labeled idiots or simpletons were usually cared for, and sometimes mistreated, by their own families and towns. Poor households had few options beyond the almshouse. In the 1840s, a group of physicians and reformers began to treat intellectual disability as a public problem. They were inspired by European claims that such children could learn. The educator Edouard Seguin, who came to the United States in 1850, shaped the first American schools. These schools promised to train pupils for productive citizenship and return them home.

The middle of the nineteenth century brings a shift in who held authority. Physicians displaced educators, and explanations moved toward heredity, pathology and degeneration. In public argument, intellectual disability was tied to immorality and crime, which was used to justify surveillance. Schools that had promised to send students home became custodial asylums. Trent shows that the system split along class lines from early on. Public institutions filled with the children of poor families, while wealthier families had private options. That pattern supports his claim that money, not diagnosis, often decided where a person lived.

A central chapter describes daily life inside institutions between 1890 and 1920. Residents were sorted into those who could work and those labeled custodial cases. The working residents did much of the labor that kept the institutions running. Training shifted from reading and writing toward habits that fit institutional routine. One reviewer singled out the letters between residents and their families as among the most powerful passages in the book. These letters let people who were rarely heard speak about separation, longing and loss in their own words.

Trent then traces the eugenics period, when intellectual disability was framed as a menace to society. Prominent psychologists promoted segregation and sterilization, and institutional populations grew several times over in the early twentieth century. After a 1927 Supreme Court decision allowed forced sterilization, thousands of people were sterilized. Trent ties these operations as much to overcrowding and the wish to release residents as to eugenic belief. A system of parole let some residents leave to work in the community, often under close control.

The final chapters follow the postwar years and the turn toward community life. Conscientious objectors who worked in institutions exposed conditions there. Parents organized to demand better services, at first largely within institutions. Federal construction money kept institutions growing into the 1960s. Then critiques of total institutions, the principle of normalization, public scandal and budget pressure drove closures. Trent judges deinstitutionalization a real gain. He also notes that some community settings came to resemble small institutions, and that some former residents ended up in jails instead.
mainPoints: Intellectual disability has been defined differently in each era, and each definition served the people who designed the services.
Economic vulnerability, more than ability, has often decided whether a person lived at home or in an institution.
Early schools promised to return pupils to their communities, and the promise faded as institutions turned custodial.
Institutions depended on the unpaid labor of the residents they claimed to care for.
Eugenic ideas justified segregation and sterilization on a large scale, with lasting harm to families.
Letters between residents and families show that people in institutions wanted connection and home.
Deinstitutionalization was a genuine advance, but community services can reproduce institutional habits if no one watches for them.
relevance: The Olmstead decision of 1999 held that unjustified segregation of disabled people is discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Minnesota's own Olmstead Plan was required by the 2011 Jensen settlement. That settlement resolved a federal lawsuit over restraint and seclusion at a state treatment program in Cambridge. Trent explains the long history behind those legal commitments. For DSD staff, the book shows why integration is a civil right rather than a service preference. It also shows why waiver design, licensing and case management need to watch for institutional patterns in small settings. And it helps staff hear what families carry from earlier generations of services. Some limits are worth naming. It is a dense academic history, and it quotes historical terms that are painful to read today. Much of what we learn about residents comes through records kept by those who held power over them. One reviewer questioned parts of its account of eugenics.
questions: Trent argues that economic vulnerability shaped where people lived. Where do cost, rates or staffing still decide where someone lives in our programs, rather than the person's own choice?
Which habits of institutional life, such as fixed routines, group schedules or restricted visitors, could appear in a four-person home, and how would we notice?
How might the history in this book shape the trust, or the fear, that older families bring to conversations with us?

title: Decarcerating Disability: Deinstitutionalization and Prison Abolition
editionNote: First published 2020 · University of Minnesota Press · 376 pages
overview: Decarcerating Disability is a study of the closure of disability institutions and psychiatric hospitals. Its author, Liat Ben-Moshe, is a scholar of criminology, law and justice at the University of Illinois Chicago and coeditor of Disability Incarcerated. Published by the University of Minnesota Press, it argues that this closure was the largest movement of people out of locked facilities in the twentieth century. Yet it is often left out of public debate about prisons. Ben-Moshe reads the history of deinstitutionalization alongside current prison abolition work. She asks what each can teach the other about freedom, care and community.
summary: The introduction makes the case for studying disability, imprisonment and deinstitutionalization together. Ben-Moshe states her approach plainly. It draws on disability studies, feminist thought and the work of scholars of color, and it centers the people who lived inside institutions. The first chapter complicates the usual origin story of deinstitutionalization. She separates the history of psychiatric hospitals, where public fear of danger shaped policy, from the history of intellectual and developmental disability services. In those services, people were more often treated as lifelong children. Both stories, she argues, involve activism as well as budgets and drugs.

The second chapter follows the shift from reforming institutions to calling for their end. It centers the activism of people who had been institutionalized. These include people in the antipsychiatry movement and people involved in the push for normalization in developmental disability services. The third chapter defines its key terms: deinstitutionalization, decarceration and abolition. Ben-Moshe argues that abolition is a way of thinking as much as a policy goal. It questions the urge to know and classify people in advance. She also recasts common objections to closing facilities as places where new ideas can grow.

The fourth chapter challenges a claim that many readers will have heard: that prisons have become the new asylums because institutions closed. Ben-Moshe argues that the rise of mass incarceration and the loss of affordable housing came from political and economic choices. Blaming deinstitutionalization hides those choices. The fifth chapter turns to neighborhood resistance to group homes and community living. She shows that fights over where disabled people could live ran parallel to fights over racial desegregation, and that the two crossed. She does this without treating one as a mere analogy for the other.

The sixth chapter studies the feelings and arguments that surround institution closures, including appeals to choice, care, safety and innocence. Ben-Moshe looks closely at the role of workers and families, and at how caring language can treat disabled adults as children. Here she offers some of the book's most concrete suggestions, such as better community jobs and higher wages for support workers. The seventh chapter examines lawsuits, from landmark institution cases to prison reform suits. She concludes that courts have often produced reform rather than freedom. So lasting change needs coalitions across affected groups.

The epilogue gathers these threads and raises open questions about current alternatives. Ben-Moshe asks whether group homes, psychiatric medication and house arrest are true alternatives to confinement or new forms of control. She does not pretend to settle these questions. A reviewer described the book as dense and demanding, and noted that its terms take effort to absorb. The book received honors from the National Women's Studies Association, the American Studies Association and the Society for the Study of Social Problems.
mainPoints: The closure of disability institutions and psychiatric hospitals was one of the largest exits from confinement in the twentieth century.
Deinstitutionalization was driven by activism, including by people who had lived inside institutions, not only by budgets.
Blaming deinstitutionalization for mass incarceration hides the political choices that built prisons and cut housing.
Resistance to group homes and community living has overlapped with resistance to racial desegregation.
Caring language can still treat disabled adults as children and justify control.
Litigation has won important changes but often settles for reform of institutions rather than freedom from them.
Community services deserve the same scrutiny as institutions: a smaller setting is not automatically a free one.
relevance: This book is useful for DSD staff who want to understand Olmstead work as part of a wider question about freedom, not only about the size of a setting. Its account of neighborhood resistance can help teams planning community housing expect opposition and respond to it with partners. Its attention to support workers' wages connects integration to workforce policy. Its link between race and disability helps staff ask a hard question. Why are some disabled Minnesotans, particularly people of color, more likely to end up in jails, crisis settings or out-of-home placements? Readers should know that it is a demanding academic book. Its abolitionist position goes further than current state policy, and it is openly critical of group homes and of relying on courts. Read it as a challenge to sharpen our questions, not as a program manual.
questions: Ben-Moshe asks whether some community settings are true alternatives to confinement. What would a person we serve say about the freedom they actually have in their home?
When a neighborhood resists a new home, who speaks for the people who will live there, and how do we prepare for that conversation?
Where do people with disabilities in Minnesota still end up in jails, emergency rooms or crisis beds because community support was missing, and who is most affected?

title: Disability Servitude: From Peonage to Poverty
overview: Disability Servitude is a history of unpaid and underpaid work by people with intellectual and developmental disabilities in the United States. Its author, Ruthie-Marie Beckwith, has taught in the disability studies program at the City University of New York. Published by Palgrave Macmillan, it traces how state institutions relied on residents' labor for decades. It shows how residents and their advocates sued to be paid, and how the thinking of that era carried into sheltered workshops and the subminimum wage. It is a short, pointed book that treats fair pay as a matter of civil rights.
summary: Beckwith begins with institutional peonage. This was the practice of making residents of state institutions work, often for nothing, under the label of therapy or training. Residents did much of the daily work of running these places, and institutions came to depend on that labor. She frames this as involuntary servitude. A following chapter is titled around fighting forest fires and the lost heritage of competence and contribution. It recovers how much skilled and valuable work disabled residents did. That record sits uneasily beside claims that they could not work.

The book then turns to the peonage cases, the lawsuits brought in the 1970s to win pay for resident workers. In Souder v. Brennan, a federal court held that federal wage law applied to resident workers in institutions. Claims of therapeutic value did not cancel the economic benefit their work provided. Beckwith shows how far that victory reached and where it stopped. A later Supreme Court decision on federal power over states weakened enforcement for workers in state institutions.

In a chapter on the aftermath, Beckwith argues that the lawsuits helped speed deinstitutionalization, but did not secure fair pay for the people who brought them. Many resident workers were simply replaced by paid staff without disabilities, and residents lost both the work and the recognition that came with it. This part of the book shows how a legal win can leave the people at its center with little, which is a lesson for anyone who designs policy remedies.

The next chapters examine what Beckwith calls the peculiar institution of subminimum wage. Since 1938, Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act has allowed certified employers to pay disabled workers below the minimum wage. She describes long-standing oversight failures under that provision and argues that segregated employment settings carried forward patterns of institutional peonage. A further chapter follows how peonage and poverty persist in the twenty-first century. At the time she wrote, hundreds of thousands of workers were in sheltered settings.

The conclusion, titled Stone Buildings and Stone Walls, draws a line from the physical walls of institutions to the policy walls that still keep many disabled workers out of ordinary jobs at ordinary pay. One reviewer called the book a persuasive case that knowing this labor history is essential to real community integration. Another praised its balance between advocacy and critique. It is brief and densely sourced, and it is best read as history with a clear argument.
mainPoints: State institutions depended on the unpaid work of the people who lived in them, often described as therapy.
Disabled residents did skilled and valuable work, which undercuts later claims that they could not work.
Lawsuits in the 1970s established that wage law applied to resident workers, but enforcement was weakened.
Legal victories sped institution closures without securing fair pay for the workers who sued.
Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act has allowed subminimum wages since 1938, with weak oversight.
Sheltered workshops carried patterns from institutional labor into community settings.
Fair pay for work is a civil rights question, not only a program design question.
relevance: Employment First asks that competitive integrated employment be the first option offered to every working-age person. Beckwith explains why that policy was needed by showing how long disabled people's work has been taken without fair pay. For DSD staff, the book gives history for conversations with families who see sheltered settings as safe. It also supports providers moving away from subminimum wages, an effort Minnesota has supported since its 2021 Task Force on Eliminating Subminimum Wages, though its 2023 session left out the proposed end date. The book can also help teams explain why informed choice must include real exposure to community jobs. It has limits. It is a history and critique rather than a guide to job development. It says less about the experiences of workers who valued their workshops, and some figures date from the time of writing. Pair it with practical resources on customized and supported employment.
questions: Beckwith shows that disabled residents did valuable work for decades without fair pay. How does that history change the way we talk about someone being ready for work?
When a family says a sheltered setting feels safer, how can we respect that concern while making sure the person has real experience of community jobs before choosing?
Which of our own rules, rates or habits still make segregated settings the easier path for providers and case managers?

title: The Boys in the Bunkhouse: Servitude and Salvation in the Heartland
overview: The Boys in the Bunkhouse is a work of narrative journalism by Dan Barry, a longtime reporter and columnist for The New York Times, expanded from his 2014 Times reporting. It tells the story of a group of men with intellectual disabilities from Texas who, for more than three decades, lived in a decaying former schoolhouse in Atalissa, Iowa, and worked eviscerating turkeys at a processing plant for food, lodging and about sixty-five dollars a month. Barry follows the men, the business that profited from them, the town that knew them, and the advocates and lawyers who finally won their freedom.
summary: Barry begins in the 1960s, when a pilot program at a Texas state school sent a small group of young men to work for a rancher and businessman, T. H. Johnson, who agreed to teach them farm skills. The arrangement saved the state money and gave Johnson cheap labor. Over time it grew into a company that supplied disabled workers to turkey processing plants, and in 1974 a crew of men was moved to Atalissa. Barry weaves in the history of farm labor programs, the turkey industry and changing public attitudes toward intellectual disability.

The heart of the book is the men's daily life. They were bused to the plant before dawn to do bloody, repetitive and dangerous work, then returned to a schoolhouse that was falling apart around them. Their pay was far below minimum wage, and room and board were taken out of it. Reviewers note that they were denied basic medical and dental care and were mistreated by the people placed over them. Barry writes about them as individuals with pride in their work, humor and friendships, not as symbols.

Barry also looks hard at the town. Residents of Atalissa liked the men, waved to them at parades and sold them candy, and that affection made it harder for anyone to see what was happening. A social worker who visited raised alarms with state officials, who concluded that the business looked legitimate. One reviewer described the town's response as a mix of kindness and paternalism that missed the conditions in plain sight. The book gives the people who ran the business room to explain themselves, which makes its judgment more persuasive.

The turning point comes when a sister worried about her brother, and a determined newspaper reporter drew public attention to the bunkhouse in 2009.
