State officials then stepped in, the men were moved out, and many of them began new lives with support from people who had once looked away. Barry follows the federal legal case that followed, in which a jury returned a very large verdict for the men that was later sharply reduced under damage caps, leaving each man with far less than the jury intended.

The closing chapters follow the men after their rescue, as they received care and support and began to build lives of their own. Barry presents their story as both a scandal and a story of repair. Kirkus called it a gripping indictment, told gently and with empathy, and the Star Tribune praised its mix of hard reporting and literary craft. The case drew national attention to subminimum wage and to the oversight of employment arrangements for disabled workers.
mainPoints: A state arrangement that saved money and supplied cheap labor became decades of servitude for disabled workers.
Subminimum wages, combined with deductions for room and board, left the men with almost nothing for hard work.
Affection from neighbors did not protect the men, and in some ways made the harm harder to see.
Oversight failed when officials accepted appearances over the conditions people actually lived in.
A family member and a persistent reporter did what the system had not done.
Legal remedies brought recognition but were limited by damage caps.
With real support, the men built new lives that showed how much they had been denied.
relevance: This book makes the stakes of Employment First concrete. It shows what can happen when disabled workers are isolated, paid below minimum wage and supervised by people who profit from them, and when monitoring checks paperwork instead of lives. DSD staff can use it in training on licensing, monitoring and case management, to ask what we would need to see to recognize exploitation, and how to listen to people who may not complain. It also supports the case for competitive integrated work with ordinary coworkers and ordinary pay. Its limits are clear. It is one extreme case, told by a journalist rather than by the men themselves, and it should not be read as a portrait of every employment setting. Read it alongside history and policy on subminimum wages, and alongside voices of self-advocates.
questions: The men in this book were proud of their work and did not complain. How do our monitoring and case management practices find out what people are actually experiencing at work?
The town liked the men and still did not see what was happening. Where might goodwill be blinding us to conditions in settings we fund or license?
What would it take for every person we serve to have a coworker, neighbor or friend outside paid services who would notice if something was wrong?

title: Beyond Behaviors: Using Brain Science and Compassion to Understand and Solve Children's Behavioral Challenges
overview: Beyond Behaviors is a practical book by Mona Delahooke, a clinical psychologist with more than thirty years of experience on multidisciplinary teams and a senior faculty member of the Profectum Foundation. Published by PESI, it treats challenging behavior as the visible tip of an iceberg, with a person's sense of safety in relationships beneath it. Delahooke draws on developmental science and on Stephen Porges's polyvagal theory to argue that many behaviors adults call defiant are stress responses, and that the most effective response is connection and support for regulation rather than punishment or rewards.
summary: Delahooke opens by asking readers to look past behavior to what drives it. She argues that many children who seem unable to behave have not yet developed the capacity to do so, and that treating every behavior as a deliberate choice leads adults to punish distress. The book is written for parents, teachers and professionals, and addresses children with a wide range of labels, including autism, anxiety, sensory processing differences, trauma and diagnoses such as oppositional defiant disorder, as well as everyday tantrums and shutdowns.

A central idea is the difference between top-down and bottom-up behavior. Top-down behavior is planned and under conscious control. Bottom-up behavior comes from the nervous system's response to stress, often before thinking can catch up. Delahooke argues that rewards and consequences may shape top-down behavior but tend to backfire with bottom-up behavior, because a person in distress cannot learn a lesson in that moment. Telling the two apart is the first job of anyone trying to help.

Delahooke then offers a simple color language for states of the nervous system, drawn from polyvagal theory. Green describes a state of safety and connection in which a person can learn and engage. Red describes fight or flight. Blue describes shutdown, when a person withdraws in response to overwhelming threat. Reviewers found this language easy to share with families and teams, because it moves the conversation from what a child is doing wrong to what state the child is in and what would help.

Much of the book is practical. Delahooke provides worksheets, charts and observation questions that help adults map a child's developmental capacities, sensory needs, sleep and health, and the relationships around them. She emphasizes co-regulation: an adult's calm, attuned presence helps a distressed person return to safety. She also asks adults to check their own state first, since a stressed caregiver can escalate a situation without meaning to. Case examples show teams changing environments and expectations instead of applying more control.

Reviews are mostly warm. Readers praised the reframing of behavior as communication and the usable tools, and many found it accessible for people new to these ideas. Critics, including a behavior analyst, found it long, repetitive and lighter on specific methods than they wanted, and some experienced clinicians found the ideas familiar. The book focuses on children, so adult services must translate its lessons rather than apply them directly, with attention to the dignity and autonomy of grown people.
mainPoints: Behavior is the visible part of a deeper story about safety, stress and capacity.
Many behaviors that look defiant are nervous-system stress responses rather than deliberate choices.
Rewards and consequences can backfire when a person is in distress and cannot learn in that moment.
A shared language for states of safety, fight or flight, and shutdown can help teams respond in the moment.
Co-regulation through a calm, attuned relationship is a primary tool, not an extra.
Caregivers need to notice their own stress, because it shapes how a situation unfolds.
Changing environments and expectations often works better than adding control.
relevance: Minnesota's positive supports requirements limit restrictive procedures and ask providers to understand the reasons behind behavior. Delahooke gives DSD staff, case managers and providers a clear, compassionate language for that work. It can support training on why restraint and punishment escalate distress, on reading signs of shutdown that are easy to miss, and on building plans around safety, sensory needs and relationships. It also helps staff talk with families who have been told their child is simply defiant. Its limits matter. It is written about children, so its tools must be adapted with care for adults, whose dignity and autonomy require different language. It is lighter on measurable methods than some teams need, and it should sit alongside person-centered positive support practice and the views of disabled people themselves.
questions: Think of a behavior support plan you know. Does it treat the behavior as a choice to be managed, or as a sign of a state the person is in?
What signs of shutdown, the quiet withdrawal Delahooke describes, might our teams miss because they do not disrupt anyone?
How do we help direct support staff notice and manage their own stress, given that it shapes the situations they are in?

title: Lost at School: Why Our Kids with Behavioral Challenges Are Falling Through the Cracks and How We Can Help Them
overview: Lost at School is a book by Ross W. Greene, a clinical psychologist and author of The Explosive Child, who developed the approach now called Collaborative and Proactive Solutions. Published by Scribner and later revised, it argues against punitive discipline for children with behavioral challenges. Its organizing belief is that kids do well if they can: when they do not, it is because they lack skills, not because they are manipulative or unmotivated. Greene shows how adults can identify those lagging skills and the specific problems that trigger behavior, then solve those problems together with the young person.
summary: Greene opens with a critique of traditional discipline. Detentions, suspensions, expulsions and zero tolerance policies, he argues, fail the students who receive them most often, because they treat challenging behavior as a problem of motivation. The students most often punished are the ones who lack the skills to meet expectations, and punishment does not teach those skills. He proposes that adults replace the question of how to make a child behave with the question of what is getting in the way.

The book's first practical tool is an assessment of lagging skills and unsolved problems. Lagging skills include flexibility, frustration tolerance, problem solving and managing emotions. Unsolved problems are the specific, predictable situations in which behavior happens, such as a transition, a type of task or a crowded space. Greene argues that behavior is highly predictable once adults list these situations, so the work can be proactive, done before the next incident rather than during it.

The core of the approach is a collaborative conversation, which Greene often calls Plan B, with three steps. First comes empathy: gathering the young person's own view of the problem and what makes it hard. Second, adults state their own concerns clearly. Third comes an invitation to find a solution together that addresses both sets of concerns and is realistic for everyone. Greene contrasts this with imposing adult will or simply dropping expectations.

Much of the book follows a running story about one student and the adults around him, with dialogues, questions and answers, and planning advice for teachers, parents and administrators. Greene addresses how to fit the approach into individualized education programs and behavior plans, how to de-escalate, and how to change school culture so the approach is not left to one patient teacher. The revised edition adds refinements to the conversation steps and to building relationships.

Readers often describe the book as eye-opening and practical. Critics found the scripted dialogues repetitive, felt it says too little about trauma, poverty and culture, and noted limited guidance for specialized settings and for teaching the missing skills. Some educators felt its time demands were unrealistic. The book itself is written about children in school, so readers who support adults or work outside schools will need to adapt its language and examples with care.
mainPoints: Kids do well if they can: challenging behavior usually signals lagging skills, not poor motivation.
Punitive discipline falls hardest on the students who most need skills, and does not teach them.
Behavior is predictable once adults identify the specific situations that trigger it.
Proactive problem solving, done before the next incident, works better than reacting during a crisis.
The young person's own view of the problem is essential information, gathered with empathy.
Solutions should address both the person's concerns and the adults' concerns, and be realistic for both.
Lasting change requires the whole organization to adopt the approach, not one committed adult.
relevance: For DSD staff and providers working to reduce restrictive practices, Greene offers a respectful, structured way to replace control with collaboration. His idea that people do well if they can fits the goals of positive supports, and his focus on predictable triggers helps teams plan ahead instead of responding to crises with restraint or removal. The collaborative conversation can be adapted for adults, making the person a partner in their own plan, which supports informed choice and dignity. Staff should know its limits. It is written for schools and children, its examples can feel scripted, and critics note it gives little attention to trauma, culture and poverty. Adult services will need to translate its language with care and pair it with person-centered planning and the experience of disabled people.
questions: If we believed that the people we support do well if they can, which parts of our current behavior plans would we change first?
What predictable situations, such as transitions, crowded spaces or staff changes, come before incidents in the settings we know, and what could be solved ahead of time?
How do we make sure the person's own explanation of a problem is gathered and used before a plan is written?

title: Supported Decision-Making: Theory, Research, and Practice to Enhance Self-Determination and Quality of Life
authors: Karrie A. Shogren, Michael L. Wehmeyer, Jonathan Martinis, and Peter Blanck
overview: Supported Decision-Making is a book by four leading figures in disability research and law. Karrie Shogren and Michael Wehmeyer of the University of Kansas study self-determination. Jonathan Martinis and Peter Blanck work at the Burton Blatt Institute at Syracuse University. Cambridge University Press published the book in its disability law and policy series. It presents supported decision-making as an alternative to guardianship. In this approach, a person keeps the legal right to make choices, while trusted people help them understand options and communicate decisions. The book draws together research from law, psychology, education and health. It offers a roadmap for states, families, attorneys and support providers.
summary: The book begins with how supported decision-making emerged. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recognized that disabled people have the right to exercise legal capacity, meaning the right to make choices the law will respect. It named support in decision-making as a way to make that right real. The authors trace how the idea moved into the disability field in the United States. This happened as growing numbers of adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities came to live under guardianship. Shogren has described the dominant guardianship approach as rooted in an outdated understanding of disability.

The next part sets out the frameworks behind the book. The authors use social-ecological understandings of disability. These place disability in the fit between a person and their environment, rather than only in the person. The authors add strengths-based approaches from positive psychology. They also use causal agency theory, which explains how people become the causal agents in their own lives. Together these frameworks change the question. Instead of asking whether a person can decide alone, they ask what supports would help them decide.

The authors then look at decision-making capacity in law and practice. They examine how courts and clinicians judge capacity. They show how the demands of a setting shape what a decision requires, and which decision-making skills and support needs matter most. In this view, capacity is not a fixed trait. It varies with the decision, the setting and the support available. This part also reviews legal frameworks for supported decision-making and state legislation, using states such as Texas and Delaware as examples.

A further section reviews research on supported decision-making and self-determination in the United States and other countries. It also covers new tools for assessment and intervention. The authors are candid that the evidence base is still developing. They describe ongoing work to measure what supported decision-making does in people's lives, including its effects on self-determination and quality of life. This makes the book useful for readers who want to know what is known and what is still uncertain.

The final chapters turn to building systems of supports. The authors offer guidance for individuals, families, support providers, schools and communities. They explain how to plan and use supported decision-making across the lifespan, including legal and financial tools and community supports. This work can happen even where state law has not yet recognized supported decision-making. A closing chapter names what all this means for future theory, research and practice. Its message, in Shogren's phrase, is that everyone needs supports to make decisions.
mainPoints: Supported decision-making lets a person keep legal rights while trusted supporters help them understand and communicate choices.
International human rights law recognizes the right of disabled people to exercise legal capacity with support.
Disability is better understood as a fit between a person and their environment than as a fixed deficit.
Decision-making capacity changes with the decision, the setting and the support available.
People become causal agents in their own lives when they have chances to make choices and learn from them.
States are building legal recognition of supported decision-making, and practice can begin even before the law catches up.
Everyone relies on support to make important decisions, so needing help is not a reason to lose rights.
relevance: For DSD staff, this book gives a rigorous foundation for talking about guardianship alternatives, informed choice and the dignity of risk. Case managers can use its frameworks to help families and teams ask a better question. The question is what support a person needs to decide, not whether they can decide alone. This matters most at the move into adulthood, when families often seek guardianship by default. Policy staff will find its review of state laws and research helpful for planning and training. The book also supports person-centered planning, because it treats choice as a skill that grows with practice. Its limits: it is an academic book from a university press, with a price and density to match. Its examples are largely about intellectual and developmental disabilities. Pair it with plain-language guides written by and with self-advocates.
questions: When a young person nears adulthood, what do we tell families about guardianship? Do we describe less restrictive alternatives first?
Think of a decision a person we serve is facing. What supports, such as time, plain-language information or a trusted person, would help them make it themselves?
Where do our own forms, meetings or timelines make it harder for a person to be the decision-maker in their own plan?

title: Beyond Guardianship: Toward Alternatives That Promote Greater Self-Determination for People with Disabilities
editionNote: First published 2018 · National Council on Disability (U.S. Government Publishing Office)
overview: Beyond Guardianship is a book-length report by the National Council on Disability. The council is the independent federal agency that advises the President and Congress on disability policy. It prepared the report with Quality Trust for Individuals with Disabilities, along with a qualitative study by the Institute on Disabilities at Temple University. Released in March 2018, the report looks at guardianship through the lens of disability civil rights. It also draws on the integration mandate of the Americans with Disabilities Act, which requires services in the most integrated setting appropriate. The report explains how guardianship works and documents its problems. It reviews less restrictive alternatives, including supported decision-making. It then makes recommendations to Congress, federal agencies and state and local governments.
summary: The report opens with the basics of guardianship and sets them against disability rights law. In guardianship, a state court finds that an adult lacks capacity to make some or all decisions. The court then appoints someone to decide for them. The council notes that guardianship is a matter of state law, yet it removes rights protected by the Constitution. People under guardianship are still protected by the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504. The council estimates that about 1.3 million people in the United States are subject to guardianship.

Early chapters trace how guardianship law has changed and describe the current system. A central finding is how little anyone knows. Reliable state and national data are largely missing, both on how many people are under guardianship and on how many new cases are filed. The report asks whether guardianship prevents abuse or sometimes leads to it. It finds that courts often lack the resources and training to monitor guardians. That gap can leave room for financial exploitation, abuse or neglect.

The report then examines capacity and the role of experts. It finds that capacity assessments often lack strong scientific or evidentiary support. The professionals asked to judge capacity vary by state. Proceedings often start from the assumption that disabled people cannot make their own decisions. The report describes gaps in due process and the difficulty of getting strong legal representation. It also notes the overuse of full guardianship when a limited order, or no order, would do. It names a school-to-guardianship pipeline, in which schools steer families of students with intellectual and developmental disabilities toward guardianship at age eighteen.

Further chapters look at life once a guardianship is in place. They cover effects on voting, relationships and sexuality, along with financial abuse and orders that reach too far. Every state has a process for restoring rights, but the council finds that people seldom use it. The report then turns to less restrictive alternatives. It argues that the Olmstead decision makes finding alternatives to guardianship a civil rights duty. It reviews options such as supported decision-making, powers of attorney, health care directives and representative payees, and it offers a practical tool for weighing them.

A chapter on stakeholder experiences draws on interviews with people with disabilities, family members and professionals in the guardianship system. One professional observed that everyone makes poor decisions sometimes. Respecting a person's right to a wrong decision, this professional said, is part of respecting them. The final chapter sets out findings and recommendations. These include better data, stronger due process, real enforcement of less restrictive alternatives and wider use of supported decision-making. Appendices list state statutes and contacts for local guardianship reform groups.
mainPoints: Guardianship removes constitutional rights, yet courts often impose it with little evidence and weak due process.
Reliable data on how many people live under guardianship, and what happens to them, are largely missing.
Capacity assessments often rest on assumptions about disability rather than strong evidence.
Students with intellectual and developmental disabilities are often steered into guardianship at eighteen by default.
Most states require courts to consider less restrictive alternatives, but the requirement is rarely enforced.
Restoration of rights is available in every state but seldom pursued.
The integration mandate of the Americans with Disabilities Act supports alternatives such as supported decision-making.
relevance: This report is one of the most authoritative United States sources on guardianship and its alternatives, and it is free to read on the council's website. DSD staff can use it to ground training on informed choice and dignity of risk. It can also help us review how our programs talk with families about guardianship during transition. And it can help us find people who might seek restoration of their rights. Its chapters on due process and capacity help case managers notice when a guardianship may be broader than a person needs. Its connection to Olmstead ties decision-making rights to community integration. Note its limits. It is a federal policy report, not a narrative book. Its findings date from 2018, and state laws, including Minnesota's, have kept changing. Its interviews are summarized rather than told at length in people's own voices.
questions: The report describes a school-to-guardianship pipeline. What happens in our transition planning, and who first raises guardianship with families?
How would we know if a person we serve has a guardianship broader than they need? What would we do to support restoration of their rights?
What would it look like in our planning meetings to respect a person's right to make a decision we disagree with?

title: A Little Book About Person Centered Planning
authors: John O'Brien (editor) and Connie Lyle O'Brien (editor)
overview: A Little Book About Person Centered Planning is a collection edited by John O'Brien and Connie Lyle O'Brien, two of the people who shaped person-centered planning in North America, and published by Inclusion Press in Toronto. It gathers short essays that passed around as handouts in the early years of the practice. The authors are among its founders, including Judith Snow, a disabled advocate and pioneer of circles of support, along with Michael Smull, Beth Mount, Marsha Forest, Jack Pearpoint, Herb Lovett and Jeff Strully. A later second edition added new chapters. Together the essays explain why person-centered planning exists and what it is for.
summary: The collection opens with Judith Snow's essay on the power in vulnerability, which places planning within interdependence and community. Snow argues that when people with different gifts and needs are connected to one another, everyone's capacity grows. The O'Briens follow with an essay on learning to listen, the foundation skill of the practice. They describe how people come to life when someone works faithfully to understand them, especially people who communicate in unusual ways or whose communication has been discounted.

Several essays warn about what happens when systems adopt the practice. In an essay asking whether person-centered planning has arrived, the O'Briens and Beth Mount caution that applying a procedure without attention to relationships and agreements will disappoint. Michael Smull's essay on thinking before you plan states a principle that runs through the book: a plan is not an outcome. The outcome is the life the person wants, and the only good reason to plan is to help someone move toward it.

The O'Briens' essay on the politics of person-centered planning argues that it is not a way to avoid conflict. Instead, it brings real conflicts among individuals, families, communities and service systems into the open, in partnership with disabled people who want change. Smull's essay on revisiting choice looks at common misunderstandings of choice and how to balance choice and safety. It also shows how staff values shape which opportunities are offered or withheld. He asks readers to notice when they say someone is not ready.

Other essays turn to everyday life. Smull writes on positive rituals and routines that build relationships, and on what happens after the plan, when listening and acting must continue because what people want will change. Beth Mount describes the benefits and limits of planning and the conditions linked to real change in people's lives. The O'Briens explore the quest for community membership, asking how planning can help communities include people as contributing members.

The closing essays address circles of support and facilitation. Snow describes building support circles, and O'Brien and Strully offer questions that circles can use to check their contribution. Forest and Pearpoint name the ethical dangers and safeguards of the MAPS and PATH processes. O'Brien and Mount contrast stories that enhance a life with stories that degrade it, and O'Brien and Lovett describe what different planning approaches share. A final guide outlines an early version of personal futures planning.
mainPoints: Person-centered planning exists to help a person move toward the life they want, so a plan is never the outcome.
Deep listening is the foundation skill, especially with people whose communication has been discounted.
Planning belongs inside relationships and community, not only inside a service system.
Requiring a procedure without attention to relationships leads to disappointing results.
Person-centered work brings real conflicts to the surface and works through them with the person, rather than avoiding them.
Staff values shape which choices are offered, so teams need to talk openly about those values.
Listening must continue after the plan, because people's wishes change over time.
relevance: Minnesota requires person-centered planning and practices across disability services, and this small book explains the purpose behind those requirements in the words of the people who created the practice. DSD staff can use its essays in training for case managers, providers and policy staff, to keep the focus on the life the person wants rather than the completed form. Smull's essays on choice and safety are especially useful for discussions of informed choice and dignity of risk, and the politics essay helps leaders expect conflict and work through it. Its limits: it is a collection of short pieces written in the 1990s. Much of it reflects intellectual and developmental disability services, and its language sometimes reflects its time. It is a statement of purpose rather than a manual for today's tools.
questions: Smull writes that a plan is not an outcome. In our work, how do we know whether a person's life is actually moving toward what they want?
When we say someone is not ready for a choice, whose values are we expressing? How could we test that judgment?
Who outside paid services takes part in planning for the people we serve, and how could we invite more of those relationships?

title: Person-Centred Teams: A Practical Guide to Delivering Personalisation Through Effective Team-Work
authors: Helen Sanderson and Mary Beth Lepkowsky
editionNote: First published 2014 · Jessica Kingsley Publishers · 168 pages
overview: Person-Centred Teams is a practical guide by two authors. Helen Sanderson is a leading developer of person-centred thinking and planning in the United Kingdom and chief executive of Helen Sanderson Associates. Mary Beth Lepkowsky runs Pathways Facilitation Services and has led training and organizational development at Tri-Counties Regional Center, a California nonprofit serving people with developmental disabilities and their families. Published by Jessica Kingsley, the book asks what happens after person-centred plans and personal budgets are introduced: how must the teams who provide support change? It turns person-centred practices inward, applying them to the team itself.
summary: The authors begin from a gap many organizations know well. Systems can adopt person-centred plans and individual budgets, yet daily support stays the same if the team delivering it works in the old way. Sanderson and Lepkowsky argue that a team can only support people in person-centred ways if it uses the same practices among its own members. They set out a framework for developing a team and recording what it learns in a person-centred team plan, a living document that sits alongside the plans of the people the team supports.

An opening chapter on profiles and plans explains the tools the rest of the book relies on. The guide is then organized around five areas. The first is purpose: helping a team become clear about why it exists and what it is trying to achieve in the lives of the people it supports. A shared, clear purpose gives the team a way to make decisions and to notice when routines have drifted away from what matters to people.

The second area is people. Here the authors describe what a manager needs to know about each team member, including their strengths, interests and what helps them do their best work, and they show how one-page profiles can capture that information. The same tool that helps staff understand a person they support also helps a team understand its own members. Work can then be matched to people's gifts, and support can be offered in ways that make sense to each staff member.

The third area is performance: getting clear on what the people who use a service expect of the team, and checking whether those expectations are being met. The fourth is process, which looks at how person-centred practices can improve the way a team works together and gets things done. The fifth is progress, which treats teamwork and performance as things to keep improving rather than settle. Each area draws on examples and illustrations from real teams.

The book closes with a conclusion and two appendices: a self-assessment that teams can use to judge how person-centred they are, and a summary of the person-centred practices used throughout. It is written for providers, managers, practitioners, students, planning coordinators and user-led organizations across health, social care, education and voluntary settings. A human resources director at a social care charity called it a usable and pragmatic guide to improving team performance.
mainPoints: Person-centred plans change little unless the teams delivering support also work in person-centred ways.
A team should use with its own members the same practices it uses with the people it supports.
A clear, shared purpose helps a team decide what matters and notice when routines have drifted.
One-page profiles help managers understand each team member's strengths and what helps them work well.
Teams should know what the people they support expect, and check honestly whether they are meeting those expectations.
A written team plan keeps learning visible and shared as staff come and go.
Being person-centred is an ongoing practice of improvement, not a box to check once.
relevance: Minnesota asks disability service providers to deliver person-centered supports. DSD staff often see that the gap between a good plan and a good day lies in how direct support teams are organized and led. This guide gives DSD trainers, licensing and quality staff, and provider partners concrete tools for closing that gap: team purpose statements, one-page profiles for staff, and self-assessment. It can also help DSD's own teams practice what they ask of others. Lepkowsky's work in a California developmental disability system gives it a United States connection. Its limits: its policy language comes from English personalisation and personal budgets, and it is a workbook rather than a study. It also does not take up wages, turnover or staffing shortages, which shape what teams can do. Use it alongside workforce and self-advocate perspectives.
questions: If the team supporting a person wrote down its purpose today, would it describe the life that person wants or the tasks of the shift?
What do managers in the settings we oversee know about the strengths and needs of each direct support worker? How do they use it?
How could our own DSD team use one of these practices, such as a team purpose statement or one-page profiles, before we ask providers to?

title: Over My Head: A Doctor's Own Story of Head Injury from the Inside Looking Out
overview: Over My Head is a memoir by Claudia L. Osborn, an internist and clinical professor of medicine who sustained a traumatic brain injury in a bicycle crash. First published in 1997 and reissued by Andrews McMeel the following year, it describes from the inside the loss of the profession she loved and of everyday abilities she had taken for granted. It also traces her long path to a new and full life. Library Journal wrote that it would help patients, families and friends facing similar difficulties, and readers with brain injuries have often said it captures their experience.
summary: Osborn begins with her life before the injury, as a respected young internist who lived with her close friend Marcia, also a physician. After a bicycle crash, she was released from the hospital within hours, and at first no one recognized how serious her brain injury was. Over the following weeks she realized that her memory, reasoning, energy and ability to think clearly had changed. Her account of trying to keep practicing medicine, and of slowly seeing that she could not, shows how invisible a brain injury can be, even to a doctor.

The middle of the book describes daily life with a changed brain. Osborn writes about forgetting, losing track of tasks, feeling overwhelmed in busy places and struggling with errands such as grocery shopping and sorting mail. She describes a state she calls flooding, when her mind filled with thoughts that never reached a conclusion and her emotions became hard to manage. She also describes fatigue, and the way other people, including colleagues, played down what they could not see.

A turning point comes when she moves from Michigan to New York City to take part in a full-time Head Trauma Program at New York University's medical center. She works in a small group of people with brain injuries, relearning skills and building strategies together. Readers remember the tools she learned to rely on, such as lists, notebooks, recorders and alarms, and the shared experience of a group whose members understood one another. The program helps her stop measuring herself only against the person she had been.

Osborn writes candidly about grief. Losing her medical practice meant losing an identity, a community and a way of being useful. She describes the work of accepting a new self, and the help of friends who stayed, especially Marcia. She also describes unexpected gains, including a sharper perception of color and new interests in painting and writing. One reviewer noted that the book shows memory and attention problems through everyday mishaps rather than clinical tests, which makes them easy to understand.

The book closes years after the injury, as Osborn reflects on a life that is different and full. Its tone mixes restraint and humor. Some readers felt the journal entries and letters were heavily edited or that parts now feel dated, and the book says little about the medical details of her injury. Its value lies in its honest view, from a physician turned patient, of what brain injury feels like day to day, what made things worse and what helped her rebuild.
mainPoints: Brain injury can be invisible to others, and sometimes to the injured person, for a long time.
Everyday tasks such as errands and mail can become the hardest part of life after a brain injury.
Fatigue, overload and emotional flooding are real effects of injury, not signs of weak effort.
Practical strategies such as lists, alarms and routines can restore independence.
Rehabilitation with peers who share the experience can matter as much as clinical treatment.
Losing a career can mean losing an identity, and grief for that loss deserves room.
A full life after brain injury is possible, though it may look different from the life before.
relevance: DSD programs serve people with brain injuries, including through the Brain Injury waiver, and many have injuries that others cannot see. Osborn helps staff understand why a person may struggle with paperwork, appointments and busy offices, and why fatigue and overload affect follow-through. That understanding can shape how assessors, case managers and providers schedule meetings, share information in writing and offer reminders, instead of treating missed steps as noncompliance. It also shows the value of peer support and of honoring grief for a changed identity. Its limits: it reflects one well-educated professional with strong personal support, written in the 1990s. It says little about people without those resources, or about how race, income and rural life shape recovery. Pair it with the voices of brain injury survivors from Minnesota communities.
questions: Osborn found errands and mail among the hardest tasks. Which of our own processes, such as forms, renewals or phone menus, would be hardest for someone with her challenges?
How do we tell the difference between a person who is not following through and a person who is overloaded or exhausted?
Where can the people with brain injuries we serve connect with peers who understand their experience?

title: Where Is the Mango Princess? A Journey Back from Brain Injury
editionNote: First published 2000 · Alfred A. Knopf · 272 pages
overview: Where Is the Mango Princess? is a memoir by Cathy Crimmins, a writer and humorist, about life after her husband, Alan, an attorney, sustained a traumatic brain injury. In 1996, during a family vacation at a lake in Ontario, a speedboat struck Alan and left him in a coma with serious damage to the frontal lobes of his brain. Published by Knopf, the book follows what happened to Crimmins, Alan and their young daughter, Kelly, after he woke up, as a family learned to live with a man whose personality had changed.
summary: Crimmins opens with the accident and the first frightening days in intensive care, when the family did not know whether Alan would live or what kind of person would wake up. She explains frontal lobe injury in plain terms as the story unfolds, and reviewers credited her with getting the medical details right. The early chapters capture the shock and confusion that families feel when a loved one's life changes in an instant. They also show how fast families must learn a new vocabulary and a new system.

Most of the book follows Alan's long rehabilitation, which proved harder than the injury itself. As he recovered, he became uninhibited in public, verbally and sexually, and his emotions ran high. Crimmins writes about worrying that she was married to a stranger. She also writes with humor about the strange and sometimes funny situations the injury created, and reviewers noted that the humor never hides the pain. Her honesty extends to herself: she admits she did not feel like a natural nurturer, and she describes the pressure on women to become caregivers in a crisis.

A strong thread in the book is Crimmins's anger at the health insurance system. She describes battles with managed care plans that would not pay for the rehabilitation she believed Alan needed. She also describes the work of advocating for him while caring for him and their daughter. Some readers questioned parts of her account of insurance and family finances. Still, the book gives a vivid picture of how much rehabilitation can depend on a family's ability to fight for it.

As Alan improves, the book traces a quieter kind of change. He becomes warmer and more easygoing, and in many ways he recovers well, yet Crimmins misses parts of the man she married, including his sharper edges. The memoir does not resolve those mixed feelings. It shows a marriage and a family reorganizing around a new reality, with grief and affection side by side, and it treats Alan as a person with his own experience, not only as a patient.

Reviews were mixed. Bookreporter praised the book as moving and long on humor. Publishers Weekly found it eye-opening in places but thought it focused too much on the author's own experience, with little attention to other families affected by brain injury or to wider research. Readers should take it as one family's story, told by a spouse with a writer's eye and a sharp sense of humor, rather than as a guide to brain injury or to the experiences of families with fewer resources.
mainPoints: Brain injury changes a whole family, not only the injured person.
Frontal lobe injury can change personality, inhibition and emotion in ways families find hard to recognize.
Rehabilitation can be longer and harder than the medical crisis that came before it.
Families often become advocates against insurance and service systems while also providing care.
Caregiving roles carry gendered expectations that can add guilt and strain.
Humor can be a way for families to survive, without denying pain.
Recovery can bring real gains and real losses at the same time.
relevance: DSD staff work with spouses, parents and children who are adjusting to a family member's brain injury, often while dealing with waivers, insurance and providers at the same time. Crimmins shows what that experience can feel like from inside a household. She captures the exhaustion of advocacy, the confusion of personality change and the mixed grief of a recovery that is real but incomplete. The book can help case managers listen for family strain, plan respite and caregiver support, and explain behavior changes without blame. It also reminds staff to keep the injured person at the center of planning, even when a spouse speaks loudest. Its limits: it is one family's story, told by a spouse, and critics found it self-focused. It reflects the insurance system of the late 1990s and a family with resources many do not have.
questions: Crimmins describes becoming an advocate while also being a caregiver. How do our processes add to, or ease, that double burden for families?
When a person's personality has changed after injury, how do we make sure their own wishes, not only their family's, guide the plan?
What supports, such as respite, peer groups or counseling, do we offer to family members adjusting to a loved one's brain injury?

title: Writing for Busy Readers: Communicate More Effectively in the Real World
overview: Writing for Busy Readers is a practical, research-based guide to writing that people actually read and act on. Todd Rogers is a behavioral scientist and professor of public policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, and Jessica Lasky-Fink is research director at The People Lab. Over about a decade, the two ran field experiments on how school districts reach busy families and how campaigns reach busy voters. During the pandemic they advised state and local leaders on communicating with the public. The book distills that work into six principles, with examples, a checklist and other tools.
summary: The authors begin from a plain fact about reading in daily life: most readers skim, are short on time, and care less about a message than the person who wrote it. Rather than blaming readers, Rogers and Lasky-Fink argue that the writer is responsible for meeting people where they are. They separate effective writing, which aims for the reader to understand and respond, from beautiful writing. They present the book as an update of classic style advice for a crowded digital world, where every email, letter and notice competes for limited attention.

The first principle, less is more, asks writers to use fewer words, include fewer ideas and make fewer requests. Cutting needless words is easy, but cutting ideas that are useful yet optional takes judgment. The authors draw on experiments, including one in which shorter emails drew noticeably higher response rates. They stress that every added request lowers the chance that the most important one gets done. The book presents deciding what matters most, and saying only that, as the hardest and most valuable part of the work.

The second principle is to make reading easy, with short and common words, straightforward sentences and a lower reading level. Rogers rejects the idea that this means dumbing down. He points out that some celebrated literature is written in very simple language. He argues that turning complex ideas into clear prose is a craft, while making simple ideas complicated takes no skill at all. Nuance can survive plain words, and it often survives better.

The third and fourth principles concern design and formatting. Readers jump around a document, so headings, a clear opening that explains what follows, and logical order help people find what they need. Formatting such as bold or highlighting signals importance. But the authors report that emphasizing one passage increases attention to it while reducing reading of everything else. They recommend enough formatting to guide the eye, and no more, so that emphasis keeps its meaning.

The final two principles ask writers to tell readers why they should care and to make responding easy. The authors suggest naming the intended audience early, so a reader knows quickly whether a message is meant for them. They also suggest removing steps between reading and acting, such as unclear instructions or hard-to-find links. The book closes with tools for building readability editing into routine practice. The goal is for clear writing to become a team habit rather than a matter of individual talent.
mainPoints: Most readers skim, so writers must design for limited time and attention rather than ideal reading.
The writer, not the reader, is responsible when an important message is missed.
Fewer words, fewer ideas and fewer requests raise the chance that readers act on the main request.
Short, common words and simple sentences carry complex ideas without talking down to anyone.
Headings and clear structure help readers who move around a document find what they need.
Formatting works only when used sparingly, because emphasis on everything signals emphasis on nothing.
Telling readers early why a message matters to them, and making the response easy, improves follow-through.
Readability editing can be a routine team practice, tested and improved like any other part of a service.
relevance: Much of what DSD staff produce, from notices and waiver letters to provider bulletins and web pages, asks busy people to understand something and act. This book gives teams a shared, evidence-based vocabulary for editing those documents, and its findings came partly from work with schools and state and local governments. It pairs well with Minnesota's plain language expectations for state agencies and with accessibility practice. Clear structure helps people using screen readers, people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, and people reading in a second language. Its limits are worth naming. The authors write mainly about general audiences and digital messages. They say little about easy read formats, translation or how disabled readers experience text. Use it alongside testing with the people who receive our materials, and with guidance from self-advocates on accessible formats.
questions: Pick one letter or notice our team sends often. How many separate requests does it make, and which one matters most to the person reading it?
Where do we rely on bold, capitals or warnings so heavily that readers may no longer notice them?
How could we test a revised document with the people who receive it, including self-advocates and people reading through an interpreter?

title: Letting Go of the Words: Writing Web Content that Works
overview: Letting Go of the Words is a standard guide to writing for the web from Ginny Redish, a linguist and one of the central figures in the United States plain language movement. Redish spent decades helping organizations communicate clearly. She co-wrote well-known books on usability testing and task analysis, and she wrote the writing guidance for the federal usability.gov site. The book first appeared in 2007. A second edition in 2012 added material on content strategy, search and social media, along with many new examples. Its core idea is that good web content works like a conversation with the person who came looking for an answer.
summary: Redish starts from the reader. People come to a website with a question or a task, and they want to finish it and move on. Redish asks writers to define their users in detail, including their backgrounds, the situations that bring them to the site and the context in which they read, so that writers can predict the questions people will ask. In her view, content is the reason a site exists, and planning content around real users and their tasks comes before any decisions about design or wording.

The heart of the book is the idea of the web as conversation. Writers should predict the main questions their users have and structure content as answers to those questions. That does not mean turning every page into a list of frequently asked questions. It means keeping the reader's question in mind throughout and putting the most important answer first, in an inverted pyramid style. It also means naming the reader's real problem rather than describing the organization's internal structure.

The middle chapters turn to the building blocks of a page. These include clear headlines, useful headings that may be phrased as questions, short sentences and paragraphs, lists and tables, meaningful link text and illustrations that earn their place. Redish shows many before-and-after examples. Short interludes address special cases, including a demonstration that legal information can be written clearly. Another gives guidance on building an organization's own style guide over time rather than all at once.

Redish also explains who benefits from this approach. Reviewers note her emphasis on people who read with difficulty, people in a hurry, people for whom English is a second language and people who scan. In practice that covers almost everyone who visits a public website, and especially people under stress seeking help from a government agency. Writing for these readers is not a special accommodation; it is the baseline for content that works.

The book ends where it began, with users: test, test, test. Redish urges writers to watch real people try to use their content and to revise based on what they see, rather than relying on internal review alone. Reviewers praise the book as a useful reference and a broad introduction to usability and clear writing, while noting that experienced web writers may find some basics familiar, and that the first edition came before social media.
mainPoints: People come to a website to answer a question or finish a task, and content should be built around that purpose.
Knowing your users, their situations and their questions comes before deciding what to write.
Treating web content as a conversation means answering the reader's questions in the order they would ask them.
The most important information belongs first, with detail following for those who need it.
Headings, lists, tables and meaningful links let readers scan and find what matters to them.
Clear writing helps people who read with difficulty, people in a hurry and people reading in a second language.
Even legal and policy information can be written clearly.
Usability testing with real readers is the only reliable check on whether content works.
relevance: DSD's public web pages, provider manuals and program guidance are often written from the agency's point of view. They are organized by program name or statute rather than by the questions that families, people receiving services, case managers and providers actually bring. Redish offers a practical method for reversing that: start from the user's task, answer the question first, and test with real readers. Her section showing that legal information can be clear is useful for policy staff who believe complexity is unavoidable. The book is older, and some technical advice about devices, search and social media has dated, so teams should pair it with current state web standards and accessibility requirements. It also does not address easy read formats or translation in depth. Its central habits, however, remain sound and fit well with person-centered practice.
questions: If a parent or a person receiving services came to our web page with one question, what would it be? How many clicks or paragraphs would it take them to find the answer?
Which of our pages are organized around how the agency is structured rather than around what readers need to do?
Who could we watch use our content this quarter, and what would we change based on what we learn?

title: Found in Translation: How Language Shapes Our Lives and Transforms the World
overview: Found in Translation is a lively, story-driven tour of the places where translation and interpreting quietly shape everyday life. It moves from hospitals and courtrooms to business, religion, entertainment and technology. Nataly Kelly has worked in language services since the 1990s as a certified court interpreter and freelance translator. She studied Spanish sociolinguistics as a Fulbright scholar and wrote an earlier book on telephone interpreting. Jost Zetzsche is a translator and writer on translation technology. Linguist David Crystal wrote the foreword. The book is aimed at general readers who may never have thought about the work interpreters and translators do.
summary: The authors open by arguing that translation is everywhere and mostly invisible. It moves goods across borders, carries news, supports diplomacy and, in their account, can prevent conflict and stop the spread of disease. They describe it as one of the oldest professions and a very large global industry. They draw on surveys of working translators, who describe their work as challenging, rewarding and too often unappreciated. The book has seven chapters, and each is a collection of real cases and short sidebars rather than a single argument.

The first chapter is the one most relevant to public service. It shows how interpreting and translation save lives and protect rights for patients, for people on trial and for people facing danger. It also tells the story of a Native American language, Wampanoag, being brought back into use. The second chapter turns to war and peace. One story follows an interpreter at the Nuremberg trials who rendered the words of the men responsible for murdering his family. Another describes the danger faced by Iraqi and Afghan interpreters who worked alongside American forces.

Later chapters widen the view. The authors show how companies lose money and trust when messages are mistranslated. They note that literary translators are among the lowest-paid members of the profession, even though they do some of its hardest work. They also show how translating sacred texts has shaped faith and language for centuries. Lighter chapters cover food, beauty products, film, sports and the large interpreting teams behind events such as the Olympic Games. The authors report that thousands of companies around the world sell translation and interpreting services, and that most internet users prefer to browse in their own language.

The last chapter looks at translation in a connected world. It covers social networks, multilingual online reference works, software in many languages and computer translation. The authors conclude that technology will change the work but not replace skilled human translators, especially where meaning, culture and stakes are high. Throughout, Kelly stresses the professional ethic of interpreters, who must stay neutral and faithful to the speaker even when the content is painful.

Reviewers differ on the result. Some praise the book as a fascinating, accessible case for the importance of language work. Others find it mostly a collection of stories without a unifying argument. For a public-sector reader, that structure is both a strength and a limit. The stories make the stakes vivid. But readers looking for standards, law or practical guidance on running a language access program will need other sources.
mainPoints: Interpreting and translation are essential, skilled work that is easy to overlook until it fails.
In health care and the courts, accurate interpreting protects safety and legal rights.
Professional interpreters are bound by ethics of accuracy, completeness and neutrality.
Interpreters can carry heavy emotional loads and sometimes face real danger because of their work.
Mistranslation has real costs, from lost trust to lost money and harm.
Language work includes reviving and sustaining endangered languages, not only moving between major ones.
Technology can support translation, but human judgment remains central when meaning and stakes are high.
relevance: This is a good starting book for DSD staff who have not worked closely with interpreters or translators. It helps teams see interpreting as professional work with its own ethics, rather than a quick add-on. That view supports better planning for assessments, person-centered planning meetings, appeals and public engagement. The stories about interpreters' emotional load can prompt teams to schedule briefings and breaks for interpreters during hard conversations. Its limits are clear. It is a general-audience book from 2012, and it does not explain federal or Minnesota language access duties. It gives little attention to sign language interpreting or Deaf communities, and reviewers fairly note that it relies on stories. Pair it with DHS language access policy, with guidance from the Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing, and with interpreters themselves.
questions: When we schedule interpreters for assessments or planning meetings, do we treat them as professionals with preparation needs, or as a last-minute logistics item?
Which of our documents would cause real harm if mistranslated, and how do we check the quality of those translations?
How do we support interpreters who carry emotionally difficult conversations on our behalf?

title: Translating Childhoods: Immigrant Youth, Language, and Culture
editionNote: First published 2009 · Rutgers University Press · 183 pages
overview: Translating Childhoods is an ethnographic study of the work immigrant children do as language and culture brokers for their families. Marjorie Faulstich Orellana is a professor of education at the University of California, Los Angeles. She followed children in Los Angeles, Chicago and a mostly white, middle-class Chicago suburb she calls Engleville. She used surveys, interviews, recorded conversations and children's own journals. With them she shows what it means to be the person in the middle, carrying meaning between parents and the institutions around them. She argues that this largely unseen work is real labor that families, and public systems, depend on.
summary: Orellana opens by looking at how people frame child language brokering. To some adults it looks like an unfair burden that reverses the usual roles between parents and children. To many of the children doing it, translating fits family values of helping and contributing, and it can be a source of pride. Parents may see it as a way to keep children connected to the home language. Orellana coins the term para-phrasing. It signals both that children speak for others and that their work is valued differently from the work of trained professionals.

The chapter on home work draws on a survey of 280 fifth and sixth graders at a Chicago public school. She finds that translating in the home is like housework: essential to the household, largely unrecognized and unpaid. Oldest children, and especially girls, tend to carry the most. Children read mail ranging from advertisements to official notices such as jury summonses and credit applications. They answer the phone and door, help younger siblings with homework and explain television and radio. Most see the work as part of family interdependence.

Tension grows when translating moves into public settings such as stores, banks, clinics, schools and public offices. There children must manage not only language but also how adults treat immigrants and children. Orellana describes children buffering open or subtle racism and noticing when staff doubt a family's ability to pay. She also describes the weight they feel when interpreting where families seek public assistance or medical care. She shows the limits placed on them as well. One boy supplied all the information for his sibling's hospital visit but was not allowed to sign anything.

In parent-teacher conferences, children are at once interpreters and the subject being discussed. Orellana shows them reframing teachers' comments in terms that fit family values, while also managing how school staff see their parents. She returned to the families years later and found that translating grows as children get older and enter more adult spaces. She describes learning that flows both ways, with adults helping with words and children teaching adults. She also reports that children who translated tended to do well on academic tests.

Orellana concludes that translating both strengthens children and sharpens their awareness of being different from the dominant culture. Their work keeps schools, hospitals and stores running, and denying its value misunderstands immigrant families. A reflective appendix describes her methods and her effort to see the world through children's eyes. Reviewers praise the book's rich data and readability, which one compared to a novel. Throughout, she treats children as agents who weigh choices and negotiate between two sets of expectations, not as passive channels between adults.
mainPoints: Children of immigrants often serve as interpreters and cultural brokers for their families, at home and in public.
This work is real labor, largely unseen and unpaid, and it often falls on the oldest children and on girls.
Many children take pride in translating as part of family values of helping and interdependence.
Translating in public institutions exposes children to stress, adult judgment and sometimes racism.
Institutions often depend on children's language work while denying them standing or authority.
Children translating in meetings about themselves are placed in a difficult and conflicted role.
Translating can build skill and confidence, and it can also sharpen children's sense of being outsiders.
Public systems shape whether this work is a burden or a strength through how they provide professional language help.
relevance: This book helps DSD staff understand why relying on children, siblings or other family members to interpret is a serious concern. That holds even when the family offers and the child is capable. Assessments, person-centered planning, eligibility decisions and talks about a family member's disability or health are exactly the high-stakes, emotionally loaded settings Orellana describes. They can place a young person in the role of both interpreter and family member. The book supports offering qualified interpreters every time and explaining that offer respectfully. It also reminds teams to honor the skill and pride many young brokers have, rather than treating families as lacking. Limits: the research focuses mainly on Mexican and Central American families in Los Angeles and Chicago. It is about children rather than adults with disabilities, and it predates current remote interpreting practice.
questions: When a family member offers to interpret during an assessment or planning meeting, how do we respond? How do we explain the offer of a qualified interpreter?
Where might young people in the families we serve be reading our notices for their parents, and what does that tell us about how we write and translate them?
How can we recognize the skill of family members who broker language while still protecting everyone's right to professional interpreting?

title: Games without Rules: The Often-Interrupted History of Afghanistan
overview: Games without Rules is a readable history of the last two centuries of Afghanistan by Tamim Ansary, an Afghan American writer born in Kabul to an Afghan father and an American mother. Ansary spent part of his childhood in Lashkar Gah and moved to the United States as a teenager. He studied for a time at Carleton College in Minnesota and later directed the San Francisco Writers Workshop. He is also the author of a memoir, West of Kabul, East of New York. Here he tells Afghanistan's story as its own, a story that outside powers have repeatedly interrupted.
summary: Ansary takes his title from buzkashi, a traditional mounted game in which riders compete to carry a goat carcass to a goal. As first played, it had no lines, no referees and no fixed teams; it ran on tradition, context and shared understanding. Ansary uses it to describe Afghan political life before the modern state. Back then, each town and village had its own sphere of influence, often with a headman and a local mullah, and was governed by customs and values rather than written rules.

The first major interruption came from the competition between the British and Russian empires in the nineteenth century. The British invaded in 1838 and again in 1878, and they could take the country but not hold it. Ansary argues that Afghans came together against outsiders in wartime, then split apart again under occupation, which made the country very hard to govern. He describes British officers who lived apart from Afghans, brought their own way of life, and understood little of the society around them.

Between foreign interventions, a second Afghanistan took shape. A series of modernizing rulers built a layer of government, officials and institutions on top of village and tribal life. This second Afghanistan, centered in Kabul, was elite, urban and drawn to Western ideas. During the Cold War, Afghan leaders attracted development money from both the United States and the Soviet Union. Ansary remembers the American-funded irrigation project where his father worked, and the peaceful mood of that era.

Ansary reads the Soviet war that began in 1979 as both a Cold War conflict and a struggle between the two Afghanistans. On one side was the modernizing Kabul elite allied with the Soviets; on the other were the villages and tribes that formed the resistance. He sees Soviet bombing campaigns that emptied the countryside as a turning point that tore apart Afghan society and released long-buried conflicts. The later civil war, the rise of the Taliban and the American intervention after 2001 follow from that break.

The book ends around 2012, during the American-led war. Ansary argues that Afghan leaders, including Hamid Karzai, faced the same trap that undid most rulers before them. Depending on foreign support angered people at home, while concessions at home angered foreign backers. He closes on a cautiously hopeful note, describing rural homes with solar panels and satellite dishes, and a society changing in ways no one fully controls. Reviewers call it accessible and illuminating, and Kirkus describes it as a breezy overview.
mainPoints: Afghanistan has its own long political story, which outside powers have repeatedly interrupted without understanding it.
Local, informal authority in villages and tribes has long existed alongside, and often competed with, a central government in Kabul.
Afghans have often united against foreign invaders and then divided again in peacetime.
Modernizing elites in Kabul built a state and institutions that many rural communities experienced as distant.
The Soviet war, and the destruction of rural life it brought, was a turning point for Afghan society.
Afghan rulers have faced a recurring trap between foreign backers and their own people.
Understanding history from an Afghan point of view helps outsiders avoid repeating past mistakes.
relevance: Many Afghan Minnesotans arrived after the 2021 evacuation, joining earlier Afghan families who came over several decades. This book gives DSD staff a clear, Afghan-authored background on that history. It helps explain why trust in central authority, family and local networks, and the experience of repeated war may shape how families approach government services. It can help staff ask better questions about where a family is from, which languages they speak, such as Dari or Pashto, and who they want involved in decisions. Its limits matter. It ends in 2012, before the Taliban's return and the large recent resettlement. It is a political history rather than a study of disability, health or life in the United States. Ansary is one voice, and Afghan communities hold many views about this history.
questions: How might a long history of distant central government and foreign intervention shape how some Afghan families view a state agency? How can we earn trust rather than assume it?
Do we know which languages and regions the Afghan families we serve come from, and do our interpreter plans reflect that?
Which Afghan-led organizations in Minnesota could help us understand recent arrivals' needs in their own terms?

title: The Story of My Life: An Afghan Girl on the Other Side of the Sky
editionNote: First published 2005 · Simon Spotlight Entertainment · 256 pages
overview: The Story of My Life is a memoir by Farah Ahmedi, written with Tamim Ansary. It tells of growing up in Kabul during war, losing a leg to a land mine as a young child, and resettling in the Chicago area as a refugee with her mother. Ahmedi's story won a national story contest run by ABC's Good Morning America, which led to the book. It was later reissued as The Other Side of the Sky. Told in a young person's voice, it brings together war, refugee life, disability, faith and the work of starting over in the United States.
summary: Ahmedi was born in Kabul near the height of the war between the Soviet-backed government and the mujahideen. Gunfire and planes were ordinary background sounds of her early childhood, and classrooms had few books and more students than seats. When she was in second grade, she took a shortcut across a field on her way to school and stepped on a land mine, and the injury led to the loss of her leg and changed the direction of her life.

She was flown to Germany for treatment with a group of other injured Afghan children, without her family, and spent close to two years there recovering and receiving care. When she returned to Kabul, she struggled to readjust and had to relearn parts of her own language. Soon after, a rocket struck her family's home while she and her mother were at the market, killing her father and two sisters, and the family lost nearly everything.

Her brothers left the country to avoid being drafted and were never heard from again. Under Taliban rule, Ahmedi and her mother, who had serious asthma, had no male relative to go out with them in public, and they rarely felt safe leaving home. They fled to Pakistan and lived for a time in hard conditions in refugee camps. Their application for resettlement was accepted, and World Relief brought them to the Chicago area, where they arrived after September 11, 2001.

The American chapters describe the shock of a new language, a fast pace of life, unfamiliar systems and a winter climate. At first her mother feared what would happen to them when they arrived. Ahmedi entered high school with only a second-grade education from Afghanistan and worked to catch up, while the family adjusted step by step, with real help from new friends, including a woman named Alyce Litz. Ahmedi again and again credits strangers whose kindness came at moments when her life could have ended.

Throughout the memoir, Ahmedi reflects on loss and on what she gained from it, speaking of hope and faith rather than bitterness. A scholarly review in Disability Studies Quarterly praised the way the book weaves together cross-cultural views of women, disability and religion. Because the book was written for a broad audience, including younger readers, it is accessible and direct. It gives fewer details about systems and services than an adult policy reader might want, though.
mainPoints: War-related disability, such as limb loss from land mines, is part of many Afghan families' experience.
Children injured in war may receive care far from their families, adding separation to injury.
Loss of family members, home and country often comes before resettlement, not only during it.
Women without male relatives faced serious limits on movement and safety under Taliban rule.
Resettlement agencies, schools and individual neighbors all shaped this family's first years in the United States.
Newcomers may enter school or services with major gaps in formal education that say nothing about their ability.
Faith, hope and relationships can be sources of strength in rebuilding a life with a disability.
relevance: For DSD staff, this memoir offers a rare Afghan voice that connects refugee experience directly with disability. It can help teams think about families who arrive with war-related injuries, limited formal schooling, grief and caregiving duties for other relatives. It also shows the difference that steady, respectful helpers can make in the first years. It invites questions about prosthetic and mobility needs, about the health of family caregivers, and about how gender and household roles may shape who attends appointments. Limits are important. It is one young woman's story from the early 2000s, written for a general and younger audience. It describes Chicago rather than Minnesota, and resettlement before the 2021 evacuation. It should not be used to assume anything about any Afghan family; use it to ask better questions.
questions: When a newly arrived family comes to us, how do we learn about disability or injuries related to war respectfully and only as needed?
Who are the steady helpers in a newly arrived family's life, and how can our services work alongside them?
How might gender, household roles or a caregiver's own health affect who can attend meetings and how we schedule them?

title: Freedom in Exile: The Autobiography of the Dalai Lama
overview: Freedom in Exile is the second autobiography of the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso. He is the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhists and was for decades the political leader of Tibetans in exile. He prepared the book with the British journalist Alexander Norman from many hours of recorded conversation. It appeared around the time he received the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize. He says he wrote it to answer what he saw as misinformation about Tibet's history. The title refers to the freedoms he found in India, where he and many Tibetan refugees have lived since 1959.
summary: The book begins with his birth in 1935 to a farming family in a small village in Amdo, in northeastern Tibet. At about age two, he was recognized as the reincarnation of the Thirteenth Dalai Lama. He describes being brought to Lhasa as a young child and starting a demanding monastic education in logic, philosophy and other subjects. He also offers a personal picture of daily life in the Tibet of his youth, which he remembers with clear affection.

The central part of the book traces Tibet's relationship with the People's Republic of China. After Chinese troops entered Tibet in 1950, he was asked to take on full political authority while still a teenager. He recounts years of trying to reach a peaceful arrangement, including a visit to Beijing in 1954 to meet Mao Zedong and other leaders. Tension kept rising until the uprising in Lhasa in March 1959. After the uprising was put down, he escaped to India.

The later chapters cover his life in exile and his care for the many Tibetan refugees who followed him. He describes the work of resettling people in India, building a government in exile based in Dharamsala and appealing to the United Nations. He discusses early steps toward democratic government for Tibetans in exile, including a draft constitution in 1963. He also describes his efforts to keep Tibetan religion, language and culture alive outside Tibet.

He also takes on disputed history directly. For example, he writes about the American intelligence agencies that supported Tibetan resistance in the 1950s and 1960s.
